statement: Premature abstraction is as harmful as premature optimization; do not make every script rely on special methods and metaprogramming.
Prefer using ready-made standard-library collections and tools before building your own equivalents, to avoid reinventing the wheel.
Become comfortable using an existing abstract base class before creating your own, because in practice you inherit from existing ABCs far more often than you define new ones.

Implementing special (dunder) methods is the mechanism that lets user-defined objects support and interact with idiomatic language constructs such as collections, iteration, operator overloading, attribute access, and managed contexts.
Special methods are meant to be invoked by the Python interpreter, not called directly by user code; write len(x) rather than x.__len__().
The only special method that user code commonly calls directly is __init__, to invoke a superclass initializer from a subclass __init__.
condition: invoking a superclass initializer

statement: When you must trigger a special method, prefer the related built-in (len, iter, str) rather than calling the dunder directly, because the built-ins also provide other services and are faster for built-in types.
Implementing just __len__ and __getitem__ makes a class behave like a standard Python sequence, gaining iteration, slicing, the in operator, reversed, sorted, and random.choice support.
Implement special methods by delegating to a wrapped built-in object via composition (for example __len__ and __getitem__ delegating to an internal list) instead of reimplementing the behaviour.
Use collections.namedtuple to build classes that are just bundles of attributes with no custom methods, such as a database record.
condition: the class is only a bundle of attributes with no custom behaviour

statement: If a collection implements no __contains__ method, the in operator falls back to a sequential scan, which works as long as the object is iterable.
condition: the collection has no __contains__ method

statement: For built-in types, len(x) reads the ob_size field directly from a C struct rather than calling a method, which is faster than a method call.
condition: x is an instance of a built-in type implemented in C

statement: __repr__ is called by the repr built-in for inspection, and its returned string should be unambiguous and, where possible, match the source code needed to recreate the object.
If you implement only one of __repr__ and __str__, choose __repr__, because the object base class provides a __str__ that falls back to calling __repr__.
condition: only one of the two methods will be implemented

statement: __str__ is called by the str built-in and implicitly by print, and should return a string suitable for display to end users.
Use the !r conversion (or %r) inside __repr__ to render the standard representation of attributes, because it reveals type differences such as Vector(1, 2) versus Vector('1', '2').
User-defined instances are truthy by default unless __bool__ or __len__ is implemented; bool(x) calls __bool__, and if absent uses __len__, treating a length of zero as False.
__bool__ must return an actual Boolean, so wrap the result in bool() when the expression (such as x or y) could return a non-Boolean operand.
condition: implementing __bool__

statement: Infix operator special methods such as __add__ and __mul__ should create and return a new object and must not mutate either operand.
Python does not require a concrete class to inherit from collections.abc ABCs; any class that implements __len__ already satisfies the Sized interface (structural typing).
Since Python 3.7 dict is officially ordered, but that guarantee only preserves key insertion order and does not let you rearrange keys arbitrarily.
A Python object should provide two usable string representations: __repr__ for debugging and logging, and __str__ for presentation to end users.

Container sequences (list, tuple, collections.deque) hold references to objects of any type, while flat sequences (str, bytes, array.array) store primitive values in their own contiguous memory, making them more compact but limited to primitive machine values.
An array.array of floats is far more compact in memory than a tuple of floats because the array stores raw machine values in a single object while the tuple holds a separate float object per item.
condition: storing many primitive numeric values

statement: Built-in concrete sequence types do not actually subclass the Sequence and MutableSequence ABCs; they are registered as virtual subclasses, so issubclass(tuple, abc.Sequence) returns True.
Use a list comprehension when the target is a list, and a generator expression to feed other sequence types.
A list comprehension is more readable than an equivalent build-up for loop because its single goal is always to build a new list, making intent explicit.
Do not use a list comprehension purely for its side effects; if you are not using the list it produces, use a plain for loop instead.
Keep list comprehensions short; if one spans more than two lines, it is probably best to break it apart or rewrite it as a plain for loop.
List, set, and dict comprehensions and generator expressions have their own local scope for variables assigned in the for clause, so those variables do not leak to the surrounding scope.
exception: a target assigned with the walrus operator := remains accessible in the enclosing scope

statement: List comprehensions do everything map and filter do without resorting to lambda, and are not necessarily slower than the map/filter equivalent.

In a multiline literal inside [], {}, or (), add a trailing comma after the last item to make future edits easier and reduce diff noise; line breaks inside these delimiter pairs need no backslash continuation.
A generator expression saves memory compared with a list comprehension by yielding items one at a time via the iterator protocol instead of building a whole list just to feed another constructor.
When a generator expression is the single argument to a function call, the enclosing parentheses of the call double as the genexp parentheses and need not be duplicated.
condition: the genexp is the sole argument of the call

statement: Tuples do double duty: they serve as immutable lists and also as records with unnamed fields.
When a tuple is used as a record, the position of each item carries its meaning, so the field count is fixed, order matters, and sorting such a tuple would destroy the information.
condition: the tuple is used as a record of fields

statement: Prefer tuple unpacking over index access to read a record's fields, which often removes the need to create a class just to name those fields.
Use tuples as immutable lists as the interpreter and standard library do, because a tuple signals that its length will never change.
Use _ as the conventional dummy variable for unpacked items you do not need.
exception: inside a match/case statement _ is a wildcard that matches any value without binding it

statement: A tuple uses less memory than a list of the same length and lets the interpreter perform some optimizations.
A tuple's immutability applies only to the references it holds (which cannot be deleted or replaced); if a referenced object is mutable and is changed, the tuple's value effectively changes.
Tuples containing mutable items can be a source of bugs and are unhashable, so they cannot be used as dict keys or set elements; an object is hashable only if its value can never change.
condition: the tuple holds a mutable item

statement: To check explicitly whether an object has a fixed value, call hash(o) and treat a raised TypeError as evidence that the object is not fixed.

Tuples are more efficient than lists because a tuple literal compiles to a single constant, tuple(t) returns the same object without copying, a tuple is allocated exactly the memory it needs, and its item references are stored inline in the tuple struct rather than through an extra indirection.
Prefer unpacking over index access to extract elements from sequences, because it avoids error-prone indexing and works with any iterable, including iterators that do not support [] notation.
Use parallel assignment (b, a = a, b) to swap the values of variables without a temporary variable.
Prefix an argument with * in a function call to unpack an iterable into separate positional arguments.
In parallel assignment, prefix one target variable with * to collect the excess items into a list; the starred target may appear in any position but only once.
exception: the * prefix may apply to at most one variable per assignment

statement: Since PEP 448, * can appear multiple times in a function call and can be used inside list, tuple, and set literals, with ** providing the equivalent for mappings.
Nested unpacking works when the target's nesting structure (for example (a, b, (c, d))) matches the value's structure.
A single-item tuple must be written with a trailing comma (for example (record,)); omitting it produces a silent bug.
match/case improves on the C switch statement chiefly through destructuring, a more advanced form of unpacking, and avoids switch's fallthrough and dangling-else problems.
A sequence pattern matches a subject only when the subject is a sequence, has the same number of items as the pattern, and each corresponding item (including nested items) matches.
In a sequence pattern, square brackets and parentheses are interchangeable and carry the same meaning.

A sequence pattern matches most actual or virtual subclasses of collections.abc.Sequence, but str, bytes, and bytearray are treated as atomic values, not sequences; convert them (for example tuple(phone)) to match their contents.
exception: str, bytes, and bytearray subjects are atomic in match/case and must be converted to match as sequences

statement: Unlike unpacking, pattern matching does not destructure iterables that are not sequences, such as iterators.
In a pattern, _ matches any single item in its position without binding to it, and is the only variable allowed to appear more than once in a pattern.
Bind any part of a pattern to a variable using the as keyword (for example (lat, lon) as coord).

Constructor-like syntax inside a pattern (for example str(name) or float(lat)) performs a runtime type check on that position rather than a type conversion, and still binds the matched value to the variable.
Use *_ in a pattern to match any number of items without binding them; use *extra instead to bind those items as a list of zero or more.
A case clause may carry an optional guard introduced by if, which is evaluated only after the pattern matches and may reference variables bound by the pattern.
Provide a catch-all case _ in a match statement, because without one a subject that matches no pattern makes the match do nothing, which can be a silent failure.
Pattern matching is a form of declarative programming: the code describes what to match rather than how to match it, so the shape of the code follows the shape of the data.

Slices and ranges exclude the last item, which fits zero-based indexing: with only a stop the length equals the stop, with start and stop the length is stop minus start, and seq[:x] plus seq[x:] splits a sequence with no overlap.
The slice notation s[a:b:c] specifies a stride or step c, and a negative step returns items in reverse order.
The a:b:c notation is valid only as a subscript inside [] and produces a slice(a, b, c) object, so evaluating seq[start:stop:step] calls seq.__getitem__(slice(start, stop, step)).
Assign names to slice objects (for example SKU = slice(0, 6)) instead of hardcoding slice literals throughout the code, which makes parsing fixed-width data far more readable.

The [] operator can take multiple comma-separated indices or slices, which __getitem__ and __setitem__ receive as a tuple (so a[i, j] calls a.__getitem__((i, j))); all built-in sequence types except memoryview are one-dimensional.

A slice on the left side of an assignment (or as the target of del) grafts, excises, or otherwise modifies a mutable sequence in place; the right side of a slice assignment must be an iterable even when it has a single item.
The + and * operators on sequences always create a new object and never modify their operands, and usually both operands of + must be of the same sequence type.
Beware of a * n when a is a sequence containing mutable items: for example [[]] * 3 creates a list with three references to the same inner list rather than three independent lists.
condition: the repeated sequence contains mutable items

statement: Build a list of independent nested lists with a list comprehension such as [['_'] * 3 for _ in range(3)], not with [['_'] * 3] * 3, which produces aliases referring to the same inner list.

+= is implemented by __iadd__ for in-place addition; if __iadd__ is absent Python falls back to __add__, so a += b behaves like a = a + b and rebinds a to a new object. For mutable sequences += is usually in place; for immutable sequences it cannot be.
Repeated concatenation of immutable sequences with += is inefficient because the interpreter copies the whole target sequence each time instead of appending in place.
exception: CPython optimizes str += in loops by over-allocating, so it avoids copying the whole string each time

statement: Avoid putting mutable items inside tuples.

Augmented assignment is not an atomic operation: it can raise an exception after already performing part of its work, as when s[a] += b mutates a referenced mutable item and then fails on the item-assignment back into an immutable container.

A function or method that changes an object in place should return None to signal that the receiver was mutated and no new object was created, as list.sort and random.shuffle do; the trade-off is that such methods cannot be cascaded in a fluent-interface style.
list.sort sorts a list in place and returns None, whereas the sorted built-in accepts any iterable and always returns a newly created list.

Both list.sort and sorted accept keyword-only arguments key and reverse, where key is a one-argument function applied to each item to produce its sort key (for example key=str.lower for case-insensitive sorting or key=len to sort by length).
Python's sort is stable: it preserves the relative ordering of items that compare equal.
The key keyword argument also works with the min and max built-ins and with standard-library functions such as itertools.groupby and heapq.nlargest.

By default Python sorts strings lexicographically by character code, so ASCII uppercase letters sort before lowercase ones and non-ASCII characters are unlikely to be ordered sensibly; sort human-readable text with locale- or Unicode-aware techniques instead.
Search a sorted sequence efficiently with the bisect module's binary search, and use bisect.insort to insert items while keeping the sequence sorted.
condition: the sequence is kept sorted

statement: Do not overuse list: prefer array.array for millions of floating-point values to save memory, collections.deque when frequently adding and removing items at both ends, and set when frequently testing membership in a large collection.

If a list holds only numbers, array.array is a more memory-efficient replacement that supports all mutable-sequence operations plus fast binary load/save methods such as frombytes, tofile, and fromfile.
condition: the sequence contains only numbers of a single machine type

statement: When creating an array.array you must supply a typecode that fixes the underlying C type of each item, and Python rejects any value that does not match that type.

Saving and loading numeric data with array.tofile and array.fromfile is far faster and far more compact than writing and reading one number per line in a text file, which also requires parsing each line.
As of Python 3.10 array.array has no in-place sort method, so sort one by rebuilding it as array(a.typecode, sorted(a)), and keep a sorted array sorted while inserting with bisect.insort.
memoryview is a shared-memory sequence type that lets you handle slices of array-like data without copying bytes, which is important for large datasets.
memoryview.cast reinterprets how the underlying bytes are grouped into units without moving any bits, returning another memoryview that shares the same memory.
Because a memoryview shares memory with its source, writing through a cast view mutates the underlying object's bytes and can corrupt its values if used carelessly.
For advanced numeric and matrix processing on large datasets, use NumPy and SciPy, which implement homogeneous multidimensional arrays and efficient element-wise operations backed by C and Fortran.
condition: the work involves heavy numeric processing on large data

statement: Vectorized NumPy operations apply a function to all elements of an array without an explicit Python loop and can run in parallel using vector instructions or multiple cores, yielding large speedups over equivalent pure-Python loops.
A list can serve as a stack or queue via append and pop, but inserting or removing at the head (index 0) is costly because the entire list must be shifted in memory.

collections.deque is a thread-safe double-ended queue optimized for fast appends and pops at both ends; it can be bounded with maxlen, in which case adding to a full deque discards an item from the opposite end.
Removing items from the middle of a deque is not fast, because a deque is optimized for appending and popping at its ends.
The deque append and popleft operations are atomic, so a deque can be used as a FIFO queue across threads without explicit locks.

The queue module's synchronized classes (SimpleQueue, Queue, LifoQueue, PriorityQueue) block on insertion when bounded and full rather than discarding items as a bounded deque does, which is useful for throttling producer threads.
The heapq module provides heappush and heappop functions that let you use an ordinary mutable sequence as a heap or priority queue.

Mixed-type lists are rarely useful in practice, because the items in a list are usually processed together and so should share at least some common operation; for example, you cannot sort a Python 3 list unless its items are mutually comparable.

The key argument of sort, sorted, max, and min is both simpler and more efficient than a two-argument comparison function, because key is invoked only once per item whereas a comparator is called for every comparison.
The dict type is a fundamental part of Python's implementation (backing class and instance attributes, module namespaces, and keyword arguments) and is highly optimized using hash tables.

Python's set and frozenset are hash-table types that implement the full set-theory operations (union, intersection, subset tests), letting algorithms be expressed declaratively and avoiding many nested loops and conditionals.
A dict comprehension (dictcomp) builds a dict by producing key:value pairs from any iterable.

Since PEP 448, ** can be applied to more than one argument in a function call (when the keys are all unique strings) and can appear multiple times inside a dict literal, where later duplicate keys overwrite earlier ones.
Since Python 3.9 the | operator creates a new merged mapping while |= updates a mapping in place, mirroring the set union operators.
match/case supports mapping subjects: a mapping pattern looks like a dict literal and matches any actual or virtual subclass of collections.abc.Mapping.

Unlike sequence patterns, mapping patterns succeed on partial matches, so extra keys present in the subject do not prevent a match; capture the remaining pairs by prefixing one variable with **, which must be last, while **_ is forbidden as redundant.

Pattern matching against a mapping uses d.get(key, sentinel) and so never triggers automatic creation of missing keys; a mapping pattern matches only if the subject already contains the required keys.

When handling semi-structured records such as JSON, include a field naming the record type, include a field identifying the schema version to allow API evolution, and provide case clauses for invalid records of a given type plus a catch-all.
Prefer isinstance(arg, abc.Mapping) over checking for the concrete dict type, so that alternative mapping implementations are also accepted.
To implement a custom mapping, extend collections.UserDict or wrap a dict by composition rather than subclassing the Mapping or MutableMapping ABCs directly.
Mapping types built on a dict (including UserDict) require their keys to be hashable; only the keys must be hashable, not the values.
An object is hashable if it has a hash code that never changes during its lifetime (a __hash__ method) and can be compared via __eq__; objects that compare equal must have the same hash code.

Numeric types, str, and bytes are hashable; a container type is hashable only if it is immutable and every object it contains is also hashable, so a tuple is hashable only when all its items are hashable and a frozenset is always hashable.
An object's hash code is guaranteed constant only within a single Python process, because it can vary with the Python version, machine architecture, and a security salt.

User-defined types are hashable by default (their hash code is their id and inherited __eq__ compares ids); if you implement a custom __eq__ based on internal state, the type is hashable only when __eq__ and __hash__ rely solely on instance attributes that never change during the object's life.
condition: a custom __eq__ is implemented based on object state

statement: d.update(m) uses duck typing: if m has a keys method it is treated as a mapping, otherwise update iterates m as (key, value) pairs; most mapping constructors reuse this logic, so they can be initialized from another mapping or any iterable of pairs.

Use d.setdefault(key, default) to fetch and update a mutable value in a single key lookup (for example index.setdefault(word, []).append(location)), instead of d.get(...) followed by reassignment, which performs two or three lookups.
In line with Python's fail-fast philosophy, d[k] raises KeyError when k is missing; use d.get(k, default) when a default value is more convenient than handling KeyError.
There are two main ways to make a mapping supply values for missing keys: use a collections.defaultdict, or subclass dict (or another mapping) and add a __missing__ method.

A defaultdict creates a default value on demand for a missing key accessed via d[k], by calling the default_factory callable supplied at construction (for example defaultdict(list) produces an empty list).
A defaultdict's default_factory is invoked only by __getitem__ (d[k]); for a missing key, d.get(k) still returns None and k in d is still False.

The standard dict.__getitem__ calls __missing__ when a key is not found instead of raising KeyError, provided a dict subclass defines __missing__; the method is not defined on base dict but dict is aware of it.
In a __missing__ that converts a key before re-looking it up, guard the conversion (for example with isinstance(key, str)) to avoid infinite recursion when the converted key is itself missing.
condition: the __missing__ implementation re-looks up a transformed key

statement: On a plain dict subclass, __missing__ is consulted only by __getitem__ (d[k]); k in d and d.get do not fall back to it, so override __contains__ and get as well if consistent missing-key behaviour is required.
k in my_dict is faster than k in my_dict.keys() because it avoids the attribute lookup for the keys method, although both are efficient since keys() returns a set-like view.

The use of __missing__ differs across standard-library base mappings: a dict subclass triggers it only on d[k], a UserDict subclass triggers it on both d[k] and d.get(k), and an abc.Mapping subclass triggers it only if its own __getitem__ calls it, so subclass carefully.

Since dict preserves key insertion order from Python 3.6/3.7, the main reason to use OrderedDict is backward compatibility; the remaining differences are that OrderedDict equality is order-sensitive, it offers move_to_end, and it is optimized for frequent reordering, making it suitable for an LRU cache.

A collections.ChainMap holds references (not copies) to a list of mappings searched in order, succeeding at the first mapping that contains the key; updates and insertions affect only the first mapping.
A collections.Counter maps each key to an integer count (updates add to the count), supports the + and - operators to combine tallies and a most_common([n]) method, and can be used as a multiset.

shelve.Shelf provides persistent storage mapping string keys to pickle-serialized Python objects: keys must be strings, values must be picklable, it subclasses MutableMapping, and it is a context manager.
Prefer subclassing collections.UserDict over dict to create a custom mapping, because dict's built-in implementation shortcuts otherwise force you to override methods you could simply inherit.
UserDict does not inherit from dict; it composes an internal dict in a data attribute, which avoids unwanted recursion when overriding special methods such as __setitem__ and simplifies __contains__.

There is no real immutable mapping in the standard library, but types.MappingProxyType wraps a mapping to return a read-only, dynamic mappingproxy: changes to the source mapping are visible through the proxy, but the mapping cannot be mutated through it.

The dict views returned by keys(), values(), and items() are read-only, dynamic projections of the dict's internal data that avoid copying; they are iterable and support len and reversed but are not subscriptable, and dict_keys and dict_items additionally support set operations.

Key consequences of dict's hash-table implementation: keys must be hashable with proper __hash__ and __eq__, key access is very fast (hash code mapped to a table index), key insertion order is preserved since Python 3.7, and a dict carries significant memory overhead because the hash table keeps at least one-third of its rows empty to stay efficient.

To save memory, avoid creating instance attributes outside __init__, because adding an attribute after __init__ returns forces Python to give that instance its own __dict__ hash table instead of using the class-shared key-sharing layout (which PEP 412 reports saves 10-20% memory).
A set is a collection of unique objects, so a basic use case is removing duplicates by passing an iterable to set().
To remove duplicates while preserving the order of first occurrence, use dict.fromkeys(iterable).keys() instead of a set, which does not preserve order.
condition: order of first occurrence must be preserved

statement: Set elements must be hashable; the set type itself is not hashable (so you cannot nest a set inside a set), but frozenset is hashable and can be an element of a set.

The set types provide infix operators for set theory (a | b union, a & b intersection, a - b difference, a ^ b symmetric difference), and using them can reduce line count and execution time while making code easier to read by removing loops and conditionals.
Create an empty set with the constructor set(), because the literal {} creates an empty dict, not an empty set.

A set literal such as {1, 2, 3} is faster and more readable than calling set([1, 2, 3]), which must look up the set name, build a list, then call the constructor; frozenset has no literal syntax and must be built with its constructor.

Because set and frozenset are hash tables: elements must be hashable, membership testing is very fast, sets carry significant memory overhead, element ordering depends unreliably on insertion order, and adding elements can reorder existing ones when the table is resized past about two-thirds full.

Set infix operators require both operands to be sets, but the equivalent named methods (union, intersection, difference, and so on) accept any iterable arguments; since Python 3.5 you can also union iterables into a new set with {*a, *b, *c}.

The dict_keys and dict_items views support the set operators &, |, -, and ^ and are compatible with set instances, so you can compare dictionary contents without explicit loops; the result of such an operation is a set.

A dict_keys view can always be used as a set because keys are hashable, but a dict_items view works as a set only when all the dict's values are hashable; otherwise a set operation on it raises TypeError.
Python 3 draws a sharp distinction between str (a sequence of human-text Unicode characters) and bytes (raw machine bytes), and performs no implicit conversion between the two.
The items of a Python 3 str are Unicode characters, and a character's identity is its code point, a number from 0 to 1,114,111 written as U+ followed by four to six hex digits.
The actual bytes representing a character depend on the encoding in use: encoding converts code points to bytes and decoding converts bytes back to code points.
Decode bytes to str to obtain human-readable text, and encode str to bytes for storage or transmission.

Python has two binary sequence types: the immutable bytes and the mutable bytearray; each item is an integer from 0 to 255, but a slice of either (even of length 1) yields a binary sequence of the same type.

For binary sequences my_bytes[0] returns an int while my_bytes[:1] returns a length-1 bytes; str is the exception where s[0] equals s[:1], so for all other sequence types a single item is not the same as a slice of length 1.

bytes and bytearray support most str methods except the formatting methods (format, format_map) and Unicode-dependent ones (such as casefold and isdecimal); the re module works on binary sequences when the pattern is compiled from bytes, and the % operator works on binary sequences since Python 3.5.
bytes and bytearray have a fromhex class method that builds a binary sequence by parsing pairs of hex digits optionally separated by spaces.
You can build a bytes or bytearray from a str plus an encoding keyword argument, from an iterable of integers in range 0 to 255, or from an object implementing the buffer protocol.
Building a bytes or bytearray from a buffer-like source always copies the bytes, whereas a memoryview shares memory between binary data structures without copying.

Python bundles more than 100 codecs for text-to-byte conversion, each with a name (such as utf_8) and often aliases, which you pass as the encoding argument to functions like open, str.encode, and bytes.decode.

Some encodings such as ASCII and GB2312 cannot represent every Unicode character, whereas the UTF encodings are designed to handle every code point; UTF-8 is by far the most common 8-bit encoding on the web.

Python's Unicode errors are specific: UnicodeEncodeError when converting str to bytes, UnicodeDecodeError when converting bytes to str, and SyntaxError when a module's source encoding is unexpected; identify the exact exception type before trying to fix the problem.

Encoding a character not defined in the target encoding raises UnicodeEncodeError unless an errors handler is passed: 'ignore' silently drops the character (usually a very bad idea causing silent data loss), 'replace' substitutes '?', and 'xmlcharrefreplace' substitutes a lossless XML entity.
ASCII is a common subset of all known encodings, so pure-ASCII text always encodes successfully; str.isascii() (Python 3.7+) checks whether a string is entirely ASCII.

Many legacy 8-bit codecs (such as cp1252, iso8859_1, and koi8_r) decode any byte stream without raising an error, so assuming the wrong 8-bit encoding silently produces garbled text (mojibake) instead of failing.

You cannot reliably determine a byte sequence's encoding from its content alone; you must be told, for example via HTTP or XML headers, although heuristic detectors like Chardet can guess the encoding of plain human text.
By UTF-8's design it is very unlikely for non-UTF-8 bytes containing codes above 127 to decode as UTF-8 without raising UnicodeDecodeError, so bytes that decode cleanly as UTF-8 are probably UTF-8.

UTF-16 may prepend a byte-order mark (b'\xff\xfe' on little-endian) to signal byte order; the explicit UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE variants generate no BOM, and UTF-8 needs no BOM because it is endianness-independent.

When reading UTF-8 files, the UTF-8-SIG codec is a safe choice because it reads files correctly whether or not they carry a BOM; when writing, prefer plain UTF-8 for interoperability, since a leading BOM breaks the Unix #! shebang convention.

Follow the Unicode sandwich for text I/O: decode bytes to str as early as possible on input, perform all business logic exclusively on str, and encode str to bytes as late as possible on output, never encoding or decoding in the middle of processing.
Python 3's open() in text mode decodes on read and encodes on write, so you exchange str objects with files, but relying on the default encoding will eventually cause bugs.

Code that must run on multiple machines or at different times should never depend on the default encoding; always pass an explicit encoding= argument when opening text files, because the default can vary by platform, locale, or over time.
Do not open text files in binary mode unless you must analyze raw bytes to detect the encoding (and even then prefer Chardet); use binary mode only for genuinely binary files such as images.

The most important encoding setting is locale.getpreferredencoding(), the default used to open text files and for sys.stdout/stdin/stderr when redirected to files; the documentation says it only returns a guess, so do not rely on encoding defaults.

sys.getdefaultencoding() is used internally for implicit binary-to-str conversions and is not meant to be changed, while sys.getfilesystemencoding() encodes and decodes filenames (not file contents) and applies when open() is given a str filename.

On GNU/Linux and macOS the I/O encodings default to UTF-8, but on Windows several different code-page encodings can be active in the same system, so Windows users are far more likely to hit encoding errors unless they are extra careful.

Write a Unicode character by its official name with the '\N{NAME}' escape, which is explicit and safe because Python raises SyntaxError if the name does not exist, unlike a hex code that could be silently wrong.

Unicode combining characters mean a visually identical string can be composed from different code-point sequences (canonical equivalents); the standard says applications should treat them as equal, but Python compares the raw code-point sequences and considers them not equal.

Normalize strings with unicodedata.normalize() before comparing them: NFC composes code points to the shortest equivalent form and NFD decomposes them, and both make canonical-equivalent strings compare equal.
NFC is the normalization form recommended for most applications and by the W3C, so normalize user-entered text with normalize('NFC', text) before saving it.

NFKC and NFKD (compatibility) normalization replace compatibility characters with a preferred representation and can lose or distort information (for example turning the squared sign 4-superscript-2 into 42), so apply them only for special cases like search and indexing, never for permanent text storage.

Use str.casefold() rather than str.lower() for case-insensitive comparison, because case folding applies extra transformations (for example the micro sign becomes Greek mu and the German Eszett becomes 'ss') and differs from lower() for nearly 300 code points.

Removing diacritics is not a proper form of normalization because it can change a word's meaning and cause false positives, but it is useful for search and for producing readable URLs in Latin-based languages; decide based on the target language, your users, and how the text will be used.
Python sorts strings by comparing their code points, which produces unacceptable ordering for non-ASCII text such as accented Latin words.
The standard-library way to sort non-ASCII text is to use locale.strxfrm as the sort key, after first calling locale.setlocale(LC_COLLATE, your_locale).

locale-based sorting has caveats: because the locale is global, set it once at process startup and never inside a library, the locale must be installed on the OS, and it must be correctly implemented by the OS, which makes locale.strxfrm unreliable across platforms.

The pyuca library, a pure-Python implementation of the Unicode Collation Algorithm, is a simpler locale-independent alternative for sorting Unicode text, working across Linux, macOS, and Windows via its Collator.sort_key method.

pyuca uses one collation order that does not respect per-language sorting rules, whereas PyICU honours language-specific collation (and Turkish dotted/dotless i casing) but requires compiling a native extension that can be harder to install.

The Unicode database records per-character metadata (whether a character is printable, a letter, a decimal digit, or numeric), which backs the str methods isalpha, isprintable, isdecimal, isnumeric, and casefold; unicodedata.category(char) returns a character's two-letter category.
unicodedata.name() returns a character's official Unicode name and unicodedata.numeric() returns the human numeric value of a numeric character, which is distinct from its code point number.

Regular expressions are dual-mode: a bytes pattern matches only ASCII for \d and \w, while a str pattern matches Unicode digits and letters beyond ASCII; force ASCII-only matching on a str pattern with the re.ASCII flag, and note the PyPI regex module offers better Unicode support than re.

os functions that accept filenames take str or bytes: a str argument is encoded and decoded with sys.getfilesystemencoding() (the usual Unicode-sandwich behaviour), but you can pass bytes to handle filenames that cannot be decoded, and os.fsencode/os.fsdecode help convert between the two.

Choose the human language that makes source code easiest for its intended audience to read (English for international or open-source teams), then use the characters needed for correct spelling, since Python 3 allows non-ASCII identifiers and defaults to UTF-8 source.

Since Python 3.3 (PEP 393), the interpreter stores each str with a fixed number of bytes per code point chosen as the most economical layout for that particular string (1 byte if all characters are in the latin1 range, otherwise 2 or 4 bytes), which allows efficient direct indexing.

A single high code point such as an emoji can inflate an otherwise all-ASCII string into a four-bytes-per-character array, and because Unicode characters combine, fast positional access is overrated and naive slicing of Unicode text can produce mojibake.

A hand-written plain class that only holds fields requires repetitive __init__ boilerplate (each attribute is named three times) and the __repr__ and __eq__ inherited from object are unhelpful, showing the memory address and comparing by identity rather than by value.

The three data class builders (collections.namedtuple, typing.NamedTuple, and @dataclass) automatically generate __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ and other useful methods, and none rely on inheritance: namedtuple and NamedTuple build tuple subclasses while @dataclass is a class decorator that does not change the class hierarchy.

collections.namedtuple and typing.NamedTuple produce immutable tuple-subclass instances, whereas @dataclass produces mutable instances by default; passing @dataclass(frozen=True) makes the class raise an exception on any attempt to assign to a field after initialization.
Only typing.NamedTuple and @dataclass support the regular class statement syntax, which makes it easier to add methods and docstrings to the data class.

The three builders provide parallel utilities: convert an instance to a dict with x._asdict() (named tuples) or dataclasses.asdict(x); read field names and defaults via ._fields/._field_defaults or dataclasses.fields(); make a modified copy with x._replace(**kw) or dataclasses.replace(x, **kw); and build a class at runtime with namedtuple()/NamedTuple() or dataclasses.make_dataclass().

To read a data class's field types at runtime, call typing.get_type_hints(cls) (Python 3.5-3.9) or inspect.get_annotations(cls) (Python 3.10+) rather than reading __annotations__ directly, because those functions resolve forward references in type hints.
Each instance of a collections.namedtuple class uses exactly the same amount of memory as a plain tuple, because the field names are stored once on the class, not per instance.

collections.namedtuple requires a class name and field names (an iterable of strings or one space-delimited string); field values are passed as separate positional arguments (unlike tuple, which takes one iterable), fields are accessible by name or position, and the class inherits __eq__ and comparison methods from tuple so instances can be sorted.

A namedtuple offers _fields (a tuple of field names), the _make(iterable) class method to build an instance from an iterable, and _asdict() which returns a plain dict (since Python 3.8) useful for JSON serialization; since Python 3.7 the defaults keyword sets default values for the N rightmost fields.

Type hints are not enforced at all by the Python compiler or interpreter at runtime; treat them as documentation that can be verified by IDEs and static type checkers such as Mypy, which you must run separately to see their effect.

In a class body, a bare annotation like a: int is recorded in __annotations__ but creates no class attribute; an annotated assignment like b: float = 1.1 is both an annotation and a class attribute; and a plain c = 'spam' is a class attribute that is not an annotation.

typing.NamedTuple and @dataclass declare instance attributes with PEP 526 variable-annotation syntax (var_name: type, optionally followed by = default), where an initial value becomes the field's default if the corresponding constructor argument is omitted.

In a typing.NamedTuple, each annotated field becomes a read-only instance attribute backed by a descriptor (because instances are immutable tuples), whereas in a @dataclass an annotated field becomes a mutable public instance attribute that exists only on instances and is not type-checked at runtime.

The @dataclass decorator takes keyword-only options @dataclass(init=True, repr=True, eq=True, order=False, unsafe_hash=False, frozen=False); the options most commonly changed from their defaults are frozen=True (protect against accidental change) and order=True (allow sorting of instances).

@dataclass(frozen=True) only emulates immutability by generating __setattr__ and __delattr__ that raise FrozenInstanceError; it is not truly immutable and a determined programmer can bypass it, though the bypass is easy to spot in a code review.
When both eq and frozen are True, @dataclass generates a __hash__ so instances are hashable; when frozen is False (the default) @dataclass sets __hash__ to None, marking instances unhashable.
Because Python does not allow a parameter without a default after one with a default, once you give a data class field a default value every field declared after it must also have a default.

A mutable default value shared through a class attribute is a common bug because all instances would share one object; @dataclass rejects a literal mutable default and requires field(default_factory=callable) so that each instance gets its own fresh value.

@dataclass's rejection of mutable defaults is only a partial safeguard: it flags list, dict, and set, but other mutable default values are not caught, so you must remember to use a default_factory for them.

Since Python 3.9 the built-in collections accept parameterized generic syntax such as list[str]; a bare list annotation means a list of any objects while list[str] means every item must be a str, letting the type checker catch some bugs. Before 3.9, import List from typing instead.

The dataclasses.field function accepts options default, default_factory, init (include the field as an __init__ parameter), repr (include it in __repr__), compare (use it in comparison methods), hash, and metadata.

Provide a __post_init__ method when a data class needs initialization beyond simple field assignment (such as validation or computing a field from other fields); @dataclass adds a call to __post_init__ as the last step of the generated __init__.
To declare a class variable rather than an instance field inside a @dataclass, annotate it with typing.ClassVar[...]; otherwise @dataclass would treat the annotated attribute as an instance field.

To pass an __init__ argument that is not an instance field (an init-only variable), declare it with dataclasses.InitVar[...]: it will not become an instance attribute and will not appear in dataclasses.fields, but it is passed to __post_init__.
Creating a hierarchy of data classes through inheritance is usually a bad idea, especially when the superclasses are not abstract.

A data class can be a code smell (Fowler and Beck): a class that has only fields with getters and setters is a dumb data holder often manipulated in too much detail by other classes, so overusing data classes may signal that behaviour belongs with the data instead.

A code smell is a quick-to-spot surface indication that often corresponds to a deeper problem, but it is not always a real problem, so a smell is an indicator to investigate rather than a defect in itself.

The core idea of object-oriented programming is to keep behaviour and data together in the same class, so a widely used class with no significant behaviour of its own tends to have its logic scattered and duplicated across the system; the remedy is to refactor that behaviour back into the class.

A behaviour-light data class is legitimate in two scenarios: as scaffolding, an initial simplistic class to jump-start a project that should later grow its own methods, and as an intermediate representation, building records for export (such as JSON) or holding just-imported data crossing a system boundary.

When a data class serves as an intermediate representation, handle its instances as immutable while in that form; if import or export requires changing values, write your own builder methods rather than using the generated as-dict methods or standard constructors.
condition: the data class is used as an intermediate representation crossing a system boundary

statement: Class patterns in match/case match a class instance by type and optionally by attributes, and the subject can be an instance of any class, not only a data class.

Write a type-matching class pattern with parentheses, as in case float(); the form case float: (no parentheses) is a bug, because Python treats the bare name as a capture variable that matches any subject and binds it.

The simple constructor-like pattern where a single argument binds the whole subject (such as float(x)) applies only to nine blessed built-in types (bytes, dict, float, frozenset, int, list, set, str, tuple); for any other class the argument-like names are patterns matched against the instance's attributes.

A keyword class pattern such as City(continent='Asia', country=cc) matches instances by attribute value and binds attributes to variables; it is very readable and works with any class that has public instance attributes, but is somewhat verbose.

A positional class pattern such as City('Asia', _, country) requires the class to define the __match_args__ class attribute (automatically created by the data class builders), which lists the attribute names in positional order; positional and keyword arguments can be combined in one pattern.

With @dataclass, type hints are not optional and PEP 526 reverses the usual class-body convention: a top-level attribute declared with a type hint becomes an instance attribute, one without a hint stays a class attribute, and to type-annotate a true class attribute you must use ClassVar.

Python variables are labels (references) attached to objects, not boxes that contain values, so b = a binds the label b to the same object that a references and mutating that object through one name is visible through the other (aliasing).

To understand a Python assignment, read the right-hand side first, where the object is created or retrieved, and only then is the left-hand variable bound to it; the object must exist before a name can bind to it, so if the right-hand side raises, the variable is never created.

The == operator compares the values of objects (their data) while is compares their identities, so two variables bound to the same object are aliases (is returns True), and two distinct objects with equal value compare == True but is False.

An object's identity never changes once it is created (you may think of it as its address in memory), the is operator compares two objects' identities, and id() returns a unique integer label for an object's identity that is constant for the object's lifetime.

Test a variable against a singleton with is; the most common case is checking None, where the recommended forms are x is None and x is not None, and the same pattern is used for sentinel objects created with object().

The is operator is faster than == because it cannot be overloaded and only compares two integer IDs, whereas a == b is syntactic sugar for a.__eq__(b), which for large collections or deeply nested structures may involve substantial processing.

Checking for None is essentially the only common correct use of the is operator; most other uses seen in code review are wrong, so when unsure use ==, which is usually what you want and also works with None.
A tuple's immutability is relative: it holds references, and if a referenced item is mutable the tuple's value can change even though the identities of the items it holds never change.

Copies are shallow by default: list(l), l[:], or the type's constructor duplicate the outer container but fill it with references to the same items, which is fine if all items are immutable but causes surprises when items are mutable.

The copy module's copy and deepcopy functions make shallow and deep copies of arbitrary objects; deepcopy does not share embedded objects and tracks already-copied objects to handle cyclic references, and you can customize both via the __copy__ and __deepcopy__ special methods (a deep copy can be too deep for objects holding external resources or singletons).

Python's only parameter-passing mode is call by sharing: each parameter receives a copy of the argument's reference and becomes an alias of it, so a function can mutate a mutable argument in place but cannot replace the caller's object with a different one.

Avoid mutable objects as parameter default values: each default is evaluated once when the function is defined and stored on the function object, so mutating it affects every later call that relies on the default; use None as the default and create a fresh object inside the function instead.

Unless a method is explicitly intended to mutate an argument, do not alias a received mutable argument by assigning it directly to an instance attribute; make a copy (for example list(passengers)), which avoids violating the principle of least astonishment and as a bonus accepts any iterable.

The del statement deletes references, not objects; the garbage collector may discard an object as an indirect result of del (or of rebinding a variable) only when the deleted reference was the last one pointing to that object.

The __del__ special method does not dispose of an instance and should not be called by your code; the interpreter invokes it when the instance is about to be destroyed to release external resources, and it is seldom needed and tricky to use correctly.

CPython's primary garbage collection is reference counting, which destroys an object immediately when its reference count reaches zero, supplemented by a generational collector for reference cycles; other Python implementations do not rely on reference counting, so __del__ may not be called promptly when references disappear.

A weak reference does not increase an object's reference count and so does not keep the target alive, which makes weak references useful in caches where you do not want cached objects kept alive merely because the cache references them.

For an immutable type, copying often returns the same object rather than a real copy: t[:] and tuple(t) return the same tuple, and str, bytes, and frozenset behave similarly (frozenset.copy() also returns the same object).

Never depend on string or integer interning: CPython may share identical small strings and integers so that is appears to work, but the criteria are undocumented, so always compare strings or integers for equality with == rather than is.

Close a file reliably with the with statement, which guarantees the file is closed even if an exception is raised; do not rely on reference-counting to close files, because open().write() is unsafe on runtimes like Jython or IronPython that do not use reference counting.

To make your own object truly immutable, every one of its attributes must also be immutable; otherwise you get tuple-like behaviour, immutable as far as identity goes but with a value that can change when a referenced mutable attribute changes.
condition: the object is intended to be immutable

statement: Mutable objects are the main reason multithreaded programming is hard to get right: threads mutating shared objects without synchronization corrupt data, while excessive synchronization causes deadlocks.
Functions in Python are first-class objects: they can be created at runtime, assigned to a variable or data-structure element, passed as an argument, and returned as the result of another function.

A higher-order function is one that takes a function as an argument or returns a function as its result; examples include map, filter, and sorted (whose key argument is a one-argument function applied to each item).

A list comprehension or generator expression replaces map and filter combined and is more readable, making lambda unnecessary; in Python 3 map and filter return generators, so a generator expression is their direct substitute.

reduce was moved from a built-in to functools in Python 3; prefer the sum built-in for summation (more readable and faster), use all and any as the other reducing built-ins (all([]) is True, any([]) is False), and call a function with dynamic arguments via fn(*args, **kwargs) since apply was removed.

A lambda creates an anonymous function, and is just syntactic sugar producing a function object exactly like def; its body is limited to a single pure expression and cannot contain statements such as while, try, or assignment with =.

The best use of a lambda is as an argument to a higher-order function; outside that context anonymous functions are rarely useful, and if a lambda is hard to read, refactor it to a named def (comment it, name the comment, convert to def, remove the comment).

Since Python 3.6 there are nine flavors of callable object (user-defined functions, built-in functions, built-in methods, methods, classes, class instances with __call__, generator functions, native coroutine functions, and asynchronous generator functions); use the callable() built-in to test whether an object can be called.

Generator functions, native coroutine functions, and asynchronous generator functions differ from other callables in that their return value is never application data but an object requiring further processing: generator functions return iterators, while coroutine and async-generator functions return objects that work only with an asynchronous framework.

Implement a __call__ instance method to make instances of a class behave like functions, which is an easy way to create function-like objects that keep internal state across invocations and is also useful for implementing decorators.
In a function signature, *name captures any number of extra positional arguments as a tuple and **name captures extra keyword arguments not named in the signature as a dict.

Declare keyword-only parameters (a Python 3 feature) by naming them after a * in the signature, or after a bare * if you do not want variable positional arguments; keyword-only parameters never capture positional arguments and may be mandatory rather than having a default.
Since Python 3.8 you can declare positional-only parameters by placing a / in the parameter list; arguments to the left of the / cannot be passed by keyword.
The operator module provides function equivalents for dozens of operators (such as operator.mul) so you do not have to write trivial lambdas like lambda a, b: a*b in functional-style code.

operator.itemgetter builds a function that extracts items by index or key (working on any object that implements __getitem__; multiple indices return a tuple), operator.attrgetter builds functions that read named attributes (a dotted name navigates nested objects), and operator.methodcaller builds a function that calls a named method, optionally freezing extra arguments.

functools.partial(callable, *args, **kwargs) produces a new callable with some of the original arguments bound to fixed values, which is useful to adapt a function to an API that requires a callback with fewer arguments; functools.partialmethod does the same for methods.

Python is not by design a functional language; it borrows ideas like first-class functions and list comprehensions, but its statement-oriented syntax forbids statements inside a lambda body and it lacks tail-call elimination, which limits functional idioms.

Type hints (PEP 484) add explicit type declarations to function arguments, return values, and variables to help developer tools find bugs by static analysis without running the code, and they should always be optional because they do not benefit all Python users equally.

PEP 484 introduced a gradual type system with three defining properties: it is optional (the checker emits no warnings for unhinted code, assuming the Any type, which is compatible with all types), it does not catch type errors at runtime, and it does not enhance performance.

Do not seek 100% type-hint coverage, because it encourages adding hints without thought just to satisfy a metric and prevents teams from using Python's flexibility; code without type hints should be accepted where annotations would make an API less user-friendly or unduly complicate its implementation.

Adopt type hints gradually with a checker like Mypy, which by default ignores functions that have no annotations; the --disallow-incomplete-defs option makes Mypy check a function once any annotation (such as a return type) is added, enabling function-by-function annotation.
Writing a parameter as color=str sets the default value to the str class rather than annotating it; the annotation must be color: str, and Python does not catch this easily-overlooked mistake.

Good type-hint style puts no space before the colon and one space after it, and spaces on both sides of the = preceding a default value, while PEP 8 says to use no spaces around = when a parameter has no type hint; rely on tools like flake8 and blue rather than memorizing the rules.

Use None as the default when an optional parameter expects a mutable type, annotating it as Optional[str] (meaning str or None) and still explicitly assigning = None; Optional does not make the parameter optional (the default value does), and import such types with from typing import X to keep signatures short.

A type is best understood as the set of operations it supports, not merely a set of values, so a type checker rejects an operation the declared type does not provide (for example x * 2 when x is annotated abc.Sequence, which has no __mul__) even though that code works at runtime for concrete sequences.

A gradual type system combines duck typing (variables are untyped and only the operations an object actually supports matter, enforced at runtime, flexible but allowing more runtime errors) with nominal typing (the checker reads only the declared types in source, so a Duck assigned to a Bird-annotated parameter cannot call a Duck-only method, rigid but catching bugs earlier).

At runtime Python ignores declared types and uses only duck typing, so a static checker can flag errors in programs that actually run; duck typing is easier and more flexible but lets unsupported operations fail at runtime, while nominal typing catches errors before runtime yet may reject code that would have run.

The value of type hints is small in tiny examples but grows with codebase size, which is why companies with millions of lines of Python (Dropbox, Google, Facebook) invest in tools and teams to type check large portions of their code in CI.

Any, the dynamic type, is the keystone of gradual typing: an unannotated function is treated as taking and returning Any, which is simultaneously the most general type (accepts every type) and the most specialized (supports every operation), so using Any prevents the checker from detecting illegal operations.

More general types have narrower interfaces and support fewer operations (object is narrower than abc.Sequence, which is narrower than abc.MutableSequence, which is narrower than list), so annotating x: object and then doing x * 2 is rejected because object has no __mul__.

A gradual type system uses the consistent-with relation, which extends subtype-of: a subtype is consistent-with its supertype, every type is consistent-with Any, and Any is consistent-with every type.

By the Liskov Substitution Principle (behavioral subtyping), an object of type T2 is a subtype of T1 if it can substitute T1 with the program still behaving correctly; a subclass supports all the superclass's operations so it can be used wherever the superclass is expected, but not the reverse.

Although int, float, and complex have no nominal subclass relationship, PEP 484 declares int consistent-with float and float consistent-with complex, so annotating a parameter as float also accepts int values and annotating as complex accepts both.

Optional[str] is shorthand for Union[str, None] (the value may be str or None); since Python 3.10 you can instead write str | None without importing from typing, and the | operator also builds the second argument of isinstance and issubclass.

Avoid creating functions that return a Union type, because it forces the caller to check the returned value's type at runtime; also Union[int, float] is redundant since int is consistent-with float, so annotating the parameter as float suffices.

Declare a generic collection's item type with parameters such as list[str] (Python 3.9+), where a bare list and list[Any] mean the same thing (a list of objects of any type); for Python 3.7-3.8 enable this with from __future__ import annotations, and for 3.5-3.6 use the now-deprecated typing aliases like List.

Annotate a tuple used as a record with fixed field types (tuple[str, float, str]); prefer typing.NamedTuple for tuples with many or frequently-reused fields; and annotate a tuple used as an immutable sequence of arbitrary length with a single type plus ellipsis (tuple[int, ...]).

Annotate a generic mapping as MappingType[KeyType, ValueType] (for example dict[str, set[str]]); use typing.TypedDict for a dict used as a record with str keys and values whose types depend on the key; and annotate a local variable when the checker cannot infer its type.

Following Postel's law for type hints, accept abstract types (collections.abc) in parameters and return concrete types: annotating a parameter as abc.Mapping lets the caller pass dict, defaultdict, ChainMap, or a UserDict subclass, whereas annotating it as dict rejects a UserDict (which is a sibling of dict, not a subclass), and use abc.Mapping rather than MutableMapping when the function does not mutate the argument.

A function's return type hint should be a concrete type (such as list[str]) because the return value is always a concrete object, while abstract collection types like Sequence or Iterable are preferred for annotating arguments.

The numbers ABCs (the numeric tower Number, Complex, Real, Rational, Integral) work for runtime type checking but are not supported by static type checkers; to annotate numbers for static checking, use the concrete types int, float, or complex, a Union, or numeric protocols such as SupportsFloat.

Iterable and Sequence are best used as parameter types and are too vague for return types; accepting an Iterable lets the caller pass a generator and save memory, but a function that must consume it fully will exhaust memory on an endless iterable, and you should require a Sequence when you need len() or indexing up front.

The standard library has no inline annotations (as of Python 3.10), so type checkers find type hints for it in the Typeshed project's stub files, which have a .pyi extension and contain annotated signatures without implementations, much like C header files.

Create a type alias by assigning a type expression to a name (FromTo = tuple[str, str]) to make complex signatures readable; since Python 3.10 the preferred, more visible form is an explicit annotation FromTo: TypeAlias = tuple[str, str].

A parameterized generic such as list[T] uses a type variable T (declared with typing.TypeVar, which must introduce the name in the namespace) that binds to a specific type on each use, allowing a parameter's type to be reflected in the return type (for example Sequence[T] -> list[T]).

A restricted TypeVar (TypeVar('NumberT', float, Decimal, Fraction)) is set to exactly one of the named types, whereas a bounded TypeVar (TypeVar('HashableT', bound=Hashable)) is set to the inferred type as long as it is consistent-with the upper boundary; the predefined AnyStr = TypeVar('AnyStr', bytes, str) supports functions accepting either bytes or str and returning the same type.

A typing.Protocol (PEP 544) defines an interface by listing one or more methods, and a type is consistent-with that protocol if it implements all the methods with matching signatures, without inheriting, registering, or declaring any relationship to the protocol; this is structural subtyping, also called static duck typing.

A key advantage of a Protocol over an ABC is that a type needs no special declaration to be consistent-with it, so a protocol can be applied to preexisting types or types you do not control (for example str, tuple, and float satisfy a SupportsLessThan protocol simply by implementing __lt__).

To constrain a generic to types that support a needed operation, define a custom protocol (such as SupportsLessThan with a __lt__ method) and use it as the upper bound of a type variable, for example LT = TypeVar('LT', bound=SupportsLessThan).

typing.TYPE_CHECKING is always False at runtime but treated as True by type checkers, so it guards code meant only for static analysis; reveal_type() is a Mypy-only debugging facility (with no import) that prints the inferred type of its argument during checking.

Annotate a callback or callable parameter with Callable[[ParamType1, ParamType2], ReturnType], using a parameter list of zero or more types; to match a function with a flexible signature, replace the whole parameter list with an ellipsis, as in Callable[..., ReturnType]. There is no syntax to annotate optional or keyword argument types.

Callable types are covariant on the return type (Callable[[], int] is a subtype of Callable[[], float]) and contravariant on the parameter types (Callable[[float], None] is a subtype of Callable[[int], None]); most parameterized generics, however, are invariant, so list[float] accepts neither list[int] nor list[complex].

NoReturn is the special type used to annotate the return type of functions that never return, which usually exist to raise an exception (for example sys.exit, whose typeshed signature returns NoReturn).

When annotating variadic parameters, *content: str means each arbitrary positional argument must be a str and the content variable is typed tuple[str, ...] inside the function, while **attrs: str means attrs is dict[str, str]; use Union or Any (for example **attrs: Any) when the values may be of different types.

Static type checkers cannot be the mainstay of software quality: they yield false positives and false negatives, cannot statically check some features (argument unpacking like config(**settings), properties, descriptors, metaclasses), lag behind Python releases, and cannot express common data or business-logic constraints; treat the type checker as one tool in a CI pipeline alongside automated tests, and use type hints where unit tests are worth writing rather than making them mandatory.

Libraries with Pythonic, dynamic APIs (such as max, requests, and SQLAlchemy) benefit least from type hints, and strict enforcement can discourage writing such powerful functions and may push teams toward code generation; any reasonable policy on type hints must allow exceptions.

A decorator is a callable that takes the decorated function as its argument and returns it or replaces it with another function or callable; the @decorate syntax above a def is exactly equivalent to defining the function and then rebinding its name with target = decorate(target).

Three essential facts about decorators: a decorator is a function or other callable, it may replace the decorated function with a different one, and it runs immediately when the module is loaded (at import time), whereas the decorated function runs only when explicitly invoked, illustrating the difference between import time and runtime.

A registration decorator adds the decorated function to a central registry (for example mapping URL patterns to handler functions) and may return it unchanged; in real code a decorator is usually defined in one module and applied to functions in other modules, and most decorators define an inner function and return it to replace the decorated function.

Python decides at compile time that a variable is local if it is assigned anywhere in the function body, so referencing that name before its assignment raises UnboundLocalError even when a global variable of the same name exists; this is a deliberate design choice, not a bug.
Use the global declaration inside a function to make the interpreter treat a name as a module-global variable so you can assign a new value to it rather than creating a local.

A closure is a function that retains the bindings of its free variables (variables referenced in its body that are neither global nor its own locals, coming from the local scope of an enclosing function) so they remain usable after the defining scope is gone; this only arises when a function is nested in another, and Python records free-variable names in __code__.co_freevars and their values in the __closure__ cells.

Rebinding an immutable free variable inside a nested function (for example count += 1, which means count = count + 1) makes it a local variable and breaks the closure with UnboundLocalError; mutable free variables like a list avoid this because you can read and mutate them (for example .append) without rebinding the name.

Use the nonlocal declaration (added in Python 3) to mark a name as a free variable even though it is assigned inside the nested function, so that reassigning it updates the binding stored in the closure.

Python's variable lookup rules: a global x declaration binds x to the module global; a nonlocal x declaration binds x to the nearest enclosing function's local; a parameter or a name assigned in the body is local; and a name referenced but not assigned is searched in enclosing function scopes, then the module global scope, then __builtins__.__dict__.

A typical decorator replaces the decorated function with a new inner function that accepts the same arguments, returns whatever the original returned, and adds extra processing; the inner function reaches the original through a closure over the func free variable.

Apply functools.wraps to a decorator's inner function to copy attributes like __name__ and __doc__ from the decorated function (a naive decorator masks them), and accept *args, **kwargs in the wrapper so it supports keyword arguments.

functools.cache (Python 3.9+) implements memoization by storing the results of previous calls to avoid recomputation, but it can consume all available memory with many entries (more suitable for short-lived scripts; use lru_cache with a maxsize in long-running processes), and all arguments of the decorated function must be hashable because the results are stored in a dict keyed by the call arguments.

Stacked decorators compose like nested calls: @alpha @beta def f is equivalent to f = alpha(beta(f)), so the decorator nearest the function (beta) is applied first and its result is passed to the outer one.

functools.lru_cache bounds memory with its maxsize parameter (default 128, ideally a power of 2, and maxsize=None disables the LRU logic for an unbounded cache like functools.cache), discarding least-recently-used entries when full; typed=False stores equal int and float arguments as one entry, while typed=True stores them separately.

functools.singledispatch turns a plain function into a generic function: a group of functions that perform the same operation differently based on the type of the first argument, with specializations registered via @base.register (using a type hint on the first parameter or by passing the type) in any module, even for third-party types you cannot edit, which supports modular extension better than a large if/elif dispatcher.

When using singledispatch, register specialized functions against ABCs (such as numbers.Integral or abc.MutableSequence) or Protocols rather than concrete types (int, list) so the code supports more compatible actual or virtual subclasses, and note that the dispatcher selects the most specific matching type regardless of registration order.
To build a decorator that accepts arguments, write a decorator factory: a function that takes those arguments and returns the actual decorator, which is then applied to the function being decorated.

A parameterized decorator is a pyramid of nested functions: a decorator factory takes the parameters (captured in a closure) and returns the actual decorator, which takes the function and returns a wrapper that replaces it; the factory must be invoked with parentheses even when no arguments are passed (for example @register()).

For nontrivial decorators, a class-based implementation with __call__ can be easier to read and maintain than nested functions: the class stores its parameters in __init__ and __call__ receives the decorated function and returns the wrapper.

Python uses lexical scope: a function's free variables are evaluated in the environment where the function is defined, not where it is invoked (which would be dynamic scope); lexical scope requires closures but keeps functions opaque so callers need not know their internals.

Python function decorators fit the Gang of Four Decorator pattern description (attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically as a flexible alternative to subclassing), but at the implementation level they differ, and the decorator design pattern itself is generally best implemented with classes rather than function decorators.

Design patterns are general recipes for common design problems and are language-independent, but not every pattern applies to every language: the implementation language determines which patterns are relevant, and many Gang of Four patterns become invisible or simpler in a dynamic language with first-class functions (for example the Iterator pattern is built into Python as generators).

In languages with first-class functions, classic patterns such as Strategy, Command, Template Method, and Visitor can be rethought so that functions do the work of classes with more readable, concise code; the Strategy pattern itself defines a family of interchangeable, encapsulated algorithms that vary independently of their clients, with participants Context, the Strategy interface, and concrete strategies.

When a concrete Strategy is a single-method class with no internal state, replace it with a plain function: a function is more lightweight than an instance of a single-method class, is created only once per Python process, and is itself a shared object usable in multiple contexts, so the Flyweight pattern (which Design Patterns recommends to share stateless strategy objects) is unnecessary.
condition: the concrete strategies have no internal state and only use data from the context

statement: Once you accept that functions are first-class objects, it naturally follows that building data structures that hold functions (such as a list of strategy functions to iterate over) often makes sense.

A metastrategy that iterates a hardcoded list of strategy functions (for example best_promo over a promos list) carries a duplication risk: adding a new strategy requires remembering to add it to the list, or it is silently ignored, introducing a subtle bug.

Prefer a registration decorator to auto-collect strategy functions (a @promotion decorator that appends each function to a list and returns it unchanged): the functions need no special naming, the decorator reveals intent and lets you disable a strategy by commenting it out, and strategies may live in any module; collecting them by introspection of globals() or inspect.getmembers is a more fragile alternative that breaks on any non-conforming function.

The Command pattern decouples an invoker from the receiver via a Command object exposing a single execute method (an object-oriented replacement for callbacks); in Python you can instead pass a plain function and call command() rather than command.execute(), and implement a MacroCommand as a class with __call__ that holds and runs a list of commands.

When a design pattern or API requires components to implement a single-method interface with a generic name such as execute, run, or do_it, it can often be implemented with less boilerplate in Python using functions as first-class objects, because every Python callable already implements a single-method interface named __call__.

When a function needs to keep state, a callable instance (a class with __call__) can hold whatever state is needed and provide extra methods, while a closure can hold the internal state of a function between calls; both are alternatives to coding single-method classes.

When an instance attribute holds a callable rather than a method (for example a strategy function stored on an object), invoking it requires passing the instance explicitly (self.promotion(self)), because the automatic method-to-instance binding does not apply to plain callable attributes.
Two widely-quoted design principles from the Gang of Four Design Patterns book are 'Program to an interface, not an implementation' and 'Favor object composition over class inheritance.'

The Python Data Model lets user-defined types behave as naturally as built-in types, achieved through duck typing by implementing the needed special methods rather than through inheritance; being Pythonic means making your classes behave the way users expect Python's built-in classes to behave.
Application classes usually do not need, and should not implement, as many special methods as a library or framework class; implement only the special methods your objects actually need.
