Python has two string representations, repr() (the developer view via __repr__, shown by the console and debugger) and str() (the user view via __str__, shown by print), plus __bytes__ for bytes() and __format__ for format(), f-strings, and str.format(); in Python 3 __repr__, __str__, and __format__ must return str, and only __bytes__ returns a byte sequence.
Convert constructor arguments to their proper types inside __init__ (for example float(x)) so errors are caught early when the class is called with unsuitable arguments.
Implementing __iter__ makes an object iterable, which is what enables unpacking such as x, y = my_object; it can be implemented simply by yielding the components with a generator expression.

Use @classmethod for a method that operates on the class rather than an instance (it receives the class as cls instead of self), most commonly to define alternative constructors that call cls(...); @staticmethod takes no special first argument and behaves like a plain function inside the class body, and good use cases for staticmethod are rare.

f-strings, the format() built-in, and str.format() all delegate formatting to a type's __format__(format_spec) method; in a replacement field the part before the colon is the field_name (an arbitrary expression in an f-string) and the part after the colon is the format specifier written in the Format Specification Mini-Language.

Extend the Format Specification Mini-Language for a user-defined type by implementing __format__ to interpret the format_spec; if a class has no __format__, the inherited object.__format__ returns str(obj) but raises TypeError when given a non-empty specifier, and when inventing a custom format code you should avoid letters already used by built-in types to reduce confusion.

To make a type hashable, implement __hash__ (which must return an int) alongside the required __eq__, and ideally compute the hash from the same attributes used in __eq__ (objects that compare equal must have the same hash), for example by returning hash of a tuple of the components.

Because a hashable object's value must never change, make such an object immutable by storing its data in private attributes and exposing read-only access through @property getters named after the public attribute (although implementing __hash__ and __eq__ correctly is technically all hashability requires).
Implement __int__ and __float__ (invoked by the int() and float() constructors for coercion) and __complex__ (for complex()) when a type has a sensible scalar numeric value.
condition: the type has a sensible scalar numeric value

statement: To support positional class patterns, add a __match_args__ class attribute listing the instance attribute names in the order they should be matched positionally; it need not include every public attribute (for example, list required __init__ arguments but not optional ones).

Python has no truly private attributes, but naming an attribute with two leading underscores (and at most one trailing) triggers name mangling, storing it as _ClassName__name in the instance __dict__, which prevents accidental clobbering of inherited attributes in subclasses; it is a safety device, not security, since the mangled name can still be accessed directly.

Many Pythonistas avoid double-underscore name mangling and instead use a single leading underscore (self._x) as a strong convention meaning the attribute should not be accessed from outside the class; the single underscore has no special meaning to the interpreter for attributes, much like ALL_CAPS marks a constant by convention.

Defining a __slots__ class attribute holding a sequence of attribute names makes Python store instance attributes in a hidden array of references instead of a per-instance __dict__, which can yield large memory savings (in one test reducing 10 million instances from about 1.55 GiB to 551 MiB) and also runs faster.

__slots__ has caveats: it must be redeclared in each subclass or that subclass's instances regain a __dict__; instances can only hold the listed attributes unless '__dict__' is added (which may negate the savings); @cached_property requires '__dict__' in __slots__; weak-reference targets require '__weakref__' in __slots__; and __slots__ must be present when the class is created.

For handling millions of objects with numeric data, prefer NumPy arrays over custom classes (even with __slots__), because NumPy is both memory efficient and provides highly optimized functions that operate on the whole array at once.
condition: the data is numeric and there are millions of objects

statement: A class attribute serves as a default value for instance attributes read via self.attr; assigning to self.attr creates a per-instance attribute that shadows the class attribute (leaving the class attribute unchanged), which allows customizing an individual instance.

To change a class attribute, set it on the class itself, not through an instance; idiomatically, subclass the class just to override a class data attribute (as Django class-based views do), and read the class name in __repr__ from type(self).__name__ so that subclasses inherit a correct __repr__ without overriding it.

An object should be as simple as the requirements dictate, not a parade of language features (simple is better than complex): application code should implement only what supports its end users, whereas library code may reasonably implement the special methods Pythonistas expect (for example __eq__, which is not always a business requirement but makes a class easier to test).
To build Pythonic objects, observe how real Python objects behave and study the API of standard Python types.

Properties reduce up-front costs: start a class with simple public attributes and, if you later need access control, convert them to read-only or managed properties without changing the public interface or breaking code that already uses those attributes, unlike Java where getters and setters must be written up front because attributes cannot later evolve into them.

Implement a user-defined sequence type by composition (store the components in an internal array or list and delegate to it) rather than inheritance, and give it a constructor that takes the data as a single iterable argument, as all built-in sequence types do, rather than arbitrary *args.

For a collection type that may hold many items, produce a limited-length repr abbreviated with '...' (for example using the reprlib module's reprlib.repr), because repr is used for debugging and a single large object should not span thousands of lines in a console or log.

Calling repr() on an object should never raise an exception, because repr is used for debugging; if something goes wrong inside __repr__, handle it and still produce some serviceable output that lets the user identify the object.

A protocol in the duck-typing sense is an informal interface defined only in documentation, not in code; a class that implements the required methods (for example __len__ and __getitem__ for the sequence protocol) can be used wherever that protocol is expected regardless of its base class, because it is a sequence by virtue of behaving like one.

Because dynamic protocols are informal and unenforced, you can implement just part of one when you know the context (for example, __getitem__ alone supports iteration without __len__); static protocols defined with typing.Protocol differ in that an implementation must provide all the methods the protocol declares.

Every built-in sequence returns slices of its own type, so to make a user-defined sequence's slices return its own type rather than the underlying array or list, analyze the argument received by __getitem__ instead of blindly delegating the slicing.

Slicing mechanics: my_seq[1:4] passes a slice(1, 4, None) object to __getitem__, and commas inside the brackets make __getitem__ receive a tuple (possibly of several slice objects); the slice type has start, stop, and step attributes plus an indices(len) method that normalizes start, stop, and stride and clips out-of-bounds or negative indices for a sequence of the given length.

To make a sequence's slices return its own type, test isinstance(key, slice) in __getitem__ and construct a new instance from the sliced underlying sequence; for integer indexing use operator.index(key) (which calls __index__) rather than int(), because operator.index is purpose-built for indexing and raises TypeError on a float instead of silently truncating it.

Excessive use of isinstance may indicate poor object-oriented design, but handling slices inside __getitem__ is a justified use case, and operator.index avoids needing a separate isinstance test for integers.

The __getattr__ special method is invoked by the interpreter only as a fallback, when normal attribute lookup (the instance, then its class, then up the inheritance graph) fails; you can implement it to provide dynamic or virtual attributes such as exposing v[0] as v.x.

Implementing __getattr__ alone often introduces inconsistency, because after an assignment like v.x = 10 the instance now has an x attribute and __getattr__ is no longer consulted for v.x even though the underlying data is unchanged; therefore when you implement __getattr__ you very often need to implement __setattr__ as well to keep the object consistent.

Use the super() function to delegate a task from a method in a subclass to a suitable method in a superclass (for example calling super().__setattr__ for default behaviour), which is necessary in a dynamic language supporting multiple inheritance like Python.

Do not use __slots__ merely to prevent the creation of new instance attributes, even though it has that side effect; because of its caveats, __slots__ should be used only to save memory, and only when memory is a real issue.

functools.reduce(function, iterable, initializer) reduces a series of values to one by applying a two-argument function cumulatively; supply the initializer (the operation's identity value, such as 0 for +, |, and ^, or 1 for * and &) to both avoid a TypeError on an empty sequence and define the result returned for an empty sequence.

Compute an aggregate hash over many components as a map-reduce: map hash over the components and reduce with operator.xor, which is cheaper than building a tuple of thousands of components; using the operator function form avoids a lambda, map is lazy in Python 3 (saving memory), and __eq__ and __hash__ should be kept together in the source because they must work consistently.

For large sequences, implement __eq__ efficiently by first checking that the operands have equal length and then comparing element-wise with zip plus all (which short-circuits on the first mismatch), rather than building two tuples that copy the entire contents of both operands.

The zip built-in iterates in parallel over two or more iterables yielding tuples, but stops silently when the shortest iterable is exhausted (a fail-fast risk that Python 3.10's strict=True turns into a ValueError on length mismatch); itertools.zip_longest fills missing values with a fillvalue (None by default), and zip(*matrix) transposes a matrix of nested iterables.

When extending the Format Specification Mini-Language with a custom code, avoid reusing the letters already used by built-in types (integers use bcdoxXn, floats use eEfFgGn%, strings use s) so the custom code does not collide with their original meaning.

When a class emulates a built-in type, implement the emulation only to the degree that makes sense for the object being modeled (a sequence may support retrieving individual elements but not slicing); implementing only the relevant part of a dynamic protocol keeps things simple and follows KISS, and you only need the stricter typing.Protocol if you want a type checker to verify the implementation.

The most Pythonic way to sum a series is sum(genexp), which is more readable than functools.reduce or a manual accumulator loop, expresses intent at a high level, and avoids the empty-sequence trap because sum([]) is 0; reduce was demoted to functools because it encouraged hard-to-explain idioms, but it still has its place for aggregations like an xor hash.

Because repr() is used for debugging and logging it must always produce serviceable output, so limit very large representations (as with reprlib), whereas __format__ is used to display output to end users who presumably want to see the whole object, so it is reasonable not to truncate a __format__ result.
Object-oriented programming is fundamentally about interfaces, so the best way to understand a type in Python is to know the methods it provides, which constitute its interface.

Since Python 3.8 there are four complementary approaches to defining and using interfaces, none of which should be dismissed: duck typing (Python's default runtime structural typing), goose typing (runtime checks of objects against abstract base classes), static typing (the typing module enforced by an external checker, nominal), and static duck typing (typing.Protocol subclasses, structural and checked by an external checker).

The Typing Map organizes the four typing approaches along two axes: runtime checking (using only the interpreter) versus static checking (requiring an external type checker or IDE), and structural typing (based on the methods an object provides regardless of its class name) versus nominal typing (based on the explicitly named class or superclass types).

Python has dynamic protocols (informal interfaces defined by convention and documentation) and static protocols (typing.Protocol subclasses from PEP 544); an object may implement only part of a dynamic protocol and still be useful, but must provide every method of a static protocol, and only static protocols can be verified by a type checker, yet for both a class never has to declare support by name or inheritance.

__getitem__ is the key to the sequence protocol: implementing it alone enables retrieving items by index and also makes the object iterable and usable with the in operator, because the interpreter falls back to calling __getitem__ with integer indexes from 0 to iterate and does a sequential scan for in when __iter__ and __contains__ are absent.

Most ABCs in collections.abc exist to formalize interfaces already implemented by built-in objects and supported implicitly by the interpreter; they are useful as base classes for new types and for runtime type checking (goose typing) and type hints, and a correct Sequence subclass need only implement __getitem__ and __len__ because the other Sequence methods are concrete and inherited.

Monkey patching is dynamically changing a module, class, or function at runtime to add features or fix bugs (for example assigning a __setitem__ function onto a class); it is powerful but the patching code is tightly coupled to the patched program and often relies on private, undocumented attributes.

Following established protocols improves your chances of leveraging existing standard-library and third-party code through duck typing, because functions like random.shuffle work on any object that implements the required protocol methods (the mutable sequence protocol's __setitem__) regardless of the object's class.

Every Python method starts life as a plain function, and naming the first argument self is merely a convention, although you should use the documented names (self, key, value, and so on) in source files.

Practice fail fast in dynamic code by raising runtime errors as early as possible: instead of type-checking a sequence argument, immediately build a list from it (self._x = list(iterable)), which accepts any iterable and fails fast with a clear TypeError at construction; if the data must not be copied use isinstance(x, abc.MutableSequence), call len() first to reject infinite generators, or call iter(x) early when any iterable is acceptable, and remember type hints (not enforced at runtime, and defeated by Any) catch some but not all problems, so fail fast is the last line of defense.

Use EAFP (easier to ask forgiveness than permission) duck typing to handle several input types without isinstance or hasattr tests: try the operation and catch the exception (for example try field_names.replace(...), except AttributeError treat the argument as an iterable), which can be more expressive than static type hints since some constraints (such as 'a string of identifiers separated by spaces or commas') cannot be spelled as a type.

Goose typing is runtime type checking that leverages abstract base classes (Python has no interface keyword); ABCs complement duck typing by defining interfaces where hasattr() would be clumsy or subtly wrong (such as with magic methods), and they introduce virtual subclasses that are recognized by isinstance and issubclass without inheriting from the ABC.

Duck typing means ignoring an object's actual type and focusing on whether it implements the method names, signatures, and semantics required for its use, which mostly means avoiding isinstance checks (and especially type(foo) is bar, which inhibits inheritance); however, shared method names do not guarantee semantic equivalence, so a knowledgeable programmer must assert that the behaviours are interchangeable.

Goose typing supplements duck typing: isinstance(obj, cls) is acceptable as long as cls is an abstract base class (its metaclass is abc.ABCMeta); subclass from an ABC to make implementing an interface explicit (a declaration of intent), and perform runtime type checks against ABCs from collections.abc or numbers rather than against concrete classes.

An ABC's key advantage is the register class method, which lets code declare a class a virtual subclass of the ABC (the class must meet the ABC's method and semantic contract but need not inherit from it), breaking the rigidity and coupling of inheritance; some ABCs whose essence is a few special methods (such as Sized via __len__) even recognize a class as a subclass with no registration at all.

isinstance and issubclass checks are more acceptable against ABCs than against concrete classes, because concrete-class checks limit polymorphism while a class can be registered to an ABC after the fact; nonetheless excessive isinstance checks are a code smell, a chain of if/elif isinstance is usually wrong (use polymorphism so the interpreter dispatches to the right method), and an isinstance-against-ABC check is justified mainly to enforce an API contract, as in plug-in architectures.

Do not define your own ABCs (or metaclasses) in production code: they are tools for building frameworks, and most developers should just use existing ABCs correctly to get nearly all the benefit without risk of misdesign.

Subclassing an ABC forces you to implement all of its abstract methods (for example collections.abc.MutableSequence demands __delitem__ and insert in addition to __setitem__); Python checks for the implementations not at import time but when you instantiate the subclass, raising TypeError if any abstract method is missing, and in return the subclass inherits the ABC's concrete methods (which you may override with more efficient implementations).

The most widely used standard-library ABCs are in collections.abc: Iterable (__iter__), Container (__contains__), and Sized (__len__) should be inherited or matched by every collection; Collection (added in 3.6, with no methods of its own) eases subclassing those three; Sequence, Mapping, and Set are the main immutable collections each with a mutable subclass; and Callable and Hashable support checking that objects are callable or hashable.

isinstance against Hashable or Iterable can mislead: isinstance(obj, Hashable) being True only means the class has __hash__ (a tuple containing unhashable items is still unhashable, so call hash(obj) to be sure), and isinstance(obj, Iterable) being False does not mean the object cannot be iterated (the only reliable test is to call iter(obj)).

Define an ABC by subclassing abc.ABC and marking abstract methods with @abstractmethod (whose body is often just a docstring); an ABC may include concrete methods provided they rely only on the ABC's own interface, an abstract method may carry an implementation that subclasses invoke via super(), and when stacking decorators @abstractmethod must be the innermost one.

A concrete ABC subclass may lazily inherit the ABC's concrete methods (which are correct but possibly suboptimal for any subclass that correctly implements the abstract methods) or override them with faster implementations.

You can register a class as a virtual subclass of an ABC with the ABC's register method even though it does not inherit from the ABC: Python trusts that the class implements the interface without checking (not even at instantiation), issubclass and isinstance then recognize it, but it inherits no methods or attributes from the ABC, the ABC is absent from its __mro__, and static type checkers cannot handle virtual subclasses. The standard library uses this to register built-ins like tuple, str, and range as virtual subclasses of Sequence.

ABCs are mostly used with nominal typing (explicit inheritance or registration links the ABC's name to the class), but some ABCs also support structural typing through a __subclasshook__ class method, for example abc.Sized recognizes any class with a __len__ in its MRO as a virtual subclass without registration.

Do not implement __subclasshook__ in your own ABCs: it is only dependable for ABCs whose essence is a single well-known special method (like Sized via __len__), because the mere presence of methods by name does not guarantee the semantic contract (mappings have __len__, __getitem__, and __iter__ yet are rightly not Sequences); instead let the programmer affirm conformance by subclassing or registering.

Static protocols make it possible to add type hints to duck-typed functions that a nominal type system could not annotate (for example double(x) returning x*2 works on any type implementing __mul__): define a typing.Protocol such as Repeatable with the required method and use it as the bound of a TypeVar so the checker verifies the argument supports the operation and the return type matches.

A typing.Protocol can be made to support runtime isinstance and issubclass checks by applying the @runtime_checkable decorator (because Protocol is an ABC with a __subclasshook__); the typing module ships runtime-checkable protocols such as SupportsComplex (__complex__) and SupportsFloat (__float__) that test numeric types for convertibility.

At runtime, duck typing (EAFP) is often the best approach to type checking: rather than calling isinstance or hasattr, just try the operation you need (for example complex(o)) and handle the exception, and if you would only raise a TypeError anyway, simply perform the operation and let Python raise a clear message.

Runtime isinstance/issubclass checks against static protocols only test for the presence or absence of methods, not their signatures or return annotations (and this will not change due to the performance cost), so they can mislead: for example complex had a __float__ method that only raises, making isinstance(c, SupportsFloat) return True even though float(c) fails; relatedly, the numbers ABCs work for runtime checks but are not recognized by static type checkers, so prefer numeric static protocols when using a checker.

Make a class consistent-with a static protocol by implementing the required special methods (for example __complex__ to satisfy SupportsComplex), and add return-type annotations to those methods so the type checker analyzes their bodies, because without a return annotation Mypy infers Any and does not check the method body.

To reference a type in an annotation before it is fully defined (such as a method whose return type is its own enclosing class), add from __future__ import annotations (PEP 563), which stores annotations as unevaluated strings; otherwise write the name as a string literal forward reference.

Single-method protocols make static duck typing more useful and flexible (as Go's Reader interface shows), and a class implements a protocol simply by providing the required methods, without importing or subclassing the protocol.

Best practices for protocol design favor narrow protocols (often a single method, a 'role interface') and sometimes defining the protocol in the client code that uses it (which eases creating new types and mock-based testing); both avoid unnecessary tight coupling in line with the Interface Segregation Principle that clients should not depend on interfaces they do not use.

Name static protocols by convention: plain names for clear concepts (Iterator, Container), SupportsX for protocols providing callable methods (SupportsInt, SupportsRead), and HasX for protocols exposing attributes or getters (HasFileno); Go additionally names a single-method protocol by appending -er to the verb (Reader, Formatter).

When a richer protocol proves useful, derive a new protocol from the existing one rather than adding methods to the original; in Python the derived protocol must explicitly name typing.Protocol as a base class in addition to the protocol it extends, must re-apply @runtime_checkable if needed (the decorator is not inherited), and only needs to declare the newly added method.

The numbers ABCs are fine for runtime type checking (isinstance(x, numbers.Integral) accepts int, bool, and externally registered virtual subclasses like NumPy's) but unsuitable for static typing because numbers.Number has no methods; the numeric static protocols (SupportsComplex, SupportsFloat) work well for static typing but are unreliable for runtime checks involving complex numbers, since built-in complex, float, and int lack __complex__ yet are still convertible via complex().

Monkey patching has a bad reputation because the patch is tightly coupled and brittle and two libraries patching the same target can clobber each other, but it is useful for making a class implement a protocol at runtime (the Adapter design pattern solves the same problem with a new class); notably, Python does not let you monkey patch built-in types, which is an advantage because a str always has the same methods.

Python's fundamental protocols are idioms: once you learn what a sequence (or other protocol) is, you can apply that knowledge across many contexts, which is why mastering the language's core idioms makes code concise, effective, and readable.

There is significant backlash against overusing inheritance in general (not only multiple inheritance) because superclasses and subclasses are tightly coupled, so changes to one part can have far-reaching effects, making systems brittle and hard to understand.

Consistent use of super() is essential for maintainable object-oriented Python: when a subclass overrides a method it usually must call the superclass version via super().method(), and in particular Python (unlike Java) does not automatically call the superclass __init__, so you must call super().__init__(...) yourself.

Do not call a superclass method directly by class name (SuperClass.method(self, ...)) instead of super(), because it hardcodes the base class (so a later change to the class statement can introduce a bug) and bypasses the multiple-inheritance logic that super() implements; the explicit two-argument super(type, obj) form is needed only to skip part of the MRO for testing or to work around a superclass.

Subclassing a built-in type such as dict, list, or str directly is error-prone because the C-coded built-in methods usually ignore user-defined overrides (for example dict.__init__ and dict.update do not call an overridden __setitem__, and dict.update bypasses an overridden __getitem__), violating late binding; instead derive your class from collections.UserDict, UserList, or UserString, which are designed to be extended.

Every class has a __mro__ attribute holding a tuple of its superclasses in method resolution order from the class itself to object; the MRO is computed by the C3 algorithm and takes into account both the inheritance graph and the order in which superclasses are listed in the subclass declaration.

A method that calls super() is a cooperative method that enables cooperative multiple inheritance; whether each class in the MRO has its implementation activated depends on whether it calls super(), so a non-cooperative method (one that omits the super() call) ends the chain and drops methods further down the MRO, which is why every method m of a non-root class should call super().m(); because resolution follows the actual instance's MRO, the same super() call can reach different classes depending on the subclass's base order.

Cooperative methods that participate in multiple inheritance must have compatible signatures, because you cannot know whether one superclass's method will be called before or after another's; the activation order depends on the order the superclasses are declared in each subclass that inherits from both.

A mixin class is designed to be subclassed together with at least one other class in multiple inheritance: it adds or customizes the behavior of sibling or child classes but does not provide all the functionality of a concrete object, so it should not be the only base class; mixins are a convention with no explicit language support in Python.

A mixin whose methods call super() depends on a sibling class that implements matching methods, so the mixin must appear first in the tuple of base classes in a subclass declaration to come before the cooperating classes in the MRO; otherwise the other base class's methods would be called instead.

A mixin whose methods call super() is brittle, because making it work with different sibling classes can require studying their internal implementations (for example Counter.__init__ uses update, which relies on dict.get, which does not call __getitem__), a stark reminder of how puzzling inheritance-based code can be even at small scale.

ABCs that provide concrete mixin methods play two roles at once, as interface definitions and as mixin classes; for example collections.UserDict relies on mixin methods provided by collections.abc.MutableMapping.

Favor object composition over class inheritance (the second design principle of the Gang of Four): composition yields more flexible designs because subclassing is a form of tight coupling and tall inheritance trees are brittle, so an object should use another object's services via delegation rather than inherit from it; composition and delegation can replace mixins but cannot replace interface inheritance used to define a type hierarchy.

Keep straight why you subclass in each case: inheritance of interface creates a subtype (an is-a relationship, best expressed with ABCs), while inheritance of implementation avoids code duplication (best done with mixins or replaced by composition); interface inheritance is the backbone of a framework, whereas implementation inheritance is an implementation detail often replaceable by composition and delegation.

In modern Python, a class intended to define an interface should be an explicit ABC or a typing.Protocol subclass, and an ABC should subclass only abc.ABC or other ABCs (multiple inheritance of ABCs is not problematic).

If a class exists to provide method implementations for reuse by unrelated subclasses without implying an is-a relationship, make it an explicit mixin class: a mixin does not define a new type, should never be instantiated, should not be a concrete class's only base, should provide a single specific behavior with few closely related methods, should keep no internal state (no instance attributes), and should be named with a Mixin suffix.

Provide aggregate classes to users: when a combination of ABCs or mixins is particularly useful, supply a class (often with an empty body, adding no structure of its own) that brings them together sensibly, as Django's ListView and tkinter.Widget do, so clients need not figure out the correct base-class order themselves.

Subclass only classes designed for subclassing: overriding the methods of a complex class is error-prone because the superclass methods may ignore the overrides, so subclass and override only classes documented or designed to be extended and only in the intended ways; since Python 3.8 the @final decorator (PEP 591) lets type checkers flag misguided attempts to subclass a class or override a method.

Avoid subclassing concrete classes, which is more dangerous than subclassing ABCs or mixins because a concrete instance's internal state can be corrupted when you override methods that depend on it (Scott Meyer's rule: all non-leaf classes should be abstract); if you must subclass for code reuse, put the reusable code in the mixin methods of an ABC or in an explicitly named mixin class.

Rejecting inheritance even single inheritance is a modern trend (Go has no class or inheritance, only struct composition and structural-typing interfaces), so the best advice is to avoid inheritance when you can, although the frameworks you use often impose their own design choices.

For reading clarity, properly-done composition is superior to inheritance, and since code is read far more often than written you should avoid subclassing in general, not mix the various types of inheritance, and not use subclassing for code sharing; more often than not, a function is all you need.

Application developers (as opposed to framework authors) almost always write leaf classes (leaves of the inheritance tree) and rarely need a class to serve as the superclass of another; if while writing an application you find yourself building multilevel class hierarchies, you are likely reinventing the wheel, using a badly designed framework, or overengineering against the KISS principle.

The @typing.overload decorator annotates the different combinations of arguments a function accepts, which is especially important when the return type depends on the types of two or more parameters; write the overloaded signatures (with ... as the body) before the actual implementation (whose signature carries no type hints), and the checker matches the call against each overload in order. Stub (.pyi) files are valid Python because ... satisfies the syntactic need for a body.

Do not aim for 100% annotated code: it can add lots of noise with little value, and refactoring to simplify type hints can produce cumbersome APIs; flexible Pythonic functions are hard to annotate (the max built-in needs six overloads), so it is sometimes better to leave a piece of code without type hints, since the expressiveness of annotations is limited compared to Python itself.

Use a unique sentinel object (for example MISSING = object()) as a parameter's default value so the function can distinguish between the argument not being provided and the argument being provided as None.

typing.TypedDict annotates a dict used as a record, where keys are field names and values have different types per key (which ordinary mapping types cannot express since they force one value type); however it is tempting but wrong to use TypedDict to validate dynamic JSON, because correct handling of JSON-like data must be done at runtime (for example with the pydantic package), which exposes the limits of static typing for dynamic structures.

typing.TypedDict exists only for the benefit of type checkers and has no runtime effect: its constructor is a placebo equivalent to calling dict(), so the fields do not become instance attributes, you cannot give them defaults or define methods, and the result is a plain dict accessed with [] rather than dotted attributes, while letting Mypy catch type mismatches and the use of undefined or deleted keys.

Without a type checker, a TypedDict is as useful as comments, in contrast to the data class builders, which are useful even without a checker because at runtime they generate or enhance a real instantiable class with useful methods.

TypedDict provides no runtime type safety for dynamically structured data such as JSON: a from_json function declared to return a BookDict passes the type checker because json.loads returns Any (consistent-with every type), yet at runtime the value may not even be a dict, and a function accepting a BookDict will process garbage with no error, so TypedDict is not a replacement for runtime data validation (use a tool like pydantic).

typing.cast(type, value) does absolutely nothing at runtime (it returns the value unchanged) but tells the type checker to blindly believe the stated type; it is used to silence spurious type checker warnings or to work around incorrect type hints in code you cannot fix.

Do not get too comfortable using cast to silence the type checker, because the checker is usually right and frequent casts are a code smell signaling misused type hints or low-quality dependencies; yet banning cast outright is unwise because the alternatives are worse, since a # type: ignore comment is less informative and Any is contagious and can undermine the checker's ability to detect errors elsewhere.

Python evaluates type annotations at import time (like parameter default values) and stores them as a dict in the __annotations__ attribute (with a 'return' key for the return type), so the stored values are actual class objects; a type hint that refers to a class defined later, including a method returning a new object of its own class, must be written as a string forward reference.

To read type hints at runtime, use typing.get_type_hints() (or inspect.get_annotations() since Python 3.10) rather than reading __annotations__ directly, because those functions resolve forward references encoded as string literals by evaluating them in the appropriate namespaces.

Adding from __future__ import annotations (PEP 563, available since Python 3.7) stores all annotations as plain strings instead of evaluating them at definition time, which reduces import-time cost and removes the need to quote forward references; however get_type_hints has limits (it cannot resolve types defined in non-global contexts such as inner classes), so reading type hints at runtime is not 100% reliable.

When you must read annotations at runtime, avoid reading __annotations__ directly (use inspect.get_annotations or typing.get_type_hints) and wrap that call in a single custom function that the rest of your codebase calls, so future changes to how annotations are read are localized to one place.

Define a generic class by subclassing typing.Generic[T] (often through multiple inheritance alongside another base class), which declares the formal type parameter T so that parameterizing the class (for example LottoBlower[int]) turns Iterable[T] into Iterable[int] in its methods and lets the type checker flag values that violate the parameterized type.

Generics terminology: a generic type is declared with one or more type variables (LottoBlower[T], Mapping[KT, VT]); the formal type parameters are the type variables in that declaration (KT, VT); a parameterized type is declared with actual type parameters (Mapping[str, float]); and the actual type parameters are the concrete types supplied (the int in LottoBlower[int]).

A generic type is invariant when there is no supertype or subtype relationship between two parameterized versions regardless of the relationship between the actual parameters (so L[A] is neither a supertype nor subtype of L[B]); Python's mutable collections such as list and set are invariant by default, and any type parameter that appears in both a method's arguments and its return type must be invariant for type safety.

A generic type is covariant (declared with TypeVar(name, covariant=True), conventionally suffixed _co) when, given A is a supertype of B, C[A] is a supertype of C[B], so the parameterized types follow the subtype direction of the parameters; immutable containers like frozenset, output-only iterators, Callable return types, and a static protocol whose only parameter appears in a return type can all be covariant.

A generic type is contravariant (declared with TypeVar(name, contravariant=True), conventionally suffixed _contra) when, given A is a supertype of B, K[A] is a subtype of K[B], reversing the subtype direction of the parameters; a contravariant container is a write-only sink, and the parameter types of Callable are contravariant.

Rules of thumb for variance: a formal type parameter for data that comes out of the object can be covariant, one for data that goes into the object after construction can be contravariant, and one used for data both coming out and going in must be invariant; to be safe, make formal type parameters invariant (which is the TypeVar default), and note that variance mostly matters to library authors, so supporting only invariant containers avoids much complexity.

Languages like Kotlin and C# declare variance on the class with out (covariant, an output type) and in (contravariant, an input type) modifiers, which makes the variance rules of thumb easy to recall; a clearer Python naming convention for variant type variables follows the same idea: T_out = TypeVar('T_out', covariant=True) and T_in = TypeVar('T_in', contravariant=True).

Using a type checker sometimes forces you to discover and import undocumented implementation-detail classes (such as asyncio.trsock.TransportSocket) solely to write a type hint; in application code, appending a # type: ignore comment to the offending line is sometimes the only cost-effective solution.

Operator overloading is necessary to support infix operator notation with user-defined or extension types (such as NumPy arrays or decimal.Decimal); because Python's infix operators work with arbitrary types, formulas stay readable (unlike Java, where switching to BigDecimal forces method-call notation), which was a key reason for Python's success in data science and financial and scientific computing, and although overloading can be abused it leads to pleasurable, readable APIs when used well.

Python limits operator overloading for safety: you cannot change the meaning of operators for the built-in types, you cannot create new operators (only overload existing ones), and a few operators (is, and, or, not) cannot be overloaded, although the bitwise operators &, |, and ~ can.

Support unary operators by implementing the matching special method (__neg__ for -, __pos__ for +, __invert__ for ~, __abs__ for abs()), each taking only self; always return a new object rather than modifying self, returning self for unary + when the receiver is immutable (otherwise a copy) and a scalar number for abs().

x == +x holds almost always, but not always: a decimal.Decimal value can differ from +x when +x is evaluated under a different arithmetic-context precision than x was computed in, and collections.Counter's unary + produces a new Counter that drops any item with a zero or negative tally.

Special methods implementing unary or infix operators must never change the value of their operands; they should produce results by creating and returning new objects, and only the augmented assignment operators are allowed to change the first operand (self).

For an infix expression like a + b, Python dispatches by first trying a.__add__(b), and if a has no __add__ or it returns NotImplemented, trying the reversed method b.__radd__(a), raising TypeError only if both fail; a reversed method like __radd__ can often simply delegate to __add__ (valid for commutative operators).

When an operator special method cannot handle an operand because of type incompatibility, it should return the NotImplemented singleton (not raise TypeError, which would abort the dispatch), so the interpreter can try the other operand's reversed method; in the spirit of duck typing, catch the TypeError from the attempted operation and return NotImplemented rather than type-checking the operand. NotImplemented (a value to return) is distinct from NotImplementedError (an exception abstract stub methods raise).

Implement scalar __mul__ and __rmul__ with duck typing rather than an explicit isinstance check: attempt to convert the operand (for example float(scalar)) and return NotImplemented if the conversion fails, which lets the operation accept int, bool, and Fraction while rejecting incompatible types.

The @ infix operator for matrix multiplication (PEP 465, since Python 3.5) is supported by __matmul__, __rmatmul__, and __imatmul__; implementing it with goose typing (checking that the operand isinstance of abc.Sized and abc.Iterable, which both work via __subclasshook__) lets it accept any object providing __len__ and __iter__ rather than only your own type.

Each arithmetic and bitwise infix operator has three special-method forms: a forward method (such as __add__), a reverse method (__radd__), and an in-place method for augmented assignment (__iadd__); the set spans +, -, *, /, //, %, divmod, **, @, &, |, ^, <<, and >>.

Rich comparison operators differ from arithmetic ones: the same method serves forward and reverse calls (a == b calls a.__eq__(b) then b.__eq__(a); a > b calls a.__gt__(b) then the reversed b.__lt__(a)), and for == and != Python falls back to comparing object identities instead of raising TypeError when the reverse method is missing or returns NotImplemented; you need not implement __ne__ because the inherited __ne__ negates the __eq__ result.

Be conservative when overloading __eq__ across types, because in the face of ambiguity you should refuse the temptation to guess and excessive liberality in evaluating operands surprises programmers; type-check the other operand (for example isinstance(other, Vector)) and return NotImplemented otherwise, mirroring the fact that in Python [1, 2] == (1, 2) is False.

If a class does not implement the in-place operator methods, augmented assignment is syntactic sugar where a += b is evaluated exactly as a = a + b, creating a new object and rebinding the left variable; this is correct for immutable types, so implementing __add__ alone makes += work without extra code.

Implement an in-place operator such as __iadd__ for a mutable type to change the left operand in place; such augmented-assignment special methods must return self (what users expect), and in-place special methods should never be implemented for immutable types.

The += operator can be more liberal than + with respect to the right operand: + usually requires both operands to be the same type to avoid confusion about the result type, whereas += updates the left object in place so the right operand may be any iterable, mirroring how list supports my_list + x (list only) versus my_list += x (any iterable, like list.extend).

If a forward infix operator method (such as __mul__) is designed to work only with operands of the same type as self, it is useless to implement the corresponding reverse method (such as __rmul__), because the reverse method is only invoked when the operand is of a different type; also, error messages should explicitly guide the user to the solution.

When overloading operators, duck typing (just attempt the operation and catch a TypeError) is more flexible while an explicit isinstance check is more predictable; libraries should generally leverage duck typing, but because operator dispatch combined with duck typing can produce misleading errors, goose typing (isinstance checks against ABCs) is often a good compromise between flexibility and safety in operator special methods.

The functools.total_ordering class decorator automatically generates all the rich comparison methods for a class that defines at least __eq__ and one ordering operator, saving you from writing them by hand.

Generator expressions are evaluated lazily, at the latest possible moment rather than where they appear in the source, so passing a genexp to a constructor defers evaluation until the consumer iterates it (an error then surfaces inside the consumer's traceback), whereas a list comprehension builds its list immediately at the point of definition.

Iteration is fundamental to data processing, and an iterator fetches items lazily, one at a time on demand, so data need not fit in memory; the Iterator design pattern is built into the Python language (you never code it by hand), and every standard collection is iterable, supporting for loops, comprehensions, unpacking assignments, and collection construction.

Whenever Python iterates over an object x it automatically calls iter(x), which first checks for __iter__ and calls it to obtain an iterator, otherwise (if __getitem__ exists) creates an iterator that fetches items by index starting from 0 and treats IndexError as the end, and otherwise raises TypeError saying the object is not iterable; this is why all sequences are iterable, since they implement __getitem__.

An object is iterable if it implements __iter__ or merely __getitem__ (an extreme form of duck typing), but isinstance(x, abc.Iterable) recognizes only __iter__ and not the legacy __getitem__, so the most accurate iterability test as of Python 3.10 is to call iter(x) and handle a TypeError; do not bother pre-checking iterability if you are about to iterate immediately, since the TypeError from iterating is already clear.

The two-argument form iter(callable, sentinel) creates an iterator that invokes the callable with no arguments repeatedly and raises StopIteration when the callable returns the sentinel value, which is useful for building things like a fixed-block file reader (for example iter(functools.partial(f.read, 64), b'')).

Python obtains iterators from iterables: an iterable is any object the iter built-in can get an iterator from (it implements __iter__ returning an iterator, or __getitem__), while an iterator is exhausted after a single pass and cannot be reset, so to iterate again you must call iter() on the original iterable, not on the iterator (whose __iter__ returns itself).

Python's iterator interface has two methods: __next__ returns the next item and raises StopIteration when exhausted, and __iter__ returns self so an iterator can be used where an iterable is expected; StopIteration is handled internally by for loops, comprehensions, and unpacking, the most accurate way to test for an iterator is isinstance(x, abc.Iterator), and you should call next(it) rather than it.__next__() directly.

Do not make an iterable be an iterator for itself (do not add __next__ to a collection class), because an iterable's __iter__ should instantiate a new, independent iterator with its own state on every call to support multiple simultaneous traversals; iterators are iterable but iterables are not iterators, and conflating the two is a common antipattern.

The Pythonic way to implement __iter__ is a generator function (a function with the yield keyword), which avoids writing a separate iterator class and its state bookkeeping; a generator function is a generator factory, returning a generator object (that implements the Iterator interface) when called, and the only syntactic difference from a plain function is the presence of yield.

When you call next() on a generator object, execution advances to the next yield and suspends there with the call evaluating to the yielded value, and when the function body returns the generator raises StopIteration; speak precisely, since a function returns values whereas a generator yields them, and a return statement inside a generator causes StopIteration (its value retrievable from the exception, usually via yield from).

Laziness is a desirable trait: a lazy implementation postpones producing values to the last possible moment, saving memory and possibly CPU cycles; for example re.finditer is a lazy generator yielding matches on demand whereas re.findall eagerly builds a whole list, and the Iterator interface is inherently lazy because next() yields one item at a time.

A generator expression builds a generator object lazily, just as a list comprehension builds a list eagerly, and is syntactic sugar that can always be replaced by a generator function; prefer a generator function when the expression spans more than a couple of lines for readability, and prefer a generator expression over a list comprehension to avoid storing an intermediate list.

An iterator is any object that implements __next__ and produces data for consuming client code, while a generator is an iterator built by the Python compiler: you create one not by implementing __next__ but with the yield keyword (a generator function being a factory of generator objects) or with a generator expression; generator objects provide __next__ so they are iterators, and in practice most iterators used in Python are generators.

When generating a numeric series, avoid the cumulative effect of floating-point errors by computing each term from a fixed base (for example begin + step*index) instead of repeatedly adding step to the previous result.

If the whole point of a class is to build a generator by implementing __iter__, replace the class with a generator function, which is itself a generator factory and needs less code; note that a function returning a generator (for example one that returns itertools.count) is not a generator function (it has no yield) but it returns a generator just as a generator function does.

Know what generator functions the standard library offers before implementing your own or you will reinvent the wheel: itertools has about twenty combinable generator functions, including count (which yields an unbounded series, so never call list() on it) and takewhile (which consumes another generator and stops when a predicate becomes falsy), and os.walk yields filenames while traversing a directory tree so a recursive filesystem search is just a for loop.

Standard-library generator functions group into categories: filtering generators (itertools compress, dropwhile, filterfalse, islice, takewhile, and the built-in filter) yield a subset of the input, most taking a one-argument predicate; mapping generators (itertools accumulate, starmap, and the built-in enumerate, map) yield one computed result per input item and stop when the shortest input iterable is exhausted; and merging generators yield from multiple inputs, with chain and chain.from_iterable consuming them sequentially while product, zip, and zip_longest consume them in parallel.

itertools combinatoric generators expand each input item into multiple outputs: product yields the Cartesian product (with repeat=N consuming each input N times), combinations yields fixed-length subsets where order is irrelevant, combinations_with_replacement allows repeated items, and permutations yields fixed-length arrangements where order matters; because these generator functions take generators and return generators, they can be freely combined.

itertools.count, cycle, and repeat are unbounded generators that conjure items from nothing, so you must limit them with islice or takewhile before building a list, or attempting list() on them will exhaust memory.

itertools.groupby assumes the input iterable is sorted by (or at least clustered by) the grouping criterion and yields (key, group-generator) tuples; the reversed built-in yields a sequence's items from last to first and requires a sequence or __reversed__ rather than an arbitrary iterable; and itertools.tee yields n independent generators that each replay every item of the input.

Reducing (folding) functions such as all, any, max, min, sum, and functools.reduce take an iterable and return a single value; all and any short-circuit, stopping as soon as the result is determined (an optimization reduce lacks), all([]) is True while any([]) is False, math.fsum gives better precision when summing floats, and sorted (unlike reversed) reads all items and returns a new list, so these functions only work on iterables that eventually stop.

yield from (Python 3.3) lets a generator delegate to a subgenerator: it pauses the delegating generator and the subgenerator takes over, its yielded values passing directly through to the client while the delegating generator is suspended, and the subgenerator's return value is captured with result = yield from sub(); a recursive generator using yield from can traverse a tree to any depth bounded by the recursion limit, and like all recursion it needs a base case (a branch that returns without recursing) to avoid infinite recursion.

Annotate a function's iterable parameters with collections.abc.Iterable[T] and a generator or iterator return value with Iterator[T] (used for both generator functions with yield and hand-written __next__ iterators); Iterator[T] is a shortcut for Generator[T, None, None], meaning a generator that yields items of type T but does not consume or return values.

A generator can be used as an iterator (it only yields) or as a coroutine (a generator function with yield used to consume and optionally return values); annotate a coroutine as Generator[YieldType, SendType, ReturnType], where SendType is the type of x in gen.send(x) and ReturnType apply only to coroutines (it is an error to call .send() on a generator coded as an iterator), and where YieldType and ReturnType are covariant while SendType is contravariant.

Keep generators and coroutines straight (per David Beazley): generators produce data for iteration, coroutines are consumers of data, coroutines are not related to iteration, and you should not mix the two concepts together.

A classic coroutine can keep its context in local variables between activations without needing instance attributes or closures, which makes coroutines attractive replacements for callbacks in asynchronous programming because they retain local state across suspensions.

Prime a classic coroutine by calling next(coro) or coro.send(None) to advance it to the first yield (you cannot send any non-None value until it is suspended at a yield); a subsequent .send(value) resolves the yield expression to value, runs to the next yield, and suspends again; .close() raises GeneratorExit at the suspended yield to terminate it, and calling .send() on a closed coroutine raises StopIteration.

A classic coroutine returns a value via a return statement whose value is smuggled out wrapped in the StopIteration exception (accessible as StopIteration.value); a delegating generator can obtain that return value directly with res = yield from subcoroutine().

Driving classic coroutines by hand with .send() and .throw() is cumbersome and confusing, so do it only when building a coroutine-based framework; productive coroutine work requires a framework such as asyncio, and native coroutines (declared with async def since Python 3.5) use await instead of yield from to delegate, with yield from being the direct precursor of await.

The Iterator design pattern is built into the semantics of Python, so a classic Iterator implemented by hand has no practical use except as a didactic example, illustrating that design patterns are not equally applicable in all programming languages.

Isolate distinct reading logic into separate generator functions (one per input format), each yielding records one by one, to decouple reading from writing and process datasets larger than memory as a stream; adding support for a new input format then only requires adding another generator function, without changing the writing logic.

The with statement sets up a temporary context and reliably tears it down under the control of a context manager object, simplifying common uses of try/finally by guaranteeing cleanup even when the block ends via return, an exception, or sys.exit; it is used well beyond automatic file closing, for example managing database transactions, acquiring and releasing locks, setting Decimal arithmetic contexts, and patching objects for testing.

The context manager interface consists of __enter__ and __exit__: Python calls __enter__ at the top of the with statement and calls __exit__ when the with block completes or terminates for any reason, just as iterators exist to control the for statement.

The context manager is the object produced by the expression after with, but the value bound by the as clause is whatever the context manager's __enter__ method returns (often self, but possibly a different object); __exit__ is always invoked on the context manager itself, not on the object returned by __enter__; a with block does not create a new scope, and the as clause is optional because some context managers return None.

__exit__ receives three arguments (exc_type, exc_value, traceback) which are all None if the with block completed without an exception; returning a truthy value from __exit__ tells the interpreter the exception was handled and suppresses it, while returning None or any falsy value lets the exception propagate. Since Python 3.10 multiple context managers can be grouped in a single parenthesized with statement.

Check the contextlib module before writing your own context manager class, because it offers ready-made utilities: redirect_stdout/redirect_stderr, closing (wrap an object that has close() but not __enter__/__exit__), suppress (ignore given exceptions), nullcontext (a do-nothing context manager for conditional logic), @contextmanager (build a context manager from a generator function), ContextDecorator (a context manager usable also as a function decorator), and ExitStack (enter a variable number of context managers, exited in LIFO order).

Use the @contextlib.contextmanager decorator to build a context manager from a generator with a single yield instead of writing a class with __enter__/__exit__: everything before the yield runs when __enter__ is called and the yielded value is bound to the as clause, and everything after the yield runs when __exit__ is called; such a decorated generator can also be used directly as a function decorator.

In a @contextmanager generator, wrap the yield in a try/finally (or with) block, because an exception raised in the with body is re-raised at the yield line inside the generator; without handling it, the code after yield never runs and cleanup is skipped, leaving the system in an invalid state. Note that @contextmanager inverts the class-based default: its provided __exit__ assumes any exception sent into the generator was handled and should be suppressed.

collections.ChainMap models nested scopes by holding a list of mappings: reading a key searches the mappings from left to right so an inner mapping shadows an outer one, while assignment with [] always writes to the first mapping; subclass ChainMap to add a method that updates an existing key in-place wherever it is defined (as needed to implement an assignment form like Scheme's set!).

A single match statement with one case clause per language form expresses an interpreter's syntax and semantics with clarity, which makes match/case an effective tool for building language processors such as an expression evaluator.

A closure is a function together with the environment captured where it was defined, which supplies the free variables (names used in the body that are not parameters, local variables, or globals) when the function is later called; because an assignment inside a function creates a local variable by default, updating a variable from an enclosing scope held in a closure requires Python's nonlocal declaration (the analogue of Scheme's set!) — without nonlocal, an assignment like x = 10 always creates a new local variable.

In a match statement, a series of subpatterns separated by | forms an OR-pattern that succeeds if any subpattern matches; all subpatterns in an OR-pattern must bind the same variables so the guard and case body can use them, and within a case clause the | operator does not invoke the __or__ special method (it carries no set-union or bitwise-or meaning); | may also be nested inside subpatterns.

The else clause applies to for, while, and try statements, not only if, with a then semantics rather than an otherwise semantics: for/else runs only if the loop completes without hitting break, while/else runs only if the loop exits because the condition became falsy (not via break), and try/else runs only if the try block raised no exception (and exceptions in the else clause are not caught by the preceding except clauses); in every case the else is skipped if break, return, continue, or an exception jumps out of the block.

Keep a try block's body limited to only the statements that may raise the expected exception, and move follow-up code that should run only on success into an else clause; this makes explicit which call is being guarded against errors and that the else code runs only when no exception was raised in the try block.

Prefer the EAFP style (easier to ask forgiveness than permission) idiomatic to Python — assume keys or attributes exist and catch exceptions if the assumption proves false, giving clean and fast code characterized by many try/except statements — over the LBYL style (look before you leap), which explicitly tests preconditions with many if statements and can introduce a race condition between the check and the use in a multithreaded environment (solvable with locks or by switching to EAFP).

The with statement is not only for resource management such as closing files: it factors out a matched pair of setup and teardown operations around an arbitrary procedure, making it the complement of the subroutine (factoring out the surrounding code rather than the inner block).

Python does not implement proper tail calls (PTC), so writing a function in tail-recursive form provides no efficiency benefit in Python; a tail call is one where a function returns the result of a call directly (so n * factorial(n - 1) is not a tail call because the result is multiplied before returning), and for factorials prefer the C-implemented, non-recursive math.factorial.

The lack of proper tail calls is the main restriction on writing Python in a functional style (more so than the limited lambda syntax); a typical Python implementation allows about 1000 levels of recursion, which is plenty for non-recursive code and for traversing a typical parse tree but not enough for a recursively written loop over a large list.

Concurrency is the ability to handle multiple pending tasks, making progress one at a time or in parallel so each eventually succeeds or fails (a single-core CPU with an OS scheduler is concurrent), whereas parallelism is executing multiple computations at the same instant and requires multiple cores, CPUs, a GPU, or a cluster; parallelism is a special case of concurrency (all parallel systems are concurrent but not vice versa), and most real-world computing is concurrent rather than parallel.

Python natively supports three kinds of execution unit: processes (isolated in private memory, so passing Python objects between them requires serializing to raw bytes over pipes/sockets/mmap, which is costly and impossible for non-serializable objects), threads (multiple within one process sharing the same memory, so data sharing is easy but concurrent updates to the same object can corrupt data, and a thread is lighter than a process), and coroutines (functions that suspend and resume, running in a single thread under an event loop and consuming the least resources of the three).

Processes and threads use preemptive multitasking (the OS scheduler periodically suspends each one so a frozen task cannot freeze the whole system), whereas coroutines use cooperative multitasking in which each coroutine must explicitly cede control with yield or await; consequently any blocking code inside a coroutine blocks the event loop and every other coroutine, so blocking calls must be kept out of coroutine bodies.

Access to object reference counts and other internal interpreter state in CPython is guarded by the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), and only one thread can hold the GIL at a time, so only one Python thread executes bytecode at any instant regardless of the number of CPU cores; the interpreter releases the GIL about every 5ms, and every standard-library function that makes a syscall (disk I/O, network I/O, time.sleep) releases it, as do some C extensions such as NumPy/SciPy compute functions and the zlib and bz2 modules.

Because contention over the GIL slows compute-intensive Python threads, use simpler and faster sequential single-threaded code for CPU-bound work and run multiple Python processes (multiprocessing or concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor) to use multiple cores; threading remains appropriate for I/O-bound tasks because I/O releases the GIL (David Beazley: Python threads are great at doing nothing), and note the GIL is a CPython implementation detail not part of the language (Jython and IronPython have none).

Python has no API to terminate a thread; you must send it a message to shut down, for which threading.Event is the simplest signalling mechanism — its internal boolean flag starts False, another thread calls Event.set() to flip it True, and Event.wait(timeout) blocks until the flag is set (returning True) or returns False when the timeout elapses; a typical supervisor starts the worker thread, runs the blocking work, then calls Event.set() and join() to let the worker notice and exit cleanly.

The multiprocessing package emulates the threading API (Process mirrors Thread) so simple thread programs convert easily to processes, and because each process has its own GIL this can use all CPU cores; but processes are OS-isolated, so objects crossing the boundary must be serialized and deserialized at a cost, and the multiprocessing.shared_memory ShareableList (Python 3.8+) can share only a fixed number of primitive items (int, float, bool, None, and str/bytes up to 10 MB each), not instances of user-defined classes.

There are three main ways to run a coroutine: asyncio.run(coro()) is called from a regular function to drive the entry-point coroutine and blocks until it returns (yielding its return value); asyncio.create_task(coro()) is called from a coroutine to schedule another to run eventually without suspending the caller, returning a Task that is already scheduled; and await coro() is called from a coroutine to transfer control and suspend the caller until coro returns. Merely calling coro() returns a coroutine object and does not run its body — driving coroutine bodies is the job of the single-threaded event loop, so time spent in any coroutine slows the loop and all others.

Never use time.sleep() inside an asyncio coroutine, because it blocks the single thread running the event loop and therefore pauses the whole program; when a coroutine needs to do nothing for a while, use await asyncio.sleep(DELAY), which yields control back to the event loop so it can drive other pending coroutines.

An asyncio.Task is roughly the asynchronous equivalent of a threading.Thread, but a Task drives a coroutine object while a Thread invokes a callable, a Task is already scheduled to run when asyncio.create_task returns whereas a Thread must be explicitly started with .start(), and a coroutine cedes control explicitly with await; to stop a Task, call Task.cancel(), which raises CancelledError inside the coroutine at the await expression where it is currently suspended.

Coroutines are synchronized by definition — only one runs at any moment and code is protected from interruption unless it explicitly awaits — so unlike threads (where the scheduler can interrupt at any time, forcing you to hold locks around critical multistep sections to avoid leaving data invalid) you do not need locks; and a coroutine can be safely cancelled precisely because it can only be suspended at an await, where cleanup can be performed by handling the CancelledError exception.

For I/O-bound work a well-designed library keeps concurrency alive because it releases the GIL (threads) or yields to the event loop (asyncio) while waiting on the network; but a CPU-intensive call behaves very differently — in an asyncio coroutine it freezes the program entirely because control never returns to the event loop, whereas under threading the default 5ms GIL switch interval lets a low-frequency secondary thread keep running, though two or more CPU-hungry threads make the program slower than sequential code.

Periodically calling await asyncio.sleep(0) inside a long CPU-bound coroutine yields control to the event loop to keep other coroutines responsive, but it slows that coroutine and the whole program, so treat it only as a stopgap before refactoring to delegate the CPU-intensive computation to another process — for example via asyncio.loop.run_in_executor or a distributed task queue.

When you delegate work to threads or processes you cannot call the worker directly and read a return value, because the worker is driven by the library and its result must be stored somewhere; the common pattern is to use queues to feed jobs to workers and collect results, terminating each worker with a poison pill (a sentinel value such as 0 enqueued once per worker so each worker's loop exits when it pulls the sentinel), and to size the worker pool with multiprocessing.cpu_count() — noting that count includes hyperthreads, so CPU-bound speedup tracks the number of physical cores rather than the reported count.

A common concurrent pattern is a worker that loops indefinitely pulling items from a queue and processing each, ending when it pulls a sentinel value (a poison pill); None is commonly used but is unsuitable if None can occur in the data stream, and object() yields a unique sentinel but does not survive inter-process serialization (a pickled-then-unpickled object() instance no longer compares equal to the original) — so for cross-process use prefer the Ellipsis built-in (...), which survives serialization with its identity intact.

Calling .get() on a queue blocks until an item is available (it can also be made nonblocking or given a timeout); because results from concurrent workers do not come back in the same order the jobs were submitted, include an identifying key (such as the original input value) in each result so you can match each result to its job.

A race condition is a bug that may or may not occur depending on the order of actions performed by concurrent execution units (fine if A happens before B, broken if B happens first); concurrent code is always hard to debug, and multiprocessing is even harder to debug because of the complexity behind its thread-like façade.

Using threading for CPU-intensive work is a non-solution in CPython: due to the GIL it is slower than sequential code and gets slower as the number of threads increases, because of GIL contention plus the cost of context switching (saving CPU registers, updating the program counter and stack pointer, invalidating CPU caches, possibly swapping memory pages); only multiple processes let Python benefit from multicore CPUs for heavy computation.

Since CPU clock speeds plateaued around 2004 (the free lunch is over), performance gains require concurrent code leveraging multiple cores or hyperthreading; but do not overestimate the GIL's impact, because many domains work around it — system administration is largely I/O-bound and suits threads or coroutines, data science offloads compute to C/C++/Fortran/Cython libraries that leverage cores, GPUs, and clusters, and C extensions need not touch the GIL at all — so the GIL chiefly limits CPU-bound pure-Python code, for which the remedy is multiple processes.

WSGI is the standard synchronous API by which a Python framework or application receives HTTP requests and returns responses, and WSGI application servers (mod_wsgi, uWSGI, Gunicorn, NGINX Unit) fork multiple Python processes to use all CPU cores — which is why traditional sequential Django/Flask/Pyramid code can scale with the application server handling concurrency transparently; ASGI is the asynchronous successor to WSGI, supporting async/await (required for WebSockets and HTTP long polling) and used by frameworks such as aiohttp, Sanic, and FastAPI.

Offload request work that takes too long (such as sending email or generating a PDF) to a distributed task queue such as Celery or RQ, which wraps a message queue: producers put job requests into the queue and decoupled consumers (workers, possibly on other machines) process them, so the web process stays free to answer the next request quickly and you scale horizontally simply by adding more workers as demand grows.

Constraints make code easier to reason about (structured programming, object-oriented information hiding, and functional immutability are each constraints that prove to be blessings), and the greatest weakness of the threads-and-locks concurrency model is its lack of constraints: threads can share arbitrary mutable data structures, the scheduler can interrupt a thread at almost any point because very few source-level operations (even a += 1) are atomic, and locks are merely advisory so nothing stops code that forgot to acquire the lock from corrupting data another thread is updating.

The actor model enforces constraints that make managing locks unnecessary: an actor can hold internal state but cannot share state with other actors, actors communicate only by sending and receiving messages, those messages carry copies of data rather than references to mutable data, and an actor handles only one message at a time (no concurrent execution inside a single actor); you can adopt this actor style in any language by agreement and discipline among everyone who touches the code.

A future is an object representing the asynchronous execution of an operation (similar to a JavaScript promise) and is the foundational primitive of both the concurrent.futures and asyncio packages; the concurrent.futures.Executor classes (ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor) encapsulate the common pattern of spawning a number of independent workers and collecting their results in a queue, making it almost trivial to use with threads and also with processes for compute-intensive tasks.

Concurrency is essential for efficient network I/O — rather than idly waiting for remote machines, the application should do other work until responses arrive — and whether you use threads or coroutines you get vastly improved throughput over sequential code (often 5x or more, scaling to 20x or more for hundreds of downloads); for HTTP clients that control how many requests they make there is no significant performance difference between threads and coroutines, though coroutines scale better on the server side because they use much less memory than threads and reduce context-switching cost.

Follow these HTTP-client practices: add a sensible timeout to network operations to avoid blocking for several minutes for no good reason; call resp.raise_for_status() (or equivalent) so a non-2XX HTTP status raises an exception instead of failing silently; pass flush=True to print for progressive output because Python output is line-buffered by default; and prefer the HTTPX library (which offers both synchronous and asynchronous APIs) over the synchronous-only, less user-friendly urllib.request.

When testing concurrent HTTP clients against public web servers you may inadvertently launch a denial-of-service (DoS) attack or be suspected of doing so, so bound the number of requests the test makes or run it against a local server (for example Python's http.server package).
