concurrent.futures provides ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor that transparently manage a pool of workers plus the queues to distribute jobs and collect results; the simplest concurrent pattern is to use the executor as a context manager (its __exit__ calls shutdown(wait=True), blocking until all workers finish) and call executor.map(fn, iterable), which behaves like the map built-in but runs fn concurrently across workers and returns a generator of results — a common refactoring being to turn the body of a sequential for loop into a function to be called concurrently.

Since Python 3.8 ThreadPoolExecutor's max_workers defaults to min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4), which preserves at least 5 workers for I/O-bound tasks, uses at most 32 cores for CPU-bound tasks that release the GIL, and avoids implicitly consuming huge resources on many-core machines (it also reuses idle worker threads before starting new ones); ProcessPoolExecutor instead defaults max_workers to os.cpu_count().

A Future represents a deferred computation that may or may not have completed (similar to a JavaScript Promise), and application code should not create or change the state of futures — the concurrency framework instantiates them (for example Executor.submit(callable) schedules the callable and returns a Future) and updates their state when the work is done; .done() nonblockingly returns whether the callable has run, .add_done_callback(fn) invokes fn (in the same worker thread or process) when the future completes, and .result() returns the result or re-raises the callable's exception — on a concurrent.futures.Future it blocks until ready (with an optional timeout that raises TimeoutError), whereas asyncio.Future.result has no timeout and you use await instead (await does not work with concurrent.futures.Future).

To process results as they become ready rather than in submission order, call executor.submit(fn, arg) to schedule each call (it returns a Future) and iterate futures.as_completed(list_of_futures), which yields each future as it finishes so future.result() will not block; this submit-plus-as_completed combination is more flexible than executor.map because you can submit different callables and arguments and even combine futures from more than one executor, whereas executor.map runs a single callable over many arguments and returns results in the order the arguments were submitted.

Because ProcessPoolExecutor and ThreadPoolExecutor both implement the same Executor interface, switching from a thread-based to a process-based solution is trivial; there is no advantage to ProcessPoolExecutor for I/O-bound work (processes use more memory and take longer to start), so reserve it for CPU-intensive jobs where it enables genuine multicore parallelism, and rewriting a hand-rolled multiprocessing-plus-queue solution with ProcessPoolExecutor is shorter because it hides the queues, worker function, and poison-pill plumbing.

Because testing concurrent HTTP clients can generate many requests per second — which is how denial-of-service attacks are made — carefully throttle clients hitting public servers and prefer a local HTTP server for testing; you can run python3 -m http.server for a basic server, plus purpose-built test servers that inject a random response delay or a configurable error rate to exercise timeout and error-handling paths.

The tqdm function consumes any iterable and produces an iterator that, while being consumed, displays an animated progress bar and estimates the time remaining; to compute that estimate it needs either an iterable with a len() or the total= argument giving the expected number of items, so when wrapping a length-less iterator such as futures.as_completed you must pass total=len(items).

A clean concurrent error-handling strategy is to handle expected per-item errors (such as HTTP 404 not found) inside the function that downloads a single item and let any other exception propagate to the caller (download_many or the supervisor): call resp.raise_for_status() to turn a non-2XX status into an HTTPStatusError, catch that to special-case 404 and re-raise everything else, then at the top level catch HTTPStatusError and RequestError (and break on KeyboardInterrupt) and tally outcomes with a collections.Counter keyed by an Enum status (OK / NOT_FOUND / ERROR) returned for the final report.

A very useful idiom with futures.as_completed is to build a dict mapping each Future to other data you will need when it completes (for example the country code being downloaded); because futures are produced out of order, this lets you recover the associated context for follow-up processing such as error reporting when each future emerges from the as_completed iterator.

Cap the maximum number of concurrent requests with a fixed MAX constant regardless of the workload size or any command-line option, as a safety precaution against launching too many threads with their significant memory overhead, and set the thread pool's max_workers to the smallest of that cap, the number of items to process, and any requested concurrency, so you never create more threads than necessary.

Asynchronous programming tends to be an all-or-nothing proposition: you must rewrite all blocking code to be nonblocking or you are wasting your time; Python's asynchronous constructs are async def, await, async with, and async for, supporting native coroutines and asynchronous variants of context managers, iterables, generators, and comprehensions, and you avoid blocking the single-threaded event loop by delegating slow or blocking operations to a thread or process executor.

A native coroutine is a function defined with async def; it delegates to another native coroutine using await (analogous to how a classic coroutine uses yield from), async def always defines a native coroutine even if its body contains no await, and await cannot be used outside a native coroutine; classic coroutines (generator functions driven by .send() and yield) cannot be driven by await and are no longer supported by asyncio, while an asynchronous generator is an async def function that uses yield, returning an async generator object whose __anext__ coroutine method retrieves the next item.

The common pattern for an asyncio script is to implement main as a coroutine and drive it with asyncio.run(main()) inside the if __name__ == '__main__': block; asyncio.run starts the event loop and returns only when the loop exits, yielding whatever the driven coroutine returns. Inside a coroutine, obtain the loop with asyncio.get_running_loop() (added in 3.7), which raises RuntimeError if no loop is running and is simpler and faster than the now-deprecated asyncio.get_event_loop().

asyncio.as_completed takes an iterable of awaitables and yields them in the order they complete (not the order submitted), similar to concurrent.futures.as_completed; because each yielded item is already done, awaiting it will not block (it just retrieves the result and re-raises any unhandled exception), and because the asynchronous operations are interleaved the total time to complete many tasks is practically the single slowest response rather than the sum of all responses.

To read asynchronous code, use Guido van Rossum's trick of squinting and pretending the async and await keywords are not there — coroutines then read like plain sequential functions that magically never block; mechanically, await suspends the current coroutine object and yields control back to the event loop (not to the coroutine's caller), so the event loop can drive other pending coroutines until the awaited operation responds and resumes this one.

Just as the for keyword works with iterables, the await keyword works with awaitables; the everyday awaitables are native coroutine objects (obtained by calling a native coroutine function) and asyncio.Task objects (obtained by passing a coroutine to asyncio.create_task). Use asyncio.create_task(coro()) to schedule a coroutine for concurrent execution without waiting for its result (you only need to keep the returned Task if you intend to cancel it or await it later), whereas await other_coro() runs the coroutine now and waits for its result because you need it before proceeding.

asyncio.gather accepts one or more awaitable arguments, waits for all of them to complete, and returns a list of their results in the order they were submitted; because it returns only when every awaitable is done, use asyncio.as_completed instead when you need to process results as they finish (for example to update a progress bar).

An asynchronous context manager implements __aenter__ and __aexit__ as coroutine methods and is used with the async with statement, which exists because the classic with statement cannot run coroutines in __enter__/__exit__; making setup and teardown coroutines (for example a database transaction's start plus commit-or-rollback, or an HTTPX AsyncClient) lets the driver perform other operations concurrently while a context is being entered or exited.

For peak asyncio performance you must replace every function that does I/O with an asynchronous version activated by await or asyncio.create_task so control returns to the event loop while it waits; if a blocking function cannot be rewritten as a coroutine, run it in a separate thread or process. In particular asyncio drives network I/O via coroutines but provides no asynchronous filesystem API, so delegate blocking file I/O to a thread with asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) (Python 3.9+) to avoid blocking the event loop.

Throttle network clients to avoid pounding a server with too many concurrent requests; a semaphore is a synchronization primitive more flexible than a lock because it can be held by up to a configurable maximum number of coroutines at once, making it ideal for limiting active concurrent coroutines, and using an asyncio.Semaphore as an asynchronous context manager (async with semaphore) suspends only that one coroutine when the counter reaches zero rather than blocking the whole program.

A semaphore is a flexible synchronization primitive (most other synchronization objects such as locks and barriers can be built on it): an asyncio.Semaphore has an internal counter set at construction, decremented when you await its .acquire() coroutine and incremented by .release() (which is not a coroutine and never blocks); awaiting .acquire() does not delay while the counter is greater than zero but suspends the coroutine when the counter is zero until another coroutine calls .release(), and it is safer to use the semaphore as an asynchronous context manager (its __aenter__ awaits acquire and __aexit__ calls release) so no more than the configured number of coroutines run at once; a BoundedSemaphore additionally forbids the counter from ever exceeding its initial value.

The await keyword lets you drive asynchronous operations one after another while sharing the local scope of the driving coroutine, which eliminates the nested-callback pyramid of doom that callback-style async required (where each callback runs in a different scope, forcing closures to carry data forward); if you are writing modern asynchronous Python application code with lots of callbacks you are probably applying outdated patterns, justified only when interfacing with legacy or low-level code that does not support coroutines.

Hold semaphores and locks for the shortest possible time (put each awaited call in its own async with block rather than wrapping several together); drive dependent requests sequentially with await when a later one is pointless if an earlier one fails, but use asyncio.gather to hit several independent APIs in parallel when there is no dependency between them.

Python is not a block-scoped language: statements such as loops and try/except do not create a local scope in the blocks they manage; however, when an except clause binds an exception to a variable (except SomeError as exc), that binding exists only within that except block, so to use the exception value later you must copy it into a variable declared outside the try/except.

Because file I/O blocks the event loop (reading or writing storage is thousands of times slower than RAM) and asyncio provides no asynchronous filesystem API, delegate blocking file I/O to a thread with asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args) (Python 3.9+, which also accepts keyword arguments) or, on 3.7/3.8, with loop.run_in_executor(None, fn, *args) where passing None selects the event loop's default ThreadPoolExecutor (use functools.partial for keyword arguments); to run a CPU-intensive function instead, pass an explicit ProcessPoolExecutor to run_in_executor so it executes in another process and avoids GIL contention (start that executor in the supervisor because of its high start-up cost).

Coroutines that use run_in_executor give merely the pretense of cancellation, because the underlying thread (with a ThreadPoolExecutor) has no cancellation mechanism; a long-lived thread started inside a run_in_executor call can prevent an asyncio program from shutting down cleanly, since asyncio.run waits for the executor to fully shut down before returning and will wait forever if the executor jobs do not stop on their own.

A common pattern in asynchronous APIs is to wrap blocking implementation-detail calls in coroutines using run_in_executor internally, presenting a consistent await-driven coroutine interface while hiding the threads used for pragmatic reasons (for example the Motor MongoDB driver is an async/await façade around a threaded core); this also disproves the myth that asynchronous approaches are always faster than threads for network I/O, since a thread pool can be more performant in some cases such as a database driver.

FastAPI is an ASGI web framework that leverages decorators, type hints, and code introspection to eliminate web-API boilerplate and automatically publish interactive OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation; its endpoints may be coroutines or plain functions, function parameters that do not appear in the route path are taken from the query string (a required parameter missing from the query string yields HTTP 422), and the response shape is declared with the response_model= keyword in the route decorator rather than a return type annotation, so the function may return a dict, generator, or database object that pydantic then validates and serializes to JSON.

The high-level asyncio Streams API provides a ready-made TCP server: await asyncio.start_server(client_connected_cb, host, port) creates and starts it, and you await server.serve_forever() to keep the driving coroutine suspended there (without that await the coroutine would return and the program would exit); the connection callback runs once per new client and must accept exactly an asyncio.StreamReader and asyncio.StreamWriter, so use functools.partial to bind any extra arguments (adapting user functions to callback APIs is the most common use of functools.partial), and because a fresh handler-coroutine instance runs per connected client, one event loop in a single thread serves many clients concurrently.

In the asyncio Streams API some I/O methods are coroutines that must be awaited and others are plain functions: StreamWriter.write and StreamWriter.writelines write to a buffer and are NOT coroutines, whereas StreamWriter.drain (which flushes the buffer and performs the network I/O), StreamReader.readline, and StreamWriter.wait_closed ARE coroutines and must be driven with await; all network I/O is in bytes, so decode received bytes and encode strings before sending (UTF-8 by default in Python 3), and below Streams there is a lower-level Transports and Protocols API inspired by the Twisted framework.

async for works with asynchronous iterables — objects whose __aiter__ is a regular method (not a coroutine) returning an asynchronous iterator, which provides an __anext__ coroutine method returning an awaitable and usually an __aiter__ returning self — mirroring the synchronous iterable/iterator distinction; implementing something like a database cursor as an asynchronous iterator lets it yield to the event loop at each __anext__ call so iterating a large result set does not block the loop while waiting for more rows.

The simple way to implement an asynchronous iterator is to write a function declared with async def that uses yield in its body, which produces an asynchronous generator object (annotatable as AsyncIterator[SomeType]); you cannot consume it with a regular for loop (that raises TypeError because it implements __aiter__ rather than __iter__) — drive it with async for or an asynchronous comprehension.

Native coroutines and asynchronous generator functions are both declared with async def but differ: an asynchronous generator always contains a yield expression (a native coroutine never does); a native coroutine may return a value other than None whereas an asynchronous generator may only use empty return statements; and native coroutines are awaitable (driven by await or passed to asyncio functions like create_task) while asynchronous generators are not awaitable but are asynchronous iterables driven by async for or asynchronous comprehensions.

To write an asynchronous context manager without a class, use the contextlib.@asynccontextmanager decorator (added in Python 3.7) on an asynchronous generator: code before the single yield becomes the __aenter__ coroutine method (the yielded value binds to the async with ... as target) and code after the yield becomes __aexit__, exactly parallel to @contextmanager; and you can experiment with such code by running python -m asyncio (Python 3.8+), an async REPL with a running event loop that accepts top-level await, async for, and async with, which are otherwise syntax errors outside a native coroutine.

PEP 530 (Python 3.6+) allows async for and await inside comprehensions and generator expressions; an asynchronous generator expression (one using async for) builds an async_generator object and may be defined anywhere in a module, but can only be consumed inside a native coroutine or asynchronous generator function, and the other asynchronous-comprehension constructs can only be both defined and used inside a native coroutine or asynchronous generator function.

PEP 530 allows await and async for inside list, dict, and set comprehensions and generator expressions (only within an async def body or the asynchronous console); using await in a comprehension is similar to asyncio.gather, but gather gives more control over exception handling through its return_exceptions argument, and it is recommended to always set return_exceptions=True (the default is False) so that one failing awaitable does not abort the whole batch.

Python's async/await constructs are not tied to any specific event loop or library (unlike JavaScript), so alternative runtimes such as Curio and Trio can drive native coroutines; a task group (Curio's TaskGroup, Trio's nursery) is an asynchronous context manager implementing structured concurrency — constraining a group of asynchronous tasks to a single entry and exit point (analogous to how structured programming replaced GOTO with block statements) so that on exiting the block all spawned tasks are completed or cancelled and any exceptions are raised — and asyncio is expected to adopt this model (PEP 654 exception groups, approved for Python 3.11).

The generic types for annotating asynchronous objects (Coroutine, Awaitable, AsyncIterable, AsyncIterator, AsyncGenerator, AsyncContextManager — use the collections.abc equivalents on Python 3.9+) are all covariant on their first type parameter (the yielded/output item type), while AsyncGenerator and Coroutine are contravariant on the send-type parameter (the input type of the low-level .send() method the event loop uses to drive them); unlike typing.Generator, AsyncGenerator has no return type, because asynchronous generators do not return values and are entirely separate from native coroutine objects (annotated with typing.Coroutine).

Blocking functions (those doing file or network I/O) must be treated fundamentally differently from nonblocking ones because I/O is orders of magnitude slower than computation: relative to a CPU cycle, an L1 cache read is a few cycles and a RAM read a few hundred, but a disk read is tens of millions of cycles and a network read hundreds of millions — which is why a disciplined asynchronous approach that cedes control to the event loop during I/O waits can yield high-performance servers.

There is no such thing as an I/O-bound system, only I/O-bound functions: any nontrivial asynchronous system has some CPU-bound parts that block the event loop (even a simple echo server's HTTP-header parsing is CPU bound), and dealing with them is the key to success; when you identify a CPU-hogging bottleneck, delegate it to a Python process pool, delegate it to an external task queue, rewrite the hot code in Cython/C/Rust that releases the GIL, or knowingly accept the performance hit and record that decision — and choose the task queue early and add automated performance-regression tests, because waiting until the slowdown hurts usually forces a major rewrite.

Data attributes and methods are collectively called attributes in Python (a method is simply an attribute that is callable), and dynamic attributes present the same obj.attr interface as data attributes but are computed on demand, honoring Bertrand Meyer's Uniform Access Principle that all services of a module should be available through a uniform notation that does not betray whether they are implemented by storage or by computation; implement dynamic attributes with the @property decorator or the __getattr__ special method, where __getattr__ enables virtual attributes that are not declared anywhere or stored in the instance __dict__ but are computed on the fly when code reads an otherwise-nonexistent attribute.

To navigate nested JSON-like data with attribute notation (obj.a.b instead of obj['a']['b']), build a read-only façade class implementing __getattr__ that first tries to delegate the name to the underlying dict's own attributes (so dict methods like .keys() and .items() still work) and otherwise treats the name as a key, recursively wrapping nested mappings and lists in more façade instances; also implement __dir__ returning the data keys to enable dir() and REPL/Jupyter autocompletion.

The __getattr__ special method is invoked by the interpreter only when the usual attribute lookup fails — that is, when the named attribute cannot be found in the instance, its class, or any superclass; a correct __getattr__ should raise AttributeError for genuinely missing names, since returning a different exception (such as KeyError from the backing storage) leaks the implementation and violates the expected protocol.

Any code that generates dynamic attribute names from arbitrary data must handle keys that are not usable as attribute names: a key that is a Python keyword causes a SyntaxError on dotted access (detect it with keyword.iskeyword and, for example, append a trailing underscore so class becomes class_), and a key that is not a valid identifier (detect it with the str.isidentifier() method) cannot be accessed with dot notation at all, so fall back to getattr(obj, key) or implement __getitem__.

In Python __init__ is an initializer, not a constructor: the object already exists when __init__ runs (it receives the existing self) and __init__ cannot return anything; the actual constructor is __new__, a special class method (which does not need the @classmethod decorator) that builds and returns the instance, which Python then passes as self to __init__ — but if __new__ returns an instance of a different class, __init__ is not called; you rarely need to override __new__ because the implementation inherited from object suffices for almost all cases.

A quick way to create an instance whose attributes come from keyword arguments is to write self.__dict__.update(kwargs) in __init__, because an object's attributes are kept in its __dict__ unless __slots__ is declared; the standard library already provides classes that do this — types.SimpleNamespace, argparse.Namespace, and multiprocessing.managers.Namespace — each giving instances an arbitrary set of attributes built from keyword arguments.

Use the @property decorator to compute or dereference a value when an attribute is read — for example an Event.venue property that converts a stored serial number into the linked Record object, analogous to how a Django ORM ForeignKey field returns the linked model object instead of the raw key; and use @staticmethod for a helper such as a fetch method that always acts on a class-level index regardless of the instance or subclass it is called from, because coding it as a classmethod would be misleading when the cls argument is unused.

When a class builds its instance attributes from arbitrary data and a method needs to call an inherited method or class attribute, reference it via self.__class__.method (or the class name) rather than self.method, because a data field of the same name (e.g. a record with a 'fetch' key) would shadow the inherited method through that instance — a subtle, dataset-dependent bug; in general, creating instance attribute names from data always risks shadowing class attributes such as methods or overwriting existing instance attributes (partly why Python dicts are not like JavaScript objects).

To select a class dynamically from data, derive a candidate class name from the record type, look it up with globals().get(name, DefaultClass), and only use it as the factory if inspect.isclass(cls) and issubclass(cls, BaseClass) (otherwise fall back to the base class); this lets you add a subclass named after a record type and have the loader automatically use it without any further changes.

A property whose method name matches a backing field of the same name must read that field through self.__dict__['name'] rather than self.name, otherwise reading self.name re-invokes the property and quickly raises RecursionError; reading or writing data directly to an object's __dict__ bypasses Python's normal attribute-lookup algorithm and is a common metaprogramming trick to avoid such recursion.

Hand-rolled property caches that create a cache attribute after __init__ defeat the PEP 412 key-sharing dictionary optimization (initialize the cache attribute to None inside __init__ to preserve it) and introduce race conditions in multithreaded code (one thread may read a half-built cache); prefer the thread-safe @functools.cached_property (Python 3.8+), but note it is a nonoverriding descriptor that allows writes, runs only on lookup when no same-named attribute exists, cannot decorate a method that depends on an instance attribute of the same name, cannot be used in a class with __slots__, and defeats key-sharing — alternatively stack @property on top of @cache (order matters).

Convert a public data attribute into a getter/setter-protected property to enforce business rules (such as weight and price being greater than zero) without changing client code, since assignment like item.weight = 12 still works: decorate the getter with @property, decorate the setter with @weight.setter, have all the property methods share the public name, store the real value in a private attribute like __weight, and raise ValueError in the setter on invalid input to prevent garbage-in/garbage-out.

The property built-in is actually a class with the signature property(fget=None, fset=None, fdel=None, doc=None), where omitting a function disallows the corresponding operation; properties are always class attributes that manage attribute access in instances, and crucially evaluating obj.attr starts the search at obj.__class__ — if the class has a property (an overriding descriptor) of that name it runs even when the instance __dict__ holds the same key, so a property is not shadowed by an instance attribute; the getter method's docstring serves as the documentation of the whole property.

Repeated near-identical property definitions are a sign of trouble whose cure is abstraction: factor them out with a property factory (a function that returns property(getter, setter) closing over the managed attribute name) or, more flexibly, with a descriptor class — and properties are in fact themselves implemented as descriptor classes.

A property factory is a function that takes a storage name and returns property(getter, setter), where the generic getter and setter are closures that read and write instance.__dict__[storage_name] directly (bypassing the property to avoid infinite recursion); each call builds a distinct property whose unique storage_name is preserved in the closure, eliminating repeated hand-coded getter/setter pairs while taking about the same number of lines as a single hand-coded property.

The del statement deletes attributes as well as variables (del obj.attr); to manage deletion through a property, decorate the deleter method with @property_name.deleter (or pass the fdel argument in the classic property() call), and alternatively attribute deletion can be handled with the lower-level __delattr__ special method — but if a class implements __delattr__, a property's deleter method is never called.

Three special attributes govern attribute handling: __class__ (equal to type(obj); Python looks for special methods such as __getattr__ here, in the object's class, not in the instance), __dict__ (the mapping of an object's writable attributes, absent if __slots__ omits '__dict__'), and __slots__ (a tuple of allowed attribute names that saves memory). Five built-ins read, write, and introspect attributes: dir (an interactive listing of interesting names, customizable via __dir__), getattr(obj, name[, default]) (fetch an attribute by name, raising AttributeError or returning default if missing), hasattr (true unless getattr raises AttributeError), setattr (assign a named attribute), and vars (return the object's __dict__, failing on __slots__-only instances that lack one).

The attribute-access special methods are __getattribute__ (always called on a read; dot notation and getattr/hasattr trigger it, and implementations must use super().__getattribute__ to avoid infinite recursion), __getattr__ (called only after __getattribute__ raises AttributeError, i.e. when normal lookup in the instance, class, and superclasses fails), __setattr__ (always on a write), __delattr__ (on del), and __dir__ (on dir); reading or writing the instance __dict__ directly does NOT trigger these methods (the usual way to bypass them), and Python looks them up on the type rather than the instance so they are not shadowed by instance attributes — and because __getattribute__ and __setattr__ fire on almost every access they are harder to use correctly than __getattr__, so prefer properties or descriptors.

In Python you can start simple by exposing data members as public attributes, because they can always be wrapped later by a property or descriptor without changing client code, so Java-style do-nothing getters and setters are an unnecessary goofy idiom; consider turning a no-argument, value-returning, side-effect-free method (such as a subtotal method) into a read-only property, but never turn a mutating method (such as list.clear) into a property — and remember that abstractions like the Uniform Access Principle trade away easy reasoning about an expression's runtime cost in exchange for accomplishing more with less code.

Because Python has no new operator, calling a function and instantiating a class use the same syntax (my_obj = foo()), so classes and functions are interchangeable in many situations and you can switch one for the other without breaking callers; the __new__ special method lets a class act as a factory that returns objects of different types or returns prebuilt/cached instances, and good reasons to replace a constructor with a factory include limiting the number of instances (as in the Singleton pattern), caching expensive object construction, and returning different types depending on the arguments.

A descriptor is a class that implements the dynamic protocol of the __get__, __set__, and __delete__ methods and is a way to reuse the same attribute-access logic across multiple attributes (for example ORM field types in Django and SQLAlchemy are descriptors mapping data between database fields and object attributes); the property class implements the full descriptor protocol, but partial implementations are fine (most descriptors implement only __get__ and/or __set__), and descriptors are core language infrastructure — even user-defined functions are descriptors, which is how methods operate as bound or unbound depending on how they are called.

You use a descriptor by declaring instances of the descriptor class as class attributes of another (managed) class; the vocabulary is: the descriptor class implements the protocol, the managed class declares descriptor instances as class attributes, a managed instance is one instance of the managed class, a storage attribute on the managed instance holds that instance's value, and a managed attribute is the public attribute handled by the combination of a descriptor instance and a storage attribute.

In a descriptor's __set__(self, instance, value), self is the descriptor instance (a class attribute such as LineItem.weight) and instance is the managed instance, and you must store the value in instance.__dict__[storage_name] rather than on the descriptor itself, because the descriptor is a single shared class attribute (there are thousands of managed instances but only one descriptor per managed attribute, so storing per-instance data on the descriptor would share it among all instances); writing via setattr(instance, storage_name, value) would re-trigger __set__ and cause infinite recursion, which is why the value is written directly into __dict__.

A descriptor's __get__ receives (self, instance, owner) where owner is the managed class; implement __get__ when the managed attribute name differs from the storage name, and note that when the managed attribute is accessed through the class (e.g. LineItem.weight) the instance argument is None — good practice is to return the descriptor instance itself in that case (if instance is None: return self) so introspection and other metaprogramming on the class works.

Because the right-hand side of a class-body assignment is evaluated before the attribute name exists, a descriptor cannot otherwise know the name it is bound to, so requiring the name to be passed explicitly (e.g. Quantity('weight')) is error-prone — a copy-paste mistake like price = Quantity('weight') silently clobbers the other attribute; the __set_name__(self, owner, name) special method (added to the descriptor protocol in Python 3.6 and called by type.__new__ for each descriptor in a class body) solves this by letting the descriptor capture name as its storage_name, removing the need for a constructor argument (and for __get__ when the storage name equals the managed name).

Define descriptors in a separate utility or model module that can be reused across applications (Django and SQLAlchemy ORM model fields are descriptors), and because descriptors are classes you can reuse logic through inheritance — for example a Validated abstract base class whose __set__ self-delegates to an abstract validate(name, value) method (the Template Method pattern, which Alex Martelli calls Self-Delegation) implemented by concrete subclasses such as Quantity and NonBlank; requiring validate to return the validated value gives subclasses an opportunity to clean, convert, or normalize the data (for example stripping surrounding blanks).

Python handles attributes asymmetrically — reading an instance attribute falls back to the class attribute if the instance lacks it, but assigning always creates the attribute on the instance — and this splits descriptors into two categories: a descriptor that implements __set__ is an overriding descriptor (a.k.a. data descriptor), whose __set__ intercepts and overrules assignment to a same-named instance attribute, whereas a descriptor with only __get__ and no __set__ is a nonoverriding descriptor (a.k.a. non-data or shadowable descriptor) that a same-named instance attribute will shadow.

An overriding descriptor (one implementing __set__) intercepts assignment to a same-named instance attribute even when the instance __dict__ already holds that key, so its __set__ stays in control of writes; a property is an overriding descriptor whose default __set__ (when you define no setter) raises AttributeError, which makes a property the easiest way to create a read-only attribute.

An overriding descriptor that implements __set__ but no __get__ controls writes only: reading the attribute through an instance returns the descriptor object itself, and if a same-named instance attribute is created via the instance __dict__, reading then returns that value (the instance attribute shadows the descriptor on read only) while __set__ still intercepts further assignments.

A nonoverriding descriptor (one implementing only __get__, with no __set__) is shadowed by a same-named instance attribute, which makes it ineffective for that instance; and any descriptor, overriding or not, can be overwritten by assigning to the class itself (a monkey-patching technique), because the writing of a class attribute cannot be controlled by a __set__ attached to the same class — controlling that requires attaching a descriptor to the metaclass.

Functions are nonoverriding descriptors because every user-defined function implements __get__: accessing a method through the class returns the plain function, while accessing it through an instance returns a bound method that wraps the function and binds the instance to the first (self) argument (like functools.partial); the bound method exposes __self__ (the instance) and __func__ (the original function), and its __call__ invokes __func__ passing __self__ as the first argument — which is how implicit self binding works — and a plain instance assignment such as obj.the_method = 7 shadows the method on that instance.

Practical descriptor tips: use the property built-in for simple cases (its default __set__/__delete__ make a read-only attribute trivial); a read-only descriptor class must implement both __get__ and a __set__ that raises AttributeError, otherwise a same-named instance attribute shadows it; a validation-only descriptor can implement just __set__, storing the validated value directly in the instance __dict__ so reads are fast and need no __get__; and a caching descriptor can implement just __get__ (a nonoverriding descriptor that sets a same-named instance attribute, which then shadows it so later reads hit the instance __dict__ directly — exactly how @functools.cached_property works).

Class metaprogramming is creating or customizing classes at runtime: because classes are first-class objects a function can build a class without the class keyword, class decorators inspect/change/replace a decorated class, and metaclasses create whole categories of classes — but metaclasses are powerful yet hard to justify and get right, so prefer class decorators or the Python 3.6 PEP 487 hooks (such as __set_name__ and __init_subclass__) that solve many of the same problems more simply, and avoid these techniques in application code (they are framework-building tools); every class also carries data-model attributes such as __bases__ (the tuple of base classes) and __qualname__ (the dotted path from the module global scope to the definition).

cls.__subclasses__() returns a list of the immediate subclasses currently in memory (it uses weak references to avoid circular references, and subclasses in modules not yet imported will not appear), while cls.mro() returns the tuple of superclasses that the interpreter stores in the __mro__ attribute when building the class (a metaclass can override mro() to customize the method resolution order); none of __subclasses__, mro, __bases__, or __qualname__ are listed by the dir() function.

type is both the function that returns an object's class and a class that builds a new class when invoked with three arguments — type(name, bases, dict), functionally equivalent to a class statement, where name is the class identifier, bases is the tuple of superclasses (or (object,) if none are given), and dict maps attribute names to values (callables become methods, other values become class attributes); type is a metaclass — a class whose instances are themselves classes — and is the default metaclass of all user-defined classes.

You can build simple data-record classes at runtime with a class factory function whose last line calls type(cls_name, (object,), cls_attrs) — the simplest possible replacement for @dataclass — and the standard library's collections.namedtuple, typing.NamedTuple, and @dataclass all leverage the same techniques; include __slots__ in the generated namespace if you want a fixed set of attributes, but note that __slots__ mainly saves memory only when you have millions of instances and carries its own drawbacks.

The __init_subclass__ special method (PEP 487, Python 3.6) is called whenever a subclass of the defining class is created, and its first argument is the NEW SUBCLASS, not the class where it is defined — so name that argument subclass rather than cls, since it is not a typical class method and @classmethod is never used with it; use it in a base class to automatically enhance every subclass at definition time (for example reading the subclass's type hints via typing.get_type_hints to install validating descriptors), and call super().__init_subclass__() to cooperate with other classes in the inheritance graph that implement it.

A class builder can validate field values at runtime by treating each field's type hint as a constructor (any callable taking zero or one argument that returns a suitable value or rejects the argument by raising TypeError or ValueError): call constructor(value) inside a descriptor's __set__ to coerce and validate, call constructor() with no argument to get a default (Python's built-in constructors return zero values — int() is 0, float() is 0.0, str() is '', list() is []), and use the Ellipsis object (...) as the sentinel for no-value-given so you can distinguish a missing argument from one explicitly set to None; note static type checkers cannot fully catch such errors because the inherited __init__ must accept arbitrary keyword arguments.

Implement __setattr__ to block setting unknown attributes after construction, but then you must invoke any overriding descriptor's __set__ explicitly, because __setattr__ intercepts every attempt to set an instance attribute including those an overriding descriptor would otherwise handle; and neither __init_subclass__ nor a class decorator can configure __slots__, because __slots__ takes effect only when it is in the namespace passed to type.__new__ and both of those hooks run after the class is already built — so to set __slots__ dynamically you must build the class namespace yourself in a class factory function or a metaclass.

A class decorator is a callable that receives the decorated class as its argument and returns a class to replace it, most often returning the same class after injecting additional methods via attribute assignment; the most common reason to choose a class decorator over the simpler __init_subclass__ is to avoid interfering with other class features such as inheritance and metaclasses (which is why @dataclass is implemented as a class decorator), and you should prefix injected helper functions with an underscore to reduce naming conflicts with the decorated class's own attributes.

At import time the interpreter parses a module's source top to bottom (where a SyntaxError may occur), compiles it to bytecode (skipped if an up-to-date .pyc exists in __pycache__), and executes the module's top-level code; the import statement is not a mere declaration but actually runs all top-level code the first time a module is imported in a process (subsequent imports use a cache and only bind names), which is why the border between import time and runtime is fuzzy — importing can trigger runtime behavior, and an import can also happen deep inside a running function.

When Python executes a class statement the order of operations is: run the class body (the class object does not exist yet) and collect its namespace, then type.__new__ creates the class object, then __set_name__ is called on each descriptor instance (with the new class as owner), then __init_subclass__ is called on the superclass (with the new class as argument), then any class decorator is applied, and finally the class object is bound to its name; both a base class's __init_subclass__ and a class decorator therefore operate on a class already built by type.__new__, so adjusting the arguments passed to type.__new__ itself requires a metaclass.

A metaclass is a class factory written as a class — a class whose instances are themselves classes — and type is the default metaclass of nearly all classes (str.__class__ and a user class's __class__ are type, and type.__class__ is type to avoid infinite regress); every class is an instance of type directly or indirectly, but only metaclasses are also subclasses of type, and inheriting from type is what gives a metaclass (such as abc.ABCMeta, the class of collections.abc.Iterable) the power to construct classes.

To use a metaclass, declare class Klass(Super, metaclass=MetaKlass); Python then calls MetaKlass.__new__(meta_cls, cls_name, bases, cls_dict), where you may inspect and change those arguments — most commonly adding or replacing items in cls_dict, the namespace of the class under construction — before calling super().__new__ (which eventually calls type.__new__), and you may process the new class further before returning it; the metaclass __new__ is the ideal place to configure __slots__, because __slots__ must be present in cls_dict before type.__new__ runs, which __init_subclass__ and class decorators cannot achieve.

A metaclass can generate __slots__ for the new class from the user's declared class attributes (whose values become the instance defaults), which blocks instantiating or later assigning undeclared attributes; copy dunder names through to the new namespace unchanged while refusing to let the user overwrite the methods the metaclass injects (such as __init__ and __repr__), slot the non-dunder names, and follow fail-fast practice by raising on unexpected keyword arguments rather than silently ignoring them — and provide a base class so users never need to reference the metaclass directly.

A metaclass can implement the __prepare__ class method — the earliest hook in class creation, which Python invokes only on metaclasses — to return the mapping that will hold the namespace of the class under construction (entries are added to it as the class body executes, before the metaclass __new__ runs); because Python 3.6+ dicts preserve insertion order, __prepare__'s main historical purpose (returning an OrderedDict so the metaclass could process attributes in source-code order) is now rarely needed.

With a metaclass, the full class-creation order is: __prepare__ returns the namespace mapping, Python adds __module__ and __qualname__ and runs the class body to populate it, then the metaclass __new__ is called, then __set_name__ on each descriptor, then __init_subclass__ on the superclass, then any class decorator, and finally the class is bound to its name; the conventional naming for metaclass methods is to call an instance method's first argument cls (because the instance is a class) and __new__'s first argument meta_cls (because __new__ behaves as a class method even without @classmethod).

A metaclass __new__ can read the type hints of the class under construction from cls_dict['__annotations__'] (you cannot call typing.get_type_hints yet because the class does not exist), build a validating descriptor for each field, overwrite the namespace entries with those descriptors, and populate cls_dict['__slots__'] — which is the only way to add __slots__ during class construction; because a class with __slots__ cannot have a class attribute and an instance attribute of the same name, give each descriptor a distinct per-instance storage_name (such as '_' + name) and implement __get__ to read it.

Metaclasses are powerful but tricky, and modern features replace most of their former uses (class decorators, __set_name__, __init_subclass__, and insertion-ordered dicts); a class can have only ONE metaclass — the metaclass of a derived class must be a non-strict subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases, otherwise you get TypeError: metaclass conflict (for example mixing abc.ABC, whose metaclass is abc.ABCMeta, with an unrelated metaclass) — and metaclasses should be implementation details, so offer users a regular base class to subclass rather than exposing the metaclass, which future-proofs the API and lets you swap the underlying mechanism without breaking it.

Combining __prepare__ (returning a custom dict subclass) with that dict's __missing__ method lets the class body itself gain magic behavior — for example an AutoConst base class can auto-number bare names (banana=0, coconut=1, ...) because the namespace dict fabricates each missing key on the fly — which is a representative wider use case of metaclasses: implementing operators and other special methods at the class level (as Enum does, or as __class_getitem__ does to enable generic type hints like list[int]).

Metaclasses, class decorators, and __init_subclass__ are useful for subclass registration and structural validation, applying decorators to many methods at once, object serialization, object-relational mapping, object-based persistence, implementing special methods at the class level, and emulating features of other languages such as traits and aspect-oriented programming, and can improve performance by doing at import time what would otherwise run repeatedly at runtime — but these tools exist primarily for library and framework development, so applications should use them (from the standard library or external packages) rather than implement them, because doing so in application code is usually premature abstraction (good frameworks are extracted, not invented).

Python is a language for consenting adults: it gets out of the way and lets you do what you must, and deliberately does not give you tools to restrict what others can do with your code and the objects it builds (so access controls like private and protected attributes are matters of convention rather than enforcement).

Python's object model embodies a coherent design ethos of giving programmers powerful, integrated abstractions: properties let you start simple by exposing public attributes (KISS), knowing any one can become a property later without pain; descriptors provide a reusable framework for abstracting away repetitive accessor logic, so effective that core Python constructs use it under the hood; functions as first-class objects combine with descriptors to unify functions and methods (a function's __get__ binds the instance to self to produce a method object on the fly); and classes as first-class objects enable class builders, class decorators, and metaclasses — all integrated in a way that does not complicate Python's suitability for casual programming.

functools.total_ordering is a simple standard-library class decorator that generates the remaining rich-comparison special methods for a class from the few you define (an __eq__ plus one ordering operator), and the third-party autoslot package provides a metaclass that automatically creates a __slots__ attribute by inspecting the bytecode of __init__ to find all assignments to attributes of self.
Python source files are UTF-8-encoded text files conventionally given a .py suffix.
The # character begins a comment that extends to the end of the line.
A #! shebang line as the first line of a script selects the interpreter; on Windows it is used to pick the Python version.
The interpreter executes statements in order until it reaches the end of the input file, then the program terminates.
A variable type annotation such as x: int is only a readability hint: it is ignored at runtime and does not prevent later assigning a value of a different type.
The / division operator produces a floating-point result even for integer operands (7/4 yields 1.75).
The // operator performs floor (truncating) division and works with both integers and floating-point numbers.
For floating-point operands the % operator returns the floating-point remainder x - (x // y) * y.
round() implements banker's rounding (round half to even): a value equidistant between two multiples rounds to the nearest even one, so 0.5 rounds to 0.0 and 1.5 rounds to 2.0.
Python integers never truncate or overflow on bitwise operations; results grow arbitrarily large, so you must size or mask the result yourself.
condition: working with raw bit patterns intended to map to native hardware integers

statement: and and or short-circuit and return one of their operands rather than a strict boolean: x or y returns x if x is true else y, and x and y returns x if x is false else y.
A value is treated as false if it is False, None, numerically zero, or empty; any other value is treated as true.
Python has no increment (++) or decrement (--) operators; use augmented assignment such as += and -= instead.
Block bodies are delimited by indentation, which need only be consistent within a given block.
Four spaces per indentation level is the conventional Python style.
An assignment expression using the walrus operator := must always be enclosed in parentheses.
The break statement aborts only the innermost enclosing loop.
The continue statement skips the rest of the loop body and returns to the top of the loop.
In interactive mode the variable _ holds the result of the last operation and is defined only interactively, so it should not be used in saved programs.
condition: running Python interactively

statement: The pass statement provides an explicit empty body where a statement is syntactically required.
String literals use single, double, or triple quotes; triple-quoted strings capture text across multiple lines whereas single- and double-quoted strings must stay on one logical line.
Immediately adjacent string literals are automatically concatenated into a single string.
An f-prefixed string evaluates any valid expression placed inside its curly braces, optionally with a format specifier.
Strings are sequences of Unicode characters indexed from zero, with negative indices counting from the end, and slicing s[i:j] returns characters whose index k satisfies i <= k < j.
The + operator always concatenates strings; Python never implicitly interprets a string as numeric, so a string must be converted with int() or float() before arithmetic.
str() produces human-readable output (as print does) while repr() produces a representation that could be typed to recreate the value and shows more type information, so prefer repr() when debugging.
open() returns a file object; using it under a with statement automatically closes the file on block exit, so prefer with over a manual close() that is easy to forget.
read() returns the whole file as one string, read(size) reads a bounded chunk, and read() returns an empty string at end of file.
Files are read and written as UTF-8 text by default; pass an encoding argument to open() to use a different text encoding.
input() returns the interactively typed text up to but not including the terminating newline.
Lists are ordered, mutable collections of arbitrary objects indexed from zero; items can be reassigned by index, appended, or inserted at a position.
Slice assignment can replace a portion of a list and may change the list's length.
List comprehensions are the preferred technique for performing simple calculations that build a new list.
A tuple is immutable: its elements cannot be replaced, deleted, or appended after creation, even though it supports indexing, slicing, and concatenation.
A one-element tuple requires a trailing comma and an empty tuple is written as ().
A set is an unordered collection of unique objects that never holds duplicates and cannot be indexed by position.
Set elements are typically restricted to immutable objects, so a list cannot be placed into a set.
Set iteration order is unpredictable and may even change between interpreter runs on the same machine.
An empty set must be created with set(), because {} creates an empty dictionary instead.
set.remove() raises KeyError when the item is absent, whereas set.discard() removes the item without raising if it is missing.
A dictionary maps keys to values; membership is tested with in, and get(key, default) returns the default instead of raising KeyError when the key is missing.
Dictionary keys may be any immutable object including numbers and tuples (allowing composite keys), but mutable structures such as lists, sets, and dictionaries cannot be used as keys.
dict.keys() returns a live keys view that reflects later changes to the dictionary, unlike the one-time snapshot from list(dict).
From Python 3.6 onward dictionaries preserve the insertion order of their keys.
exception: the ordering is not guaranteed in Python versions before 3.6, nor necessarily after many interleaved deletions and insertions

statement: range(i, j[, step]) represents the integers from i up to but not including j, with the start defaulting to 0 and an optional step (which may be negative).
A range object computes its values on demand, so it is memory-efficient even over very large ranges.
A function conventionally includes a documentation string as its first statement, which feeds the help() command and developer tools.
Function parameter and return type annotations are merely informational and are not enforced at runtime, so a function can still be called with mismatched types.
Returning a tuple lets a function return multiple values that the caller can unpack into separate variables.
Omitted arguments take their declared default values, and keyword arguments (whose order does not matter) are recommended when a function has many optional parameters to preserve readability.
Variables assigned inside a function are local and destroyed when the function returns, though a function may read module-global variables defined in the same file.
An uncaught exception terminates the program and prints a traceback showing the error type and its location.
try/except catches an exception; the 'except T as e' form binds the error details to e and transfers control to the handler, while an exception whose type is not matched still crashes the program.
After an exception is handled, execution resumes at the statement following the last except block and never returns to the location where the exception was raised.
Use try-finally for actions that must execute no matter what happens, such as releasing a lock to avoid deadlock.
Prefer the with statement to manage system resources such as files, connections, and locks, since it acquires and releases them automatically even when an exception occurs.
A program terminates when no statements remain or an uncaught SystemExit is raised; raise SystemExit(message) forces an exit, and cleanup actions can be registered with the atexit module.
All values in a Python program are objects, where an object bundles internal data together with methods that operate on that data.
The dir() function lists the methods and attributes available on an object, which is useful for interactive experimentation.
Special methods whose names begin and end with double underscores implement operators and protocols; for example __add__ implements the + operator.
In a method the first argument always refers to the instance itself and is named self by convention, and every access to the object's attributes must go explicitly through self.
Python has no mechanism for hiding or protecting data; a single leading underscore is only a convention marking a name as internal/private and is not actually enforced.
It is good practice to always define __repr__ on a class because it simplifies debugging by controlling how instances are displayed.
Inheritance extends or overrides the behavior of an existing class, and super() invokes the base class's prior definition of a method.

Prefer composition over inheritance when the new type is conceptually a different kind of object rather than a specialization, as with a Calculator that holds an internal Stack instead of subclassing Stack.
The import statement creates a new namespace and executes the associated .py file within it; the module's contents are then accessed using the module name as a prefix.
import X as Y imports a module under an alias, and 'from X import name' brings specific definitions into the current namespace.
When an import fails with ImportError, verify the module file exists and that it resides in one of the directories listed on sys.path.
Guard top-level script code with `if __name__ == '__main__'` so the same file can be both imported as a library and run as a script.
The built-in __name__ variable equals '__main__' when the file is run directly and equals the module's own name when the file is imported.
Use sys.argv for simple command-line argument handling, and the argparse standard library module for more advanced argument parsing.
A package is a hierarchical directory of modules that contains an __init__.py file, which may be empty.

Imports between files within the same package must be fully qualified (from package import module) or package-relative (from . import module); a bare top-level import of a sibling module breaks once the files are moved into a package.
Prefer package-relative imports (from . import ...) so the package name is not hardcoded, making the package easier to rename or relocate later.
Organize large codebases into packages and choose a unique top-level package name so your code's namespaces stay isolated from other code.
Keep tests, examples, and documentation in directories separate from the source package, all gathered under a single top-level project directory.
Do not install third-party packages into the system Python; create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv as an isolated sandbox so you cannot break the system installation.
The small core language plus the built-in lists, sets, and dictionaries can solve a vast range of problems, so prefer the simple solution using existing built-in features when one exists.

Integer literals represent signed integers of arbitrary size and may be written in binary (0b), octal (0o), or hexadecimal (0x); the base is not stored, and bin(), oct(), and hex() convert an integer to a based string.
Floating-point numbers are stored internally as IEEE 754 double-precision (64-bit) values.
A single underscore may be used as a visual separator between digits in a numeric literal and is not stored as part of the number.

Plain assignment is a statement and not an expression, so = cannot be embedded inside an expression; the := assignment expression combines evaluation and assignment, requires surrounding parentheses, and is normally used with if or while.
Standard operators are overloaded for non-numeric types: + concatenates sequences, * replicates a sequence, and % performs string formatting.
Operator dispatch is dynamic, and mixed-type numeric operations generally work along the numeric hierarchy of Booleans, integers, fractions, floats, and complex numbers.
exception: some type combinations are unsupported and raise TypeError, such as adding a Fraction to a Decimal

statement: For a mutable object, augmented assignment such as += mutates the object in place rather than creating a new one, so every other reference to that object also observes the change.

The == operator compares values: sequences are equal when they have the same length, elements, and order; dictionaries when they have the same keys with equal values; and sets when they have the same elements.
An == comparison between incompatible types returns False instead of raising an error, yet numerically equal values of different numeric types compare equal (2 == 2.0 is True).
The is and is not operators test object identity (whether two names refer to the same object in memory), which is distinct from == value equality, so x == y can be True while x is y is False.
Comparing objects with is is almost never what you want; use == for comparisons unless you have a specific reason to test identity.

Ordered comparison operators return Booleans; for sets x < y tests a strict subset, sequences are compared element-by-element lexicographically, and strings and bytes are ordered by character code-point.
Not all types support ordered comparison; applying it to dictionaries or between incompatible types such as a string and a number raises TypeError.
Boolean expressions are evaluated left to right and short-circuit, consuming the right operand only when needed: a and b evaluates b only if a is true, and a or b evaluates b only if a is false.

Relying on implicit truthiness causes hard-to-find bugs because an empty container evaluates as false, so write precise conditional checks and compare explicitly against None when None is the intended sentinel.
The in operator tests membership and returns a Boolean; for strings it also tests substrings, but it never supports wildcards or pattern matching.

Iterable unpacking requires the number of target locations to exactly match the number of produced items; the targets may be any assignable locations, and nested targets must mirror the data's structure.
Extended unpacking with one starred target (such as a, *rest) captures the surplus items as a list, and at most one starred target may appear when unpacking a single iterable.

Star-expansion (splatting) pastes an iterable's items into a list, tuple, or set literal, but splatting a one-time iterable such as a file or generator consumes it so it yields no further values afterward.

any(s) returns True if any item of s is true and all(s) returns True if every item is true; many built-ins (sum, min, max, sorted) accept any iterable, with min, max, and sorted taking an optional key function.
A sequence is a sized iterable whose items are accessed by integer index starting at 0, such as strings, lists, and tuples.

The s * n repetition operator makes shallow copies that replicate element references, so repeating a sequence containing mutable objects makes every copy share the same object; build independent copies with a comprehension such as [list(a) for _ in range(n)].
Indexing a sequence out of range raises IndexError, and negative indices count from the end of the sequence.
Extended slicing s[i:j:stride] selects every stride-th element; the stride may be negative, and omitted bounds default to the start or end of the sequence according to the stride's sign.
Elaborate slices can make code hard to understand later, so use judgment; a slice can be named with slice() for reuse and clarity.

Slice assignment s[i:j]=r can grow or shrink a list, but a strided slice assignment requires the right-hand side to contain exactly as many elements as the slice it replaces, otherwise it raises ValueError.
The slicing semantics described for the built-in list are not universal; third-party types such as numpy arrays may define different rules for slice reassignment, deletion, and object sharing.
Set operators (|, &, -, ^) also apply to a dictionary's keys() and items() views, for example to compute which keys two dictionaries have in common.
A list comprehension builds a new list from an iterable and supports optional filter conditions and multiple nested for/if clauses.
Variables bound inside a comprehension are private to that comprehension and do not overwrite outer variables of the same name.
Changing a comprehension's square brackets to curly braces produces a set comprehension of distinct values, and using key:value pairs produces a dictionary comprehension.
In set and dictionary comprehensions a later entry overwrites an earlier one, so a duplicate key retains only the last value.

A comprehension cannot contain exception handling; wrap a risky operation in a function, and use := to avoid evaluating that function twice when it appears in both the filter condition and the result expression.
A generator expression uses parentheses and computes its values lazily on demand instead of building a list, which can greatly reduce memory use and improve performance on large data.
A generator expression can be iterated only once; a second iteration produces no values.
A generator expression is not a sequence: it cannot be indexed and list methods such as append do not apply, though its items can be materialized with list().
When a generator expression is the sole argument to a function, its surrounding parentheses may be omitted, as in sum(x*x for x in values).
All of a call's argument expressions are fully evaluated from left to right before the function is invoked (applicative-order evaluation).

Operator precedence and associativity are fixed and independent of operand types: all operators except ** evaluate left to right, ** is right-associative, and overloading an operator on a user-defined type cannot change its precedence or evaluation order.

Using bitwise & or | where logical and/or is intended is a common bug because bitwise operators bind tighter than comparison operators, so parenthesize the comparisons; this arises often in numpy and pandas where and/or cannot be overloaded.

Nearly every Python construct, including assignment, expressions, and function, class, and import definitions, is a statement of equal status that can appear almost anywhere (so a function may even be defined inside a conditional), though a few statements such as return are restricted to specific contexts.
The while statement repeats until its expression is false, and the for statement iterates over any object implementing the iterator protocol, not only built-in sequences.
A for loop's iteration variable is not private to the loop: it overwrites any existing variable of the same name and retains its final value after the loop completes.
enumerate(s) yields (index, value) tuples and accepts a start keyword to set the initial count, replacing a manually maintained counter.
zip(s, t, ...) iterates several iterables in parallel producing tuples and stops at the shortest one; its result is a one-pass iterator, so wrap it in list() to materialize the pairs.
break and continue affect only the innermost loop, and since Python has no goto statement, breaking out of deeply nested loops is done by raising and catching an exception.
The continue statement skips to the next loop iteration and is useful for avoiding deeply nested code by reversing a test rather than indenting another level.

A loop's else clause executes only if the loop runs to completion without hitting break (or never iterates at all), so it is skipped on an early break; its primary use is detecting premature exit without a manual flag variable.
When no except clause matches a raised exception, it continues propagating to an enclosing try-except, and if it reaches the top level uncaught the interpreter aborts with an error message.
As a matter of style, only catch exceptions from which your code can actually recover; if recovery is not possible it is better to let the exception propagate.
A bare raise statement re-raises the exception currently being handled, and is only valid inside an except block.
The variable in 'except T as e' is accessible only inside that except block and becomes undefined once control leaves the block.
Multiple except clauses can handle different exception types, and a single clause can catch several types by listing them as a tuple, such as 'except (TypeError, ValueError) as e'.
Silently ignoring an exception with 'except ...: pass' is dangerous and a source of hard-to-find bugs, so it is wise to at least log or report the error somewhere for later inspection.

'except Exception' catches all normal program-related errors but not exit-related ones; when catching broadly, always report accurate exception information including the exception value, or debugging becomes very difficult.
A try statement's else clause must follow the last except clause and runs only when the try block raised no exception.

A finally clause defines cleanup code that always executes regardless of whether an exception occurred; it is not for catching errors, and any exception still pending after finally runs is reraised for an outer handler.
An exception's e.args holds the tuple of arguments passed when raising it (usually a one-item string), while OSError uses a 2- or 3-tuple of an integer error number, message, and optional filename.

Built-in exceptions are organized into an inheritance hierarchy, so it is often better to catch a general base category than to enumerate specific types; for example LookupError catches both IndexError and KeyError without being overly broad.
Exceptions are not recorded in a function's signature and there is no compiler check that they are handled, so the exceptions a piece of code may raise often cannot be determined in advance.

Avoid catching BaseException because it matches every exception including control-flow ones such as SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, and StopIteration; catch Exception instead for normal program errors.

Key base exception categories are ArithmeticError for math errors, LookupError for container lookups, OSError for operating-system and environment errors (with IOError and EnvironmentError as aliases), and ValueError for bad input values (with UnicodeError as a subclass).
SystemExit terminates a program on purpose; given an integer it is used as the exit code, and given a string it is printed to sys.stderr and the program exits with code 1.

KeyboardInterrupt is raised asynchronously on a SIGINT (typically Ctrl-C) and may occur on almost any statement; Python's default is to terminate, and the signal module can be used to control SIGINT delivery.
StopIteration is part of the iteration protocol and is raised to signal the end of iteration.
Define a new exception as a class inheriting from Exception, and the optional values passed to raise become the arguments to the exception class's constructor.

When a custom exception overrides __init__, it must assign a tuple of its constructor arguments to self.args, because that attribute is used to render traceback messages; leaving it undefined hides useful error information.
Organize custom exceptions into a hierarchy so a base class can catch a whole family of errors, and use type(e) inside the handler to identify the specific subclass that was raised.
Writing 'raise NewError(...) from e' chains exceptions, setting the new exception's __cause__ to e and producing a traceback that shows both, reserved for when a failure was anticipated.
Writing 'raise NewError(...) from None' raises the new exception without including the chain of prior exceptions.

An unexpected exception raised while handling another is recorded in __context__ rather than __cause__; __cause__ is set only for an anticipated, explicitly-chained failure, while __context__ is set in both cases.
An exception's stack traceback is stored in its __traceback__ attribute, and the traceback module (for example traceback.format_exception) builds the traceback message for custom reporting.

Do not catch an exception that cannot be handled at that location; unlike languages built on error codes or result types, Python lets an unrecoverable operation fail so the exception propagates to code responsible for handling it.
Make except clauses as narrow as reasonable; catching a broad Exception also catches legitimate programming errors that should not be ignored and makes debugging difficult.

When raising exceptions explicitly, define your own exception types so intentional application errors can be distinguished from genuine programming bugs, which usually surface as Python's built-in exceptions such as TypeError or ValueError.

The with statement runs a block inside a context managed by an object, calling obj.__enter__() on entry and obj.__exit__(type, value, traceback) on exit; __exit__ runs no matter how the block is left, guaranteeing resource release even when an exception occurs.
If a context manager's __exit__ returns True the exception that left the block is treated as handled and suppressed, whereas returning None or False lets the exception propagate.
In 'with obj as var', var receives the value returned by obj.__enter__(), which is commonly obj itself so an object can be constructed and used as a context manager in one step.
The 'assert test[, msg]' statement raises AssertionError with the optional message when test evaluates to false.

Never use assert for logic the program needs to be correct or to validate user input or important operations, because assertions are skipped when Python runs in optimized mode (-O); use assert only for internal invariants whose violation indicates a bug rather than a user error.
Every object has an identity (a number representing its memory location), a type (its class), and a value, and an object's identity never changes after it is created.

An object is mutable if its value can be modified and immutable otherwise; an object that holds references to other objects is a container, and attributes (data or methods) are accessed through the dot operator.
isinstance(value, type) is the preferred way to check a value against a type because it is aware of subtypes and can also check against a tuple of candidate types.

Explicit type checking is often less useful than it appears: excessive checks hurt performance and do not recognize duck-typed objects that share an interface without inheriting from the type (for example collections.deque is not a list subclass).

Python reference-counts all objects: the count rises when an object is bound to a new name or placed in a container and falls on del, reassignment, or scope exit, and the object is collected when its count reaches zero.
For immutable data such as numbers and strings the interpreter aggressively shares a single object across the program to conserve memory, so reference counts are often higher than expected.
Reference cycles among unused objects are not freed by reference counting alone; a periodic cycle detector reclaims them, and gc.collect() can invoke the cyclic collector immediately.

The del statement only removes a name and decrements an object's reference count; explicitly del-ing a large data structure once it is no longer needed can free memory sooner rather than waiting until the variable goes out of scope.
An assignment such as b = a creates a new reference to the same object rather than a copy, so for mutable objects a change made through one name is visible through the other.
A shallow copy (for example list(a)) makes a new container populated with references to the original's items, so mutating a shared nested element is visible through both copies.

A deep copy (copy.deepcopy) recursively copies all contained objects, but its use is discouraged because copying is slow and often unnecessary and it fails on objects holding system or runtime state such as open files, connections, threads, and generators; reserve it for when you must mutate data without affecting the original.
In string formatting the !r conversion produces a value's repr() instead of its normal str() conversion.
