All Python objects are first-class, meaning functions, modules, classes, exception types, and bound methods can all be stored in variables and containers, passed as arguments, and returned from functions like any other data.

Storing functions or classes in a dictionary keyed by a selector value is a common technique to replace a long if-elif-else dispatch, and it is more flexible because new cases are added by inserting dictionary entries rather than editing a large conditional.

None is a singleton representing an optional or missing value: it is returned by functions that do not explicitly return, is commonly used as a sentinel default argument, has no attributes, and evaluates to False.
Because None is a singleton, test for it with the is operator (value is None); testing with == also works but is not recommended and may be flagged by code-checking tools.

Most Python language features are defined by protocols of special (double-underscore) methods that the interpreter dispatches dynamically as a program runs, so an object's behavior depends entirely on which special methods it implements.

Unlike a static-language compiler, Python does not verify correct behavior in advance: a function works for any operands whose types support the required operations (numbers, fractions, decimals, numpy arrays, even strings), and unsupported type combinations fail only at runtime with TypeError.

Creating an instance with SomeClass(args) runs __new__ to create the object and then __init__ to initialize it; __init__ is the common method to define, while defining __new__ signals advanced instance-creation logic such as singletons or caching and can bypass __init__.

__del__ is invoked when an instance is about to be garbage-collected, not necessarily at a del statement (which only decrements the reference count), and it is rarely defined unless an instance must perform extra resource cleanup on destruction.

By convention __repr__ (called by repr()) returns an expression string that could be evaluated to recreate the object, falling back to an angle-bracketed <...> form when no such expression is possible.

For x + y the interpreter normally tries x.__add__(y) first (but tries y.__radd__(x) first when y is a subtype of x); if the first attempt returns NotImplemented it tries the reversed y.__radd__(x), and if that also fails the whole operation fails.
In-place arithmetic methods such as __iadd__ back operators like += and may mutate an object in place for efficiency; if they are left undefined, a += b falls back to a = a + b.

The logical and, or, and not operators cannot be customized through special methods because their short-circuit evaluation, which skips the right operand when unnecessary, cannot be expressed as a normal method call.
Truth-value testing uses __bool__ if defined, falls back to __len__ if not, and otherwise treats the object as True.
The default __eq__ compares objects by identity, so define __eq__ to get value equality; defining __ne__ is usually unnecessary as long as __eq__ is defined.
To sort objects or use min()/max(), at minimum define __lt__; the functools.total_ordering class decorator can generate the remaining comparison methods given __eq__ and one other comparison.

Comparison methods may return any type, not just a Boolean (for example an element-wise matrix result), and should return the built-in NotImplemented object (distinct from the NotImplementedError exception) when a comparison is not possible.

Define __hash__ for instances meant to go into a set or be used as dictionary keys; it must return equal integers for objects that compare equal, and __eq__ must be defined alongside __hash__ since equality resolves hash collisions.

Python never performs implicit type conversion through the conversion special methods: even if an object defines __int__, an expression like 3 + x still raises TypeError, and __int__ runs only through an explicit int(x) call.

The __index__ method supplies the integer an object should yield where an integer is required, such as sequence indexing (items[x] becomes items[x.__index__()]) and base conversions like oct() and hex().
Container behavior is implemented by special methods: len() calls __len__, s[k] calls __getitem__, s[k]=v calls __setitem__, del s[k] calls __delitem__, and the in operator calls __contains__.

Slicing is implemented through __getitem__, __setitem__, and __delitem__ with a slice instance passed as the key, and an extended or multidimensional slice passes a tuple of slice and Ellipsis objects instead.
Multidimensional slicing and the Ellipsis are not used anywhere in Python core or its standard library; those features are reserved for third-party libraries such as numpy.
To support iteration an object provides __iter__() returning an iterator whose __next__() yields the next item or raises StopIteration at the end; the for statement is built on this protocol.

The easiest way to make a class iterable is to implement __iter__ as a generator function using yield, because generators already conform to the iterator protocol and supply the rest of the machinery.

Attribute access first invokes __getattribute__, and only if the attribute is not found does __getattr__ run (whose default is to raise AttributeError); __setattr__ and __delattr__ always handle setting and deleting, and these blunt hooks can be refined with properties and descriptors.
An object can be made callable like a function by defining __call__, so that x(arg1, arg2) invokes x.__call__(arg1, arg2); types, bound methods, and functools.partial all rely on this.

Writing Pythonic code means following Python's established protocols, and three deserve special attention: define __repr__ for observable objects, support iteration so objects work with the for statement, and use context managers for setup/teardown patterns like acquiring and releasing resources.
When a function is called, the number and order of arguments must match the parameters in its definition, or a TypeError is raised; this structure is the function's call signature.
A parameter with a default value and all parameters following it are optional, and a parameter without a default may not appear after one that has a default.

Default parameter values are evaluated once when the function is defined, not on each call, so a mutable default such as [] is shared across calls and accumulates prior changes; use None as the default and create the object inside the function instead.
As a general practice, use only immutable objects (numbers, strings, Booleans, None) as default argument values to avoid shared-mutable-default surprises.
A parameter prefixed with * (the last positional parameter) collects all extra positional arguments into a tuple usable with normal sequence operations.

Keyword arguments are matched by parameter name so their order does not matter, but an unknown name or a missing required argument raises TypeError, positional arguments must come before keyword arguments, and no argument may receive more than one value.
Including a bare * in a parameter list forces every parameter after it to be keyword-only, which often improves call-site readability (for example def read_data(filename, *, debug=False)).

A parameter prefixed with ** collects all keyword arguments that match no other parameter into a dictionary (preserving the order they were supplied), which is useful for open-ended configuration options.

Combining *args and **kwargs lets a function accept any combination of arguments and forward them unchanged, which is the standard pattern for writing wrappers, decorators, and proxies that need not know the wrapped function's signature.
Parameters listed before a / in the signature are positional-only and cannot be passed by keyword (Python 3.8+); this is useful to prevent name clashes when a function also forwards **kwargs.

The naming convention for functions is lowercase words separated by underscores, and a single leading underscore marks a function as an internal helper not meant to be used directly, though these are conventions only.

Type hints have no effect on how a function evaluates (no performance benefit or runtime checking); function hints are stored in __annotations__ for external tools, while hints on local variables are ignored entirely and not even stored.
Adding type hints is not advised unless you actively use code-checking tools that consume them, because incorrect hints go undiscovered without such a tool.

Function parameters are local names bound to the passed objects with no copying, so if a mutable object such as a list or dictionary is passed and modified, the change is reflected in the caller's original object.

Functions that mutate their inputs or change other program state have side effects, which are best avoided because they cause subtle bugs as programs grow and interact poorly with threads and concurrency.
Reassigning a parameter name inside a function does not change the caller's object: assigning a name rebinds it to a different object, which is distinct from mutating the object the name referred to.
By convention a function with side effects returns None (for example list.sort() sorts in place and returns nothing), so a missing return value is a strong indicator of a side effect.

At a call site, * unpacks a sequence into positional arguments and ** unpacks a mapping into keyword arguments; both may be used more than once, and Python rejects any call that fails to satisfy the function's signature.

A return with no value, or an omitted return, returns None; to return multiple values place them in a tuple that the caller can unpack, and a NamedTuple behaves like a tuple while also allowing access by named attributes.

A function that may fail can either return None to signal a missing result (the caller checks, conveniently with :=) or raise an exception (the caller uses try/except); exceptions are the more common choice but are expensive when they occur frequently, so returning a sentinel like None, False, or -1 may be better in performance-critical code.

Each function call creates a local namespace; names assigned anywhere in the body are local, while names used but not assigned (free variables) are resolved in the enclosing module's global namespace.

Referencing an undefined global/free name raises NameError, while reading a local variable before it has been assigned raises UnboundLocalError, often the result of a control-flow bug or a careless in-place operator like n += 1 before n is initialized.

A variable's scope is fixed at function-definition time: assigning a name anywhere in the body makes it local throughout the function, so reading it before that assignment raises UnboundLocalError even when a same-named global exists.
Assigning a name inside a function binds a new local variable and does not modify the module-level global of the same name; to rebind a global you must declare it with the global statement.

Use of the global statement is usually considered poor Python style; when a function must mutate shared state, prefer encapsulating that state in a class and mutating an instance or class variable instead.

Nested functions use lexical scoping fixed at definition time (resolving names from innermost to outermost scope), and an inner function cannot reassign a variable owned by an outer function unless it declares that name nonlocal; nonlocal cannot refer to a global, for which the global statement is still required.

Nested functions and nonlocal declarations are not a common style because inner functions have no outside visibility, complicating testing and debugging, but they are useful for breaking complex calculations into parts and hiding implementation details.

Recursion depth is limited (default 1000, adjustable via sys.getrecursionlimit and sys.setrecursionlimit); exceeding it raises RuntimeError, raising the limit too high can crash the interpreter with a segmentation fault, and the limit mainly becomes an issue with deeply nested recursive data structures such as trees and graphs.
A lambda defines an anonymous function whose body must be a single expression (no statements such as try or while), and it is mainly used for small callback functions like a sorted() key.

A lambda's free variables use late binding: they are evaluated when the lambda runs, not when it is defined, so the value may differ from definition time; bind the value as a default argument to capture it at definition time.

Python functions are higher-order and first-class: they can be passed as arguments, stored in data structures, and returned from functions, and a function supplied to be invoked by another is called a callback function.

A closure is a function together with the environment of variables it needs to execute, so a nested function that is passed or returned remembers its defining environment, which enables lazy or deferred evaluation patterns such as event handlers.

A closure binds to a variable name dynamically rather than capturing a snapshot, so functions created inside a loop all observe the loop variable's final value; capture a per-iteration value by binding it as a default argument.
Wrapping an expression in a zero-argument lambda (a thunk) defers its evaluation until the thunk is later called, a general way to delay evaluation to a later point in time.

functools.partial pre-binds and caches some of a function's arguments to make a nonconforming function match an expected calling signature; with partial the bound arguments are evaluated at definition time, whereas a zero-argument lambda evaluates them when it runs later.
Callables created by functools.partial are fully evaluated and can be serialized (for example with pickle) to be saved or sent to other processes or machines, which is not possible with a lambda.

When a wrapper invokes a callback, distinguish errors raised by the wrapper itself from errors raised by the callback; wrapping callback failures in a dedicated exception (raise CallbackError(...) from err) makes the attribution of blame precise and the wrapper easier to document.

Boxing a callback's outcome into a result object that holds either a value or an exception, unwrapped later via a result() method, defers error reporting to the moment the result is requested; this is the pattern behind Future objects returned by thread and process pools.
A decorator is a function that wraps another function to alter or enhance its behavior; '@decorate' above a definition of func is shorthand for func = decorate(func).

A naive wrapper hides the wrapped function's metadata such as its name, docstring, and type hints, so it is best practice to apply functools.wraps to the wrapper, which copies that metadata from the original function.

Stacked decorators are applied innermost-first, so '@decorator1 @decorator2 def func' is equivalent to func = decorator1(decorator2(func)), and the order can matter, for example @classmethod and @staticmethod usually must be the outermost decorator.

A decorator that takes arguments is a decorator factory: the outer function receives the arguments and returns the actual decorator, which is then applied to the function; calling the factory once and reusing its result avoids repeating the arguments.
A decorator need not replace the original function; it may simply perform an action such as registering the function, for example building a registry of event handlers.
List comprehensions and generator expressions cover most map and filter needs: map(f, s) is equivalent to a generator expression applying f, and filter() yields matching values lazily.
Prefer the built-in reductions sum(), min(), and max() over functools.reduce for common operations because reduce (a left-fold) is often confusing, and the built-ins are clearer and usually faster.

Because functions are objects, they expose introspectable attributes such as __name__, __qualname__, __doc__, __annotations__, __globals__, __closure__, and __code__, which are useful for debugging and logging.

Arbitrary attributes can be attached to a function to store metadata (function tagging); they are not visible inside the function body, and frameworks use this technique, as @abstractmethod does by merely setting __isabstractmethod__ for a metaclass to check.

inspect.signature(func) returns a Signature object describing a function's parameters and annotations; signatures can be compared to check conformance to an expected prototype and overridden by assigning func.__signature__.

globals() returns the dictionary serving as the global namespace, while locals() returns a collected copy of the current local and closure variables; modifying the locals() dictionary has no effect on the actual local variables.

exec(string) runs arbitrary Python code in the caller's namespaces, but changes it makes to local variables have no effect because locals is a collected dictionary rather than the real local variables.

exec() can accept explicit globals and locals dictionaries to run code in custom namespaces, and dynamic code creation with exec underlies standard-library features such as namedtuple() and @dataclass.
Calling an async def function does not run it; it returns a coroutine object that never executes on its own and requires a manager or event loop such as asyncio.run() to actually run.

Apart from needing a managing environment, an async function evaluates like a normal function, and an await expression (valid only inside an async function) is required to call and drive another async function.

An async function cannot be called from a non-async function, so combining async and non-async code requires special-case support; Python provides this for protocols via asynchronous context managers (__aenter__/__aexit__ with async with) and async iterators (__aiter__/__anext__ with async for).
Unless you have deliberately chosen to work in an asynchronous environment such as asyncio, you should ignore async functions.
A function containing yield defines a generator: calling it executes none of its code but returns a generator object that runs the function body only as it is iterated with next() or a for loop.

On each next() call a generator runs up to the next yield, returns that value, and suspends while retaining all its local variables and execution state, resuming at the statement after the yield on the following call.

A generator stops when it returns or reaches the end of the function, raising StopIteration; a non-None return value is attached to StopIteration.value and can only be retrieved by driving the generator manually with next(), not through a for loop.

If a generator needs cleanup when only partially consumed, place the cleanup in a try-finally or a context manager inside it; the finally or with cleanup is guaranteed to run even if the generator is abandoned, executing when the abandoned generator is garbage-collected.
A generator function runs only once; to allow repeated iteration, define a class whose __iter__ method is itself a generator, so each iteration creates a fresh generator.
The yield from statement delegates iteration to a sub-iterable, replacing a manual re-yield loop, and is especially useful for recursively iterating nested iterables such as flattening nested lists.

Generators can restructure deeply nested loops and conditionals into small, composable pipeline stages, each handling a single task and accepting any iterable as input, which improves code reuse, testability, and ease of reasoning.

A deeply recursive generator is still subject to Python's recursion limit; rewriting it to drive iteration with an explicit stack of iterators avoids the limit because data is kept on an internal list rather than on the interpreter call stack.

Using yield as an expression creates an enhanced generator that receives values sent to it with send() rather than producing them, and an initial send(None) is required to advance it to the first yield.
A generator's close() raises GeneratorExit at its current yield, normally terminating it silently though it may be caught for cleanup, and sending further values after close raises StopIteration.
A generator's throw(type[, value[, tb]]) raises the given exception inside the generator at its current yield, which the generator may catch and handle or let propagate to a higher level.

The contextlib @contextmanager decorator turns a generator into a context manager: code before the single yield runs on entry, code after it runs on exit, and an error in the block is reported as an exception raised at the yield.

An enhanced generator can encapsulate a long-lived worker task, and because access to its local variables is much faster than instance attribute lookups, such a generator can run about 40-50% faster than an equivalent class implementation.

In modern Python there is almost no reason to implement an iterator any way other than a generator, and if you define a generator that is not performing iteration you should reconsider the approach since there is likely a better or more modern way (such as async functions).

A class statement defines a blueprint of methods but creates no instances by itself; an instance method receives the instance as its first argument (conventionally self), __init__ initializes a new instance's state, and the optional __repr__ eases debugging.

Calling a class object creates an instance and passes it to __init__; each instance carries its own state (viewable with vars()), while the methods live on the class, and every instance links to its class through its type.

The only three basic operations on an instance are getting, setting, and deleting an attribute, and because attribute access is dynamic, new attributes can be added to an object at any time after it is created.

The getattr, setattr, and delattr functions access an attribute by string name and hasattr tests for its existence; getattr also accepts an optional default value to return when the attribute is missing.
Accessing a method as an attribute yields a bound method that bundles the instance and the underlying function, so calling it automatically passes the instance as the first (self) argument.

A class namespace does not act as a scope for resolving names inside methods, so a method must reference instance attributes and call sibling methods explicitly through self (self.balance, self.deposit()); Python has no implicit class-level scope, unlike the implicit this of C++ or Java.

Implement the relevant special methods (such as __len__, __getitem__, and __iter__) on a custom class so it works with Python operators like indexing and iteration, which is what makes a class Pythonic.

Inheritance creates a derived class that specializes or modifies a base class, inheriting its attributes while able to override existing ones or add new ones; a class with no explicit base implicitly inherits from object, the root class providing defaults such as __str__ and __repr__.

When a derived class overrides __init__, it is the child's responsibility to initialize the parent by calling super().__init__(...) with the required arguments; forgetting this leaves a half-initialized object that breaks.
Avoid hardcoding a class name inside methods such as __repr__; use type(self).__name__ so that the output remains correct for subclasses created through inheritance.
Inheritance establishes an is-a relationship in the type system, so a child instance type-checks as its parent and isinstance(child_instance, Parent) is True.

Organizing objects into type taxonomies through inheritance is often difficult and error-prone (it can be unclear where a new class belongs), and although Python supports multiple inheritance by listing several parents, that further complicates such hierarchies.

Avoid implementation inheritance, such as defining Stack(list) to reuse list code, because the subclass also exposes many irrelevant inherited features (a stack should not offer sorting or insertion), confusing users.

Prefer composition: build the type as its own class that merely contains the other object as a private implementation detail, which gives clarity of purpose and the freedom to change the internal representation later without affecting users.

Injecting the internal container as an optional argument (dependency injection) promotes loose coupling, because the class then depends only on any object implementing the required interface rather than on a hardwired concrete type.

To decide whether to use inheritance, ask whether the object you are building is a specialized version of the parent class (use inheritance) or merely uses it as a component in building something else (do not use inheritance).

If you find yourself writing many single-method classes, use plain functions instead (passing the customizable function as an argument), because that is simpler, just as flexible, and easier to test; premature abstraction is often not a good thing.

Dynamic binding (duck typing) resolves an attribute lookup like obj.name on any object that has that attribute regardless of its type, because variable names have no associated type; this lets you write loosely coupled code that works with any object implementing the required methods, which is why diverse iterables work with for without inheriting a common base class.

Subclassing a built-in type such as dict is dangerous because built-ins are implemented in C and many of their methods (for example dict.update) bypass your overridden Python methods like __setitem__, so the override only appears to work.

Use collections.UserDict, UserList, and UserString to safely subclass dict, list, and str; most of the time, however, subclassing a built-in is best avoided in favor of building a new class by composition.

A class variable defined in the class body (outside __init__) is shared by all instances and should be modified through the class; instance attribute lookup falls back to the class when the name is not found on the instance, the same mechanism by which methods are found.

A @classmethod operates on the class itself (first argument conventionally cls) and is most commonly used to define alternate constructors; because the actual class is passed as cls, the same classmethod called on a subclass correctly creates an instance of that subclass.

The conventional name for a class method that builds an alternate constructor uses a from_ prefix (for example from_timestamp), a convention seen throughout the standard library and third-party packages.
A @staticmethod takes no self or cls argument and is just an ordinary function defined inside a class, used to group related functions or to provide swappable, configurable behavior.

Delegating an object's methods to a swappable policy or strategy class (often a bundle of static methods held in an instance attribute) is a common implementation strategy for state machines and configurable behavior, and it allows the behavior to be changed on an instance at runtime.

Many classic design patterns exist to work around the strict static type systems of C++ or Java and are often unnecessary, overkill, or obsolete in dynamic Python; prefer general principles such as debuggable/testable/extensible code, useful __repr__, composition over inheritance, dependency injection, and Pythonic protocols.

All attributes and methods of a Python class are public; a single leading underscore is only a convention marking a name as internal (treat it like a protected attribute that a subclass may still use), and it is not enforced.

A double-leading-underscore attribute name is automatically mangled to _Classname__name, which prevents a subclass from accidentally overriding a superclass's private name; mangling happens once at class definition with no runtime overhead and does not apply when the attribute name is given as a string to getattr/setattr/hasattr/delattr.

Do not overthink name privacy: single-underscore names are common and double-underscore names less so, and the practical takeaway is simply that a leading underscore signals an internal detail best left alone.

User-defined class attributes have no constraints on type or value (any value can be assigned), and attribute type hints add no runtime checking, only aiding editors and external tools; accurate hinting is difficult, so do not guess unless you are actively running a type checker.

A property intercepts access to a normally-named attribute and routes it through user-defined getter, setter, and deleter methods (defined with @property, @name.setter, and @name.deleter), enabling validation or computation without changing existing code that uses the attribute.

A property must store its underlying value under a different (private) name than the property itself, because accessing the property name inside its getter or setter would otherwise cause infinite recursion.

Properties are commonly used for read-only computed attributes (such as a shape's area), giving a uniform interface where computed values are accessed like plain attributes without a trailing call ().

Methods are themselves implicitly handled as a kind of property: a function placed in a class intercepts attribute access to create a bound method behind the scenes, whereas @staticmethod returns the function as-is without that wrapping.
isinstance(obj, cls) returns True when obj belongs to cls or any class derived from it, and issubclass(A, B) returns True when A is a subclass of B.

A base class can specify a programming interface as methods that raise NotImplementedError, which subclasses then implement; the base class can be used for type hinting or for defensive interface enforcement via isinstance().

An abstract base class (using abc.ABC and @abstractmethod) defines an interface that cannot be instantiated until every abstract method is implemented, so a missing or misnamed required method is caught early at instantiation rather than at a late call site.

Multiple inheritance combines all parents' features but is perilous when parents define conflicting methods or __init__; treat it as a specialized tool for organizing type and interface relations or for mixins, not as a general-purpose way to combine unrelated classes.

A mixin class modifies or extends other classes' behavior by calling super() and only works when combined with a class that supplies the missing functionality; by convention include the word Mixin in its name for clarity.

Inheritance builds a linear Method Resolution Order (available as __mro__) that defines the attribute-lookup search order, with each class checked in turn and the first match winning; object always appears last because all classes inherit from it.

Python uses cooperative multiple inheritance, computing the MRO by the C3 linearization under two rules: a child class is checked before its parents, and multiple parents keep the order written in the inheritance list; a hierarchy with no consistent ordering is rejected with a TypeError.

super() delegates attribute lookup to the next class on the instance's MRO relative to where super() is used, so which method runs depends on the instance's type rather than a fixed named parent class.

When designing for cooperative multiple inheritance, give mixins a common parent that provides default or error-raising implementations, keep every implementation of a mixin method signature-compatible, and always use super() instead of direct superclass calls so the cooperative call chain is not broken.

Replace a large isinstance if-elif dispatch chain with a dictionary keyed by type; to honor inheritance, walk type(obj).__mro__ to find a handler, and using getattr(self, f'handle_{typename}') is a common method-based dispatch pattern.

A class decorator takes a class and returns a possibly-modified class, used for registration, rewriting methods, code generation, or validation as a common alternative to mixins or multiple inheritance; because the modification happens once at definition time, the resulting methods can run faster.

Generating code with exec() (as @dataclass does to build __init__ and __repr__ from type hints) bypasses Python's normal compilation optimizations, so defining a large number of such classes can significantly slow down importing your code.

A base class's __init_subclass__(cls) class method is triggered automatically whenever any subclass is defined (even deep in the hierarchy), enabling implicit registration, method rewriting, or validation across a whole hierarchy without decorating each class; under multiple inheritance call super().__init_subclass__() so all such hooks run.

It is rarely necessary to define __del__; reserve it for extra cleanup such as closing files or network connections, and even then do not rely on it because its timing is not guaranteed. Provide an explicit close() method and support the context-manager protocol instead.

Objects that reference each other form a reference cycle whose counts never reach zero, so their __del__ methods never fire under reference counting; only the periodic cyclic garbage collector reclaims them at an unpredictable time (forceable with gc.collect()).

Because garbage-collection timing is unpredictable, __del__ has restrictions: an exception propagating out of it is printed to sys.stderr and otherwise ignored, and it should avoid acquiring locks or other resources to prevent deadlock, so keep any __del__ simple.

A weak reference (weakref.ref) refers to an object without increasing its reference count, so the object can still be garbage-collected; you retrieve the target by calling the weakref like a function, which returns the object or None, and you must check for None before use.
Weak references are commonly used with caching so that cached objects can be reclaimed once no other references exist, preventing a cache from growing without bound.

Supporting weak references requires a __weakref__ attribute, which user-defined classes have by default but built-in types and classes using __slots__ or named tuples do not, so those need a variant that adds __weakref__.

An instance's state is stored in its __dict__, where setting attributes and editing __dict__ are equivalent unless the attribute is managed by a property or descriptor; the instance links to its class through __class__, and the methods live in the class's own __dict__.

Setting obj.name calls __setattr__, deleting it calls __delattr__, and reading obj.name calls __getattribute__, which checks properties and descriptors, the instance __dict__, and the class dictionaries along the MRO, then falls back to __getattr__ if defined, and otherwise raises AttributeError.

A class that overrides __setattr__, __getattribute__, or __delattr__ should call the super() default implementation to perform the actual work, because the defaults handle advanced features such as properties and descriptors.

A proxy exposes another object's interface without inheriting from it; implementing __getattr__ to forward attribute lookups to an inner object provides proxying or delegation as an alternative to inheritance, redefining some methods while delegating the rest.

Forwarding attribute lookups through __getattr__ does not cover operations mapped to special methods, so operators such as len() and indexing will not work on a delegating wrapper unless you explicitly implement the required special methods like __len__ and __getitem__.

Defining __slots__ with the fixed instance attribute names replaces the per-instance __dict__ with a compact array-based layout, which can substantially reduce memory use and modestly improve speed for programs creating many instances; only instance attributes are listed, not methods or class variables.

__slots__ interacts tricky with the rest of the language: a subclass of a slotted base must also define __slots__ (even empty) or it loses the benefit and uses more memory; __slots__ is incompatible with multiple inheritance from several nonempty-slot bases (TypeError); and it removes the instance __dict__, which can break tools that expect one.

A descriptor is a class-level object that manages access to an attribute by implementing __get__, __set__, or __delete__; properties are built on this lower-level mechanism, and a descriptor can be defined only at the class level (not per instance), with __set_name__ informing it of its attribute name after the class is defined.

A data descriptor that implements __set__ takes precedence over a matching entry in the instance __dict__, whereas a method descriptor that implements only __get__ is weaker and runs only when there is no matching instance-dict entry; method descriptors are how instance, class, and static methods, as well as lazy or cached computed attributes, are implemented.

A class body executes as a script in a fresh namespace that becomes the class __dict__, and any statement is allowed there (conditionals, imports, nested classes); however, the class-body namespace is not a variable scope, so names referenced inside methods must be fully qualified.

Classes can be created without the class statement by populating a namespace, preferably with types.new_class(name, bases, exec_body=callback), which is useful for data-driven class generation; prefer types.new_class over the older type(name, bases, namespace) because type() ignores advanced metaclass machinery.

A class definition is itself an object created by a metaclass (the built-in type by default); a custom metaclass is selected with the metaclass keyword or inherited from the first base class's type, and metaclasses propagate to all subclasses.

Most code does not need a metaclass; prefer __init_subclass__, class decorators, descriptors, or mixins, and reserve a metaclass for low-level control that must occur during class creation, such as setting __slots__ from the __init__ signature or rejecting duplicate name definitions, which decorators and __init_subclass__ cannot do because they run only after the class already exists.

When writing classes, keeping it simple is often the best strategy: a plain class is usually good enough, and readability, observability/debuggability (including use of the REPL), and testability suffer when too many layers of abstraction such as metaclasses, descriptors, decorators, and multiple inheritance are piled on.

Importing a module locates its source (raising ImportError if not found), creates a module object that serves as a namespace, executes the source within that namespace, and binds the module name in the caller; the module file must be on sys.path and is named without the .py suffix in the import.
Importing a module executes all of its top-level statements, so a module that performs a computation or produces output does so as a side effect of being imported.

import module as name renames a module only within the context where the import appears, while other modules can still import it under its original name; this is useful for selecting between platform- or implementation-specific modules behind a common name.

A module's source is loaded and executed only once no matter how many times it is imported; subsequent imports bind to the cached object in sys.modules, and Python never reloads an already-imported module even if its source code has changed.

An import inside a function is cheap because after the first load it is only a cached dictionary lookup; the convention is to list imports at the top of a file, but deferring a rarely-used module's import into the function that needs it can speed up program startup.

The from module import name statement still loads and caches the entire module and then copies the named object into the local namespace, so it is not more efficient than a plain import and does not load only part of a module.

Importing a function with the from form does not change its scoping: the function looks up its global variables in the module where it was defined, not in the namespace into which it was imported and called.

Reassigning a name imported with from module import a rebinds only the local name and does not change the module's variable, so to share mutable global state you must import the module and reference it explicitly as module.a.

from module import * loads all definitions not starting with an underscore (only at module top level) and a module's __all__ list controls exactly what it exports; using import * in a program is discouraged because it pollutes the namespace and causes confusion, so prefer importing explicit names.

Two modules that mutually import each other work through the cache but create an order dependency, because a partially-evaluated module may not yet have defined a name another module needs; circular imports almost always indicate a code-organization problem, best fixed by extracting the shared definition into a separate module.

There is no reliable support for reloading or unloading modules: removing one from sys.modules does not free it because references persist elsewhere, and importlib.reload does not update existing instances, is not recursive, and is not seen by from-imports, so reloading is unsafe in production code.

Modules are compiled to interpreter bytecode cached in a __pycache__ directory as .pyc files and regenerated automatically when the source changes, which speeds up imports; however, exec-based code generation such as dataclasses is not cached, so a module of many dataclasses can import far slower than equivalent hand-written classes.

Imports search the directories and .zip archives listed in sys.path in order, where the first entry is usually the current working directory ('') or the running script's directory; extend the search path by appending to sys.path or by setting the PYTHONPATH environment variable.

The top-level module run as a program or interactively is named __main__, so guarding code with if __name__ == '__main__' lets a library file include optional test or demo code that runs only when executed directly; a directory or zip archive containing a __main__.py can also be run with python3 on that directory or archive.

Importing any part of a package first executes the __init__.py files encountered along the path, so they can perform package initialization; a directory missing __init__.py becomes a namespace package, which is rarely desired, so always create proper __init__.py files when defining a package.

All imports, including those inside a package, require an absolute or fully qualified path; prefer package-relative imports (from . import x or from ..sub import y) so the package name is not hardwired, and note that relative imports work only in the from ... import symbol form and only from within a package.

A package submodule cannot be run directly because its relative imports fail; run it as a script with python -m package.module, which sets up the correct package environment, and python -m package runs that package's __main__.py.

A bare import of a package runs only its top-level __init__.py and makes no submodules accessible; use __init__.py to curate the public top-level namespace by importing selected high-level names from submodules, hiding the internal code organization from users.

Package submodules declare their exports in an __all__ list, and __init__.py files use from .submodule import * to propagate those exports upward, so each exported name is listed in only one place; an import * is acceptable inside a package __init__.py because it is controlled by __all__, even though it is discouraged in ordinary user code.

Do not load package data files with open() and __file__, which can be unreliable or undefined when a package is bundled in a zip or unusual environment; use pkgutil.get_data(__package__, resource) to get the resource as raw bytes, and reserve package resources for configuration and small data rather than giant files.

To distribute pure Python code, place it all in a uniquely named package and write a minimal setup.py calling setuptools.setup with name, version, packages, and scripts; python setup.py sdist then builds an archive that others install with pip.

Get in the habit of starting every program as a package from the onset (a directory with __init__.py and __main__.py, run via python -m program) rather than a single file, so all code stays isolated from name collisions and you avoid the pain that arises when a growing script must later be split.

Avoid advanced hacking of the module and import system; much of the historical pain in managing Python modules, packages, and distribution is a direct consequence of such hacks, so keep the module structure simple.

Python represents I/O data with two fundamental kinds: bytes (an immutable string of integer byte values) and bytearray (its mutable form) for binary data, and str (an array of Unicode code points) for text; indexing a bytes or bytearray yields integer byte values, not single-character strings, which is a common usage error.

Python maintains a strict separation between bytes and text: there is never automatic conversion, comparisons between the two evaluate as False, and any operation mixing them raises an error, so use text strings for text and bytes for binary data.
When working with text, all input must be decoded and all output encoded, using str.encode(encoding) and bytes.decode(encoding) with an explicit encoding name such as 'utf-8' or 'latin-1'.

encode and decode accept an errors policy: the default 'strict' raises UnicodeError, while 'ignore', 'replace', 'backslashreplace', 'xmlcharrefreplace', and 'surrogateescape' offer alternatives; 'surrogateescape' lets malformed bytes survive a decode/encode round trip intact, which is useful for system interfaces where the encoding cannot be guaranteed.

The built-in format(value, spec) function, f-strings, and str.format all share a common format specifier of the form [[fill][align]][sign][0][width][,][.precision][type], controlling fill character, alignment (< > ^), sign, a thousands separator comma, precision, and a type code (defaulting to s for strings, d for integers, f for floats).

f-strings allow arbitrary expressions and nested specifier parts (for example f'{y:{width}.{precision}f}'), ending an expression with = includes its literal text in the output, and the !r and !s conversions format the value's repr() or str() respectively.

bytes and bytearray are formatted with the C-sprintf-style % operator rather than .format or f-strings, and text strings are not accepted there (they must be explicitly encoded first); the logging module uses this %-style lazy formatting.

Command-line arguments arrive in sys.argv as strings with argv[0] holding the program name; for testability write a dedicated main(argv) function that takes the list rather than reading sys.argv directly, raise SystemExit with a usage message on error, and use the argparse module for non-trivial option handling.
Environment variables are accessed and modified as text strings through the os.environ mapping, and modifications to os.environ affect both the running program and any subprocesses created later.

A relative filename given to open() is resolved against the current working directory (os.getcwd(), changeable with os.chdir()), and a filename may be a text string (encoded per sys.getfilesystemencoding()), raw bytes (passed unencoded, useful for degenerate names), an object implementing __fspath__ (the mechanism behind pathlib), or an integer file descriptor.

The core file modes are 'r' (read), 'w' (write, replacing existing content), and 'a' (append, positioned at end); 'x' writes only if the file does not already exist (raising FileExistsError otherwise to prevent accidental overwrite); append 't' or 'b' to select text versus binary, and add '+' for in-place update.

Files are I/O-buffered by default to batch operations into larger chunks; buffering=0 disables buffering (binary mode only) and buffering=1 is line buffering. Buffering can cause two communicating processes to deadlock when data sits unflushed, which is fixed with unbuffered I/O or an explicit flush() call.

For text-mode files, pass encoding and errors arguments (with the same meanings as str.encode and bytes.decode); because the default encoding varies by system, it is better to specify the encoding explicitly even when it matches the system default.

By default text files use universal newline mode, translating '
', '
', or '' to a standard '
' on reading and back to the operating system's default ending on writing; the newline argument to open() overrides this behavior.

read() and readline() signal end-of-file by returning an empty string, readline() includes the terminating newline, write() and writelines() add no newlines (so output must already include needed formatting), and iterating a file with a for loop reads it line by line.

sys.stdin, sys.stdout, and sys.stderr are file-like objects (print writes to stdout, error messages go to stderr) that can be reassigned to redirect I/O, with their originals preserved in sys.__stdin__, sys.__stdout__, and sys.__stderr__; input() reads a line from stdin without the trailing newline, unlike reading sys.stdin directly.

List a directory with os.listdir(path), where passing a bytes path returns undecoded byte filenames; match filenames by pattern (globbing) with pathlib Path.glob() or, recursively, rglob(), both of which return generators.
The print() function accepts keyword arguments end to change the line ending, sep to change the separator between items, and file to redirect output to a given file object.

A generator can emit an output stream as a sequence of fragments using yield in place of write() or print(), which decouples output production from its destination (file, socket, or joined string) and can substantially reduce memory use by processing the stream in small fragments.

An enhanced generator driven by send() can decode a protocol from input fragments while containing no I/O operations itself, which externalizes the actual reading so the same parser can be reused unchanged across files, sockets, and asynchronous channels.

The pickle module serializes Python objects to bytes (dump/load with files, dumps/loads with byte strings) in a Python-specific format; objects carrying runtime state such as open files, threads, closures, and generators cannot be pickled unless the class defines __getstate__ and __setstate__.

pickle encodes only a name reference to an object's class rather than its source code, so unpickling requires the matching class source to be installed; moreover pickle is inherently insecure because unpickling untrusted data is a known remote-code-execution vector, so use it only when the runtime environment is fully secured.

I/O is fundamentally blocking: an operation such as sock.recv() returns immediately if data is ready but otherwise stops and waits while nothing else in the program runs, so doing other work during a blocked operation requires a concurrency approach.

Nonblocking I/O (enabled with sock.setblocking(False)) raises BlockingIOError instead of waiting when an operation would block, but relying on it alone is clumsy and inefficient because it forces a busy-spin loop that constantly retries.

I/O polling with the select or selectors module lets a single loop wait on many I/O channels and dispatch a callback when one is ready, blocking efficiently instead of busy-spinning; this is the foundation of async frameworks such as asyncio.
The threading module runs independent tasks concurrently under operating-system management, and a blocking operation in one thread does not block the execution of other threads.

The asyncio module provides concurrency through an event loop built on I/O polling, with a high-level programming model resembling threads but expressed with async functions; when a library advertises asynchronous support it usually means concurrency via asyncio or a similar module.

Read and write CSV files by opening the file with newline='' and wrapping it with csv.reader/csv.writer (or csv.DictReader to get header-keyed dictionaries); the csv module correctly handles quoting and special-character edge cases, while data analysis is better done with a library such as pandas.

System-level errors are reported as OSError or one of its subclasses such as PermissionError or FileNotFoundError, and every OSError carries a numeric errno attribute (with symbolic constants in the errno module, like ENOSPC) that specialized handlers can inspect.

The io module's StringIO and BytesIO classes provide a file-like interface over in-memory strings or bytes, which is useful for testing code that expects a file object or for capturing output without a real file.

The logging module is the de facto standard for program diagnostics and print-style debugging: create a per-module logger with logging.getLogger(__name__), emit messages at the five increasing-severity levels (debug, info, warning, error, critical), and configure logging once at program startup, where the chosen level filters out less-severe messages.

The pathlib module is the modern, portable, object-oriented way to manipulate pathnames (centered on the Path class) and largely replaces the legacy os.path module, though os.path remains widespread; both handle the difference between UNIX and Windows path separators.
The shutil module performs common file and directory operations (copy, move, copytree, rmtree) and is a safer and more portable alternative to executing shell commands directly with os.system().

The struct module packs and unpacks data between Python values and binary byte structures using format codes, for interacting with C code, binary file formats, and network protocols; packing a Python float into a 32-bit field loses precision because Python represents floats as 64-bit doubles.

Running python -m http.server starts a standalone static-file web server for the current directory, which is useful for local testing and debugging of web-related programs but not for running a real website.

The subprocess module runs an external program with control over its environment: check_output(args) runs a command and returns all its output as bytes (decode it for text; it raises CalledProcessError on failure), while the Popen class with stdin/stdout PIPEs allows interactive communication with the subprocess.
The tempfile module's TemporaryFile and TemporaryDirectory, typically used with a with statement, create temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted at the end of the block.

A thread is launched with start() and waited on with join(); mark it daemon=True if you will never join it, and because there is no forced kill, stopping a thread requires signaling it through a flag or variable that the thread is programmed to check.

When threads share mutable data, protect it with a threading.Lock (used as a context manager); use an Event when one thread must wait for another to do something, and a Queue when threads need to communicate.

The time module provides sleep(seconds), time() (seconds since the epoch as a UTC float), localtime() and gmtime() (returning a struct_time), and ctime()/asctime() for printable strings; the datetime module is preferred for date computations and timezone handling.

urllib.request.urlopen fetches basic HTTP and HTTPS pages and APIs, and urllib.parse handles URL encoding and parsing, but for requests involving cookies, advanced authentication, or other layers most programmers should use a third-party library such as requests or httpx.

The same visually-rendered Unicode text can have different code-point representations (fully composed versus decomposed combining characters), which can make equal-looking strings unequal and produce surprises such as two seemingly-identical dictionary keys; normalize with unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s) or 'NFD' for consistent comparison.

Keep textual and binary data strictly separated and concentrate encoding and decoding at the application's edges, the boundary between the program and the outside world, because that is where most I/O complexity around encodings and Unicode arises.

Avoid asynchronous coding unless you are certain you need it (and if unsure, you almost certainly do not), because synchronous code is far easier to reason about, debug, and test, and adopting async usually forces the rest of the application into the async style as well.

Floating-point error handling is tricky: FloatingPointError is only raised if Python was specially configured and built to enable it, and far more commonly a failed floating-point operation silently produces a result such as float('nan') or float('inf').

A frozenset is an immutable set whose values must also be immutable; because it is hashable it can be used as a dictionary key or placed inside another set (where ordinary mutable sets cannot), supporting all set operations except those that mutate in place.

The collections module supplements the built-in containers with data-handling types worth reaching for: deque (a double-ended queue), defaultdict (a dictionary that auto-initializes missing items), and Counter (for tabulation).
The itertools module provides reusable iteration patterns such as chaining iterables, Cartesian products, permutations, and grouping, which are worth preferring over hand-rolled equivalents.
The unittest module provides built-in support for writing unit tests (Python itself is tested with it), but many programmers prefer the third-party pytest library for testing.

Given a choice, prefer Python's built-in functions, datatypes, and standard-library modules over adding a third-party package dependency, because a wide range of common programming problems can be solved with nothing beyond what Python already provides.
